which has its three sides equal." -/
def Equilateral (A B C : Point) : Prop :=
  Triangle A B C ∧ ‖A B‖ = ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C A‖

state.lean_proof:
/-- On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle. -/
theorem Prop1 (A B : Point) (hAB : A ≠ B) (P : Point) :
    ∃ C : Point, Equilateral A B C ∧ (¬ Collinear A B P → SameSideOf C P A B) := by
  -- Let AB be the given finite straight line.
  -- Thus it is required to construct an equilateral triangle on the straight line AB.
  -- With centre A and distance AB let the circle BCD be described; [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨BCD, hA_BCD, hB_BCD⟩ := Postulate3 A B hAB
  -- again, with centre B and distance BA let the circle ACE be described; [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨ACE, hB_ACE, hA_ACE⟩ := Postulate3 B A hAB.symm
  -- and from the point C, in which the circles cut one another, to the points A, B let the
  -- straight lines CA, CB be joined. [Post. 1]
  /- Euclid never says why the circles cut one another. Each passes through the
     other's centre, and a centre lies inside its circle, so they must cross
     (System E, Intersection 5). They cross on both sides of AB, so C may
     be taken on whichever side we please: on P's side, when P is off AB
     (System E, Intersections 8). Our proof uses only the point C; the
     straight lines CA, CB are drawn for the eye. -/
  have hmeet := circles_meet hB_BCD (centre_inside hA_BCD) (centre_inside hB_ACE) hA_ACE
  obtain ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, hside⟩ : ∃ C : Point, OnCircle C BCD ∧ OnCircle C ACE ∧
      (¬ Collinear A B P → SameSideOf C P A B) := by
    by_cases hP : Collinear A B P
    · obtain ⟨C, -, -, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, -⟩ := hmeet
      exact ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, fun h => absurd hP h⟩
    · obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
      obtain ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, hCP⟩ :=
        circles_meet_same_side hmeet hA_BCD hB_ACE hA_AB hB_AB (Triangle.off_line hP hA_AB hB_AB)
      exact ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, fun _ => SameSideOf.of_line hAB hA_AB hB_AB hCP⟩
  -- Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle CDB,
  -- AC is equal to AB. [Def. 15]
  have hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ := Definition15 hA_BCD hC_BCD hB_BCD
  -- Again, since the point B is the centre of the circle CAE,
  -- BC is equal to BA. [Def. 15]
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖B A‖ := Definition15 hB_ACE hC_ACE hA_ACE
  -- But CA was also proved equal to AB;
  have hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm C A).trans hAC
  -- therefore each of the straight lines CA, CB is equal to AB.
  have hCB : ‖C B‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm C B).trans (hBC.trans (len_symm B A))
  -- And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]
  -- therefore CA is also equal to CB.
  have hCA_CB : ‖C A‖ = ‖C B‖ := CommonNotion1 hCA hCB
  -- Therefore the three straight lines CA, AB, BC are equal to one another.
  have hAB_BC : ‖A B‖ = ‖B C‖ := (hBC.trans (len_symm B A)).symm
  have hBC_CA : ‖B C‖ = ‖C A‖ := (len_symm B C).trans (hCA_CB.symm)
  -- Therefore the triangle ABC is equilateral; and it has been constructed on the given finite
  -- straight line AB.
  exact ⟨C, ⟨Prop1.figure hAB hCA hCB, hAB_BC, hBC_CA⟩, hside⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to do.

Judge this unit's uses of the supplied helper signatures; helper bodies are outside this question. Heath's sentences stand as `--` lines and `cited` gives exact enunciations. state.commentary:
**Must the circles meet?** Euclid's very first step takes for granted something none of his postulates says: that the two circles cut one another. "It is a commonplace that Euclid has no right to assume, without premising some postulate, that the two circles *will* meet in a point C" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 242). We supply it as a named rule, [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean), from System E, a modern list of the facts Euclid reads off his figures (its Intersection 5): if each circle passes through a point inside the other, they cross. Here each passes through the other's centre.

**Could AC and BC run together?** Heath recalls Zeno's remark "that the problem is not solved unless it is taken for granted that two straight lines cannot have a common segment" (vol. 1, p. 242): AC and BC might meet short of C and run on together, and the triangle would not be equilateral. Heath's answer is Postulate 2. Our proof never meets the worry, since it uses only the point C, not the straight lines CA, CB that Euclid joins. Zeno's other doubt, that the two circumferences might have a common part, waits for III.10; meanwhile "it is enough for the purpose of this proposition if *one* equilateral triangle can be found with the given base" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 243).

**Is ABC a triangle, and on which side?** Euclid never says that C is off the straight line AB, though only that makes ABC a triangle. Lean wants it said, so `Prop1.figure` proves it: were C on AB, one of the three points would lie between the other two, and some length would equal itself taken twice, which Common Notion 5, the whole greater than the part, forbids. The circles cross on both sides of AB, and I.9 and I.11 need a particular side, so our I.1 lets the side be named. That means naming the straight line AB, by Postulate 1, and calling on the rule that the circles cross on each side of it (System E, Intersections 8).

**The modern way.** Put $\mathrm{A} = 0$ and $\mathrm{B} = 1$ in the complex plane, and $\mathrm{C} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i = e^{i\pi/3}$, the point reached by turning AB through $\pi/3$. Everything turns on that $\sqrt{3}$. In the plane of points with rational coordinates all five of Euclid's postulates hold, yet the two circles of I.1 slip past each other without meeting, as Robin Hartshorne's *Geometry: Euclid and Beyond* explains beautifully. So the tacit rule is doing real work: it says the plane has the square roots that ruler and compass need.

     straight lines CA, CB are drawn for the eye. -/
  have hmeet := circles_meet hB_BCD (centre_inside hA_BCD) (centre_inside hB_ACE) hA_ACE
  obtain ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, hside⟩ : ∃ C : Point, OnCircle C BCD ∧ OnCircle C ACE ∧
      (¬ Collinear A B P → SameSideOf C P A B) := by
    by_cases hP : Collinear A B P
    · obtain ⟨C, -, -, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, -⟩ := hmeet
      exact ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, fun h => absurd hP h⟩
    · obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
      obtain ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, hCP⟩ :=
        circles_meet_same_side hmeet hA_BCD hB_ACE hA_AB hB_AB (Triangle.off_line hP hA_AB hB_AB)
      exact ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, fun _ => SameSideOf.of_line hAB hA_AB hB_AB hCP⟩
  -- Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle CDB,
  -- AC is equal to AB. [Def. 15]
  have hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ := Definition15 hA_BCD hC_BCD hB_BCD
  -- Again, since the point B is the centre of the circle CAE,
  -- BC is equal to BA. [Def. 15]
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖B A‖ := Definition15 hB_ACE hC_ACE hA_ACE
  -- But CA was also proved equal to AB;
  have hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm C A).trans hAC
  -- therefore each of the straight lines CA, CB is equal to AB.
  have hCB : ‖C B‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm C B).trans (hBC.trans (len_symm B A))
  -- And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]
  -- therefore CA is also equal to CB.
  have hCA_CB : ‖C A‖ = ‖C B‖ := CommonNotion1 hCA hCB
  -- Therefore the three straight lines CA, AB, BC are equal to one another.
  have hAB_BC : ‖A B‖ = ‖B C‖ := (hBC.trans (len_symm B A)).symm
  have hBC_CA : ‖B C‖ = ‖C A‖ := (len_symm B C).trans (hCA_CB.symm)
  -- Therefore the triangle ABC is equilateral; and it has been constructed on the given finite
  -- straight line AB.
  exact ⟨C, ⟨Prop1.figure hAB hCA hCB, hAB_BC, hBC_CA⟩, hside⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to do.

state.heath_proof:
Let A be the given point, and BC the given straight line.

Thus it is required to place at the point A (as an extremity) a straight line equal to the given straight line BC.

From the point A to the point B let the straight line AB be joined; [Post. 1]

and on it let the equilateral triangle DAB be constructed. [I. 1]

Let the straight lines AE, BF be produced in a straight line with DA, DB; [Post. 2]

with centre B and distance BC let the circle CGH be described; [Post. 3]

and again, with centre D and distance DG let the circle GKL be described. [Post. 3]

Then, since the point B is the centre of the circle CGH,

BC is equal to BG.

Again, since the point D is the centre of the circle GKL,

DL is equal to DG.

And in these DA is equal to DB;

therefore the remainder AL is equal to the remainder BG. [C.N. 3]

But BC was also proved equal to BG;

therefore each of the straight lines AL, BC is equal to BG.

And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]

state.lean_proof:
/-- To place at a given point (as an extremity) a straight line equal to a given straight
line. -/
theorem Prop2 (A B C : Point) (hBC : B ≠ C) :
    ∃ L : Point, ‖A L‖ = ‖B C‖ := by
  /- If the given point A is B itself, BC already does the job. Euclid's figure
     has A apart from B, and that is the case his proof treats. -/
  by_cases hAB' : A = B
  · exact ⟨C, by rw [hAB']⟩
  have hAB : A ≠ B := hAB'
  -- Let A be the given point, and BC the given straight line.
  -- Thus it is required to place at the point A (as an extremity) a straight line equal to
  -- the given straight line BC.
  -- From the point A to the point B let the straight line AB be joined; [Post. 1]
  -- and on it let the equilateral triangle DAB be constructed. [I. 1]
  /- Either side of AB will do, so no side is named: the point given for a side
     is A itself, which is on AB. -/
  obtain ⟨D, ⟨hABD, -, hBD_DA⟩, -⟩ := Prop1 A B hAB A
  have hDA_DB : ‖D A‖ = ‖D B‖ := hBD_DA.symm.trans (len_symm B D)
  have hDB : D ≠ B := hABD.ne₂₃.symm
  have hDA : D ≠ A := hABD.ne₁₃.symm
  -- Let the straight lines AE, BF be produced in a straight line with DA, DB; [Post. 2]
  obtain ⟨DF, hD_DF, hB_DF⟩ := Postulate1 D B hDB
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hA_DE⟩ := Postulate1 D A hDA
  -- with centre B and distance BC let the circle CGH be described; [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨CGH, hB_CGH, hC_CGH⟩ := Postulate3 B C hBC
  /- Euclid's point G is where DB, produced beyond B, meets the circle CGH
     (System E, Intersections 5): B is the centre, so it lies inside. -/
  obtain ⟨G, hG_CGH, -, hGBD⟩ :=
    line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hB_CGH) hB_DF hD_DF hDB
  have hDBG : Between D B G := between_symm hGBD
  have hDG : D ≠ G := ne_of_between_ends hDBG
  -- and again, with centre D and distance DG let the circle GKL be described. [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨GKL, hD_GKL, hG_GKL⟩ := Postulate3 D G hDG
  /- And L is where DA, produced beyond A, meets the circle GKL. That needs A
     inside GKL, which holds because DA is equal to DB, and DB is only a part
     of DG. -/
  have hDB_BG : ‖D B‖ + ‖B G‖ = ‖D G‖ := len_add_of_between hDBG
  have hA_GKL : InsideCircle A GKL := by
    apply inside_of_len_lt hD_GKL hG_GKL
    rw [hDA_DB, ← hDB_BG]
    exact CommonNotion5 (len_pos (ne_of_between hGBD).symm)
  obtain ⟨L, hL_GKL, -, hLAD⟩ := line_circle_beyond hA_GKL hA_DE hD_DE hDA
  -- Then, since the point B is the centre of the circle CGH,
  -- BC is equal to BG.
  have hBC_BG : ‖B C‖ = ‖B G‖ := Definition15 hB_CGH hC_CGH hG_CGH
  -- Again, since the point D is the centre of the circle GKL,
  -- DL is equal to DG.
  have hDL_DG : ‖D L‖ = ‖D G‖ := Definition15 hD_GKL hL_GKL hG_GKL
  -- And in these DA is equal to DB;
  have hDA_AL : ‖D A‖ + ‖A L‖ = ‖D L‖ := len_add_of_between (between_symm hLAD)
  -- therefore the remainder AL is equal to the remainder BG. [C.N. 3]
  have hAL_BG : ‖A L‖ = ‖B G‖ := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ‖D A‖) (d := ‖D B‖) _ hDA_DB
    rw [add_comm, hDA_AL, hDL_DG, ← hDB_BG, add_comm]
  -- But BC was also proved equal to BG;
  -- therefore each of the straight lines AL, BC is equal to BG.
  -- And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]
  -- therefore AL is also equal to BC.
  have hAL_BC : ‖A L‖ = ‖B C‖ := CommonNotion1 hAL_BG hBC_BG
  -- Therefore at the given point A the straight line AL is placed equal to the given straight
  -- line BC.
  exact ⟨L, hAL_BC⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to do.

state.commentary:
Why not simply draw a circle about A with radius BC? Postulate 3 does not allow it: it draws a circle with a given centre through a given point, and nothing more, and Proclus calls the short cut a *petitio principii*, a begging of the question (Heath, vol. 1, p. 246). Augustus De Morgan, quoted by Heath, asks us to "suppose the compasses to close of themselves the moment they cease to touch the paper. These two propositions [I. 2, 3] extend the power of construction to what it would have been if *all* the usual power of the compasses had been assumed" (vol. 1, p. 246). I.2 does its share with an equilateral triangle and two circles.

Proclus sorts the proposition into cases by where A lies. Heath answers that "Euclid's method is to give one case only, for choice the most difficult, leaving the reader to supply the rest for himself" (vol. 1, p. 246). Our proof covers every position at once, because the rules that find G and L say only that DB and DA, produced, cut their circles, wherever they lie. Nor does it produce them, as Euclid does by Postulate 2: our straight lines DA and DB are whole already, and G and L come straight from the rule that a straight line through the inside of a circle meets it (System E, Intersections 5). For L that rule wants A inside the circle GKL, which holds because DA is equal to DB, and DB is only part of DG: the whole is greater than the part, Common Notion 5, used here without a word from Euclid. One case must still be set apart, A at B itself, with no straight line AB to build on. There, as Heath says of Proclus' point at an end, "we are given what we are required to find" (vol. 1, p. 245).

**The modern way.** Sliding BC over to A, parallel to itself, gives the point $\mathrm{A} + \overrightarrow{\mathrm{BC}}$, as far from A as C is from B; but that the copy keeps the length of BC is, in Euclid's terms, I.34, whose proof uses Postulate 5. Euclid's L uses no parallels. It lies on DA produced, at $\mathrm{L} = \mathrm{A} + \mathrm{BC} \thinspace \mathbf{u}$, where $\mathbf{u}$ is the unit vector from D towards A.
state.heath_proof:
Let A be the given point, and BC the given straight line.

Thus it is required to place at the point A (as an extremity) a straight line equal to the given straight line BC.

From the point A to the point B let the straight line AB be joined; [Post. 1]

and on it let the equilateral triangle DAB be constructed. [I. 1]

Let the straight lines AE, BF be produced in a straight line with DA, DB; [Post. 2]

with centre B and distance BC let the circle CGH be described; [Post. 3]

and again, with centre D and distance DG let the circle GKL be described. [Post. 3]

Then, since the point B is the centre of the circle CGH,

BC is equal to BG.

Again, since the point D is the centre of the circle GKL,

DL is equal to DG.

And in these DA is equal to DB;

therefore the remainder AL is equal to the remainder BG. [C.N. 3]

But BC was also proved equal to BG;

therefore each of the straight lines AL, BC is equal to BG.

And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]

therefore AL is also equal to BC.

Therefore at the given point A the straight line AL is placed equal to the given straight line BC.

(Being) what it was required to do.
state.lean_proof:
/-- To place at a given point (as an extremity) a straight line equal to a given straight
line. -/
theorem Prop2 (A B C : Point) (hBC : B ≠ C) :
    ∃ L : Point, ‖A L‖ = ‖B C‖ := by
  /- If the given point A is B itself, BC already does the job. Euclid's figure
     has A apart from B, and that is the case his proof treats. -/
  by_cases hAB' : A = B
  · exact ⟨C, by rw [hAB']⟩
  have hAB : A ≠ B := hAB'
  -- Let A be the given point, and BC the given straight line.
  -- Thus it is required to place at the point A (as an extremity) a straight line equal to
  -- the given straight line BC.
  -- From the point A to the point B let the straight line AB be joined; [Post. 1]
  -- and on it let the equilateral triangle DAB be constructed. [I. 1]
  /- Either side of AB will do, so no side is named: the point given for a side
     is A itself, which is on AB. -/
  obtain ⟨D, ⟨hABD, -, hBD_DA⟩, -⟩ := Prop1 A B hAB A
  have hDA_DB : ‖D A‖ = ‖D B‖ := hBD_DA.symm.trans (len_symm B D)
  have hDB : D ≠ B := hABD.ne₂₃.symm
  have hDA : D ≠ A := hABD.ne₁₃.symm
  -- Let the straight lines AE, BF be produced in a straight line with DA, DB; [Post. 2]
  obtain ⟨DF, hD_DF, hB_DF⟩ := Postulate1 D B hDB
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hA_DE⟩ := Postulate1 D A hDA
  -- with centre B and distance BC let the circle CGH be described; [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨CGH, hB_CGH, hC_CGH⟩ := Postulate3 B C hBC
  /- Euclid's point G is where DB, produced beyond B, meets the circle CGH
     (System E, Intersections 5): B is the centre, so it lies inside. -/
  obtain ⟨G, hG_CGH, -, hGBD⟩ :=
    line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hB_CGH) hB_DF hD_DF hDB
  have hDBG : Between D B G := between_symm hGBD
  have hDG : D ≠ G := ne_of_between_ends hDBG
  -- and again, with centre D and distance DG let the circle GKL be described. [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨GKL, hD_GKL, hG_GKL⟩ := Postulate3 D G hDG
  /- And L is where DA, produced beyond A, meets the circle GKL. That needs A
     inside GKL, which holds because DA is equal to DB, and DB is only a part
     of DG. -/
  have hDB_BG : ‖D B‖ + ‖B G‖ = ‖D G‖ := len_add_of_between hDBG
  have hA_GKL : InsideCircle A GKL := by
    apply inside_of_len_lt hD_GKL hG_GKL
    rw [hDA_DB, ← hDB_BG]
    exact CommonNotion5 (len_pos (ne_of_between hGBD).symm)
  obtain ⟨L, hL_GKL, -, hLAD⟩ := line_circle_beyond hA_GKL hA_DE hD_DE hDA
  -- Then, since the point B is the centre of the circle CGH,
  -- BC is equal to BG.
  have hBC_BG : ‖B C‖ = ‖B G‖ := Definition15 hB_CGH hC_CGH hG_CGH
  -- Again, since the point D is the centre of the circle GKL,
  -- DL is equal to DG.
  have hDL_DG : ‖D L‖ = ‖D G‖ := Definition15 hD_GKL hL_GKL hG_GKL
  -- And in these DA is equal to DB;
  have hDA_AL : ‖D A‖ + ‖A L‖ = ‖D L‖ := len_add_of_between (between_symm hLAD)
  -- therefore the remainder AL is equal to the remainder BG. [C.N. 3]
  have hAL_BG : ‖A L‖ = ‖B G‖ := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ‖D A‖) (d := ‖D B‖) _ hDA_DB
    rw [add_comm, hDA_AL, hDL_DG, ← hDB_BG, add_comm]
  -- But BC was also proved equal to BG;
  -- therefore each of the straight lines AL, BC is equal to BG.
  -- And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]
  -- therefore AL is also equal to BC.
  have hAL_BC : ‖A L‖ = ‖B C‖ := CommonNotion1 hAL_BG hBC_BG
  -- Therefore at the given point A the straight line AL is placed equal to the given straight
  -- line BC.
  exact ⟨L, hAL_BC⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to do.

statement.note: Proved wherever the point A lies; when A is B itself, BC already serves.

state.heath_proof:
Let AB, C be the two given unequal straight lines, and let AB be the greater of them.

Thus it is required to cut off from AB the greater a straight line equal to C the less.

At the point A let AD be placed equal to the straight line C; [I. 2]

and with centre A and distance AD let the circle DEF be described. [Post. 3]

Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle DEF,

AE is equal to AD. [Def. 15]

But C is also equal to AD.

Therefore each of the straight lines AE, C is equal to AD; so that AE is also equal to C. [C.N. 1]

Therefore, given the two straight lines AB, C, from AB the greater AE has been cut off equal to C the less.

state.lean_proof:
/-- Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the
less. -/
theorem Prop3 {A B C₁ C₂ : Point} (hC : C₁ ≠ C₂) (h : ‖C₁ C₂‖ < ‖A B‖) :
    ∃ E : Point, Between A E B ∧ ‖A E‖ = ‖C₁ C₂‖ := by
  -- Let AB, C be the two given unequal straight lines, and let AB be the greater of them.
  have hAB : A ≠ B := ne_of_len_gt h
  -- Thus it is required to cut off from AB the greater a straight line equal to C the less.
  -- At the point A let AD be placed equal to the straight line C; [I. 2]
  obtain ⟨D, hAD⟩ := Prop2 A C₁ C₂ hC
  have hAD' : A ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq hAD hC
  -- and with centre A and distance AD let the circle DEF be described. [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨DEF, hA_DEF, hD_DEF⟩ := Postulate3 A D hAD'
  /- Euclid does not say where the circle DEF meets AB. B lies outside it, since
     AB is the greater, and A, the centre, lies inside; so the straight line AB
     cuts the circle at a point E between A and B (System E, Intersections 4). -/
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  have hB_out : OutsideCircle B DEF := outside_of_len_gt hA_DEF hD_DEF (by rw [hAD]; exact h)
  obtain ⟨E, hE_DEF, -, hAEB⟩ := line_circle_between (centre_inside hA_DEF) hA_AB hB_out hB_AB
  -- Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle DEF,
  -- AE is equal to AD. [Def. 15]
  have hAE_AD : ‖A E‖ = ‖A D‖ := Definition15 hA_DEF hE_DEF hD_DEF
  -- But C is also equal to AD.
  have hC_AD : ‖C₁ C₂‖ = ‖A D‖ := hAD.symm
  -- Therefore each of the straight lines AE, C is equal to AD; so that AE is also equal to C.
  -- [C.N. 1]
  have hAE_C : ‖A E‖ = ‖C₁ C₂‖ := CommonNotion1 hAE_AD hC_AD
  -- Therefore, given the two straight lines AB, C, from AB the greater AE has been cut off
  -- equal to C the less.
  exact ⟨E, hAEB, hAE_C⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to do.

state.commentary:
Here I.2 goes to work. To cut off from AB a straight line equal to C, Euclid places AD equal to C at the point A, and lets the circle about A through D do the cutting. With that, the compasses that close of themselves, which Augustus De Morgan pictures under I.2, can do all that an ordinary pair does: carry a length and lay it off along a straight line.

Proclus finds eight figures here, but only, Heath remarks, "by practically incorporating the construction of the preceding proposition, instead of assuming it as we are entitled to do. If Prop. 2 is assumed, there is really only one 'case' of the present proposition" (vol. 1, p. 247). In Lean, citing I.2 is exactly assuming it: `Prop2` is a finished result, whatever its own figure looked like. Heath also sets aside Robert Potts' two cases, cutting from one end of AB or the other, and so do our proofs: when I.6 cuts from the end B, it cites `Prop3` with the letters exchanged.

Why should the circle DEF meet AB at all, and between A and B? Its centre A is inside it and B, farther from A than the radius, is outside; a straight line from inside a circle to outside crosses it (System E, Intersections 4). Our proof says so, after naming the straight line AB as in I.1, and our `Prop3` keeps E between A and B, as cutting off from AB means, since I.5 and I.6 rely on it. Where Euclid names the less straight line by one letter, C, our representation, which knows a finite straight line only by its two ends, gives C a pair of them.
state.heath_proof:
Let AB, C be the two given unequal straight lines, and let AB be the greater of them.

Thus it is required to cut off from AB the greater a straight line equal to C the less.

At the point A let AD be placed equal to the straight line C; [I. 2]

and with centre A and distance AD let the circle DEF be described. [Post. 3]

Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle DEF,

AE is equal to AD. [Def. 15]

But C is also equal to AD.

Therefore each of the straight lines AE, C is equal to AD; so that AE is also equal to C. [C.N. 1]

Therefore, given the two straight lines AB, C, from AB the greater AE has been cut off equal to C the less.

(Being) what it was required to do.
state.lean_proof:
/-- Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the
less. -/
theorem Prop3 {A B C₁ C₂ : Point} (hC : C₁ ≠ C₂) (h : ‖C₁ C₂‖ < ‖A B‖) :
    ∃ E : Point, Between A E B ∧ ‖A E‖ = ‖C₁ C₂‖ := by
  -- Let AB, C be the two given unequal straight lines, and let AB be the greater of them.
  have hAB : A ≠ B := ne_of_len_gt h
  -- Thus it is required to cut off from AB the greater a straight line equal to C the less.
  -- At the point A let AD be placed equal to the straight line C; [I. 2]
  obtain ⟨D, hAD⟩ := Prop2 A C₁ C₂ hC
  have hAD' : A ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq hAD hC
  -- and with centre A and distance AD let the circle DEF be described. [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨DEF, hA_DEF, hD_DEF⟩ := Postulate3 A D hAD'
  /- Euclid does not say where the circle DEF meets AB. B lies outside it, since
     AB is the greater, and A, the centre, lies inside; so the straight line AB
     cuts the circle at a point E between A and B (System E, Intersections 4). -/
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  have hB_out : OutsideCircle B DEF := outside_of_len_gt hA_DEF hD_DEF (by rw [hAD]; exact h)
  obtain ⟨E, hE_DEF, -, hAEB⟩ := line_circle_between (centre_inside hA_DEF) hA_AB hB_out hB_AB
  -- Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle DEF,
  -- AE is equal to AD. [Def. 15]
  have hAE_AD : ‖A E‖ = ‖A D‖ := Definition15 hA_DEF hE_DEF hD_DEF
  -- But C is also equal to AD.
  have hC_AD : ‖C₁ C₂‖ = ‖A D‖ := hAD.symm
  -- Therefore each of the straight lines AE, C is equal to AD; so that AE is also equal to C.
  -- [C.N. 1]
  have hAE_C : ‖A E‖ = ‖C₁ C₂‖ := CommonNotion1 hAE_AD hC_AD
  -- Therefore, given the two straight lines AB, C, from AB the greater AE has been cut off
  -- equal to C the less.
  exact ⟨E, hAEB, hAE_C⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to do.

/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles
contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the
triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining
angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend. -/
theorem Prop4 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hA : ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F) :
    ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ ∧ △ A B C = △ D E F ∧ ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F ∧ ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF
  -- respectively, namely AB to DE and AC to DF, and the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF.
  have hBA : B ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₂.symm
  have hCA : C ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₃.symm
  have hCB : C ≠ B := hABC.ne₂₃.symm
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hDEF.ne₁₂
  have hFE : F ≠ E := hDEF.ne₂₃.symm
  -- I say that the base BC is also equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC will be equal to the
  -- triangle DEF, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively,
  -- namely those which the equal sides subtend, that is, the angle ABC to the angle DEF, and
  -- the angle ACB to the angle DFE.
  -- For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF,
  /- Euclid lays the triangle along the straight line DE, on the side where F
     is. Our superposition rule takes that line by name, and F off it. -/
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE⟩ := Postulate1 D E hDE
  have hF_DE : ¬ OnLine F DE := fun hF => hDEF ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE, hF⟩
  -- and if the point A be placed on the point D
  -- and the straight line AB on DE,
  /- This is superposition, the one rule that moves a figure (System E §3.7, in
     LeanEuclid's form). The triangle ABC, laid down with A on D, becomes the
     triangle DB'C': B' is on the ray from D through E, C' is on the same side
     of DE as F, and every side and angle is kept. -/
  obtain ⟨B', C', hB'_DE, hB'_ray, hC'_side, hDB', hB'C', hC'D, hB'DC', hDC'B', hC'B'D⟩ :=
    superposition hABC hD_DE hE_DE hDE hF_DE
  have hB'D : B' ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq ((len_symm B' D).trans hDB') hBA.symm
  have hC'D' : C' ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq hC'D hCA
  have hB'C'' : B' ≠ C' := ne_of_len_eq hB'C' hCB.symm
  -- then the point B will also coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE.
  /- The converse of C.N. 4 that Heath points out: on the ray from D through E,
     the one point as far from D as E is, is E itself. This is Savile's argument,
     `OnRay.eq_of_len_eq` in Book Zero. -/
  have hDB'_DE : ‖D B'‖ = ‖D E‖ := hDB'.trans hAB
  have hB'E : B' = E :=
    OnRay.eq_of_len_eq ⟨hDE, hB'D, ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE, hB'_DE⟩, hB'_ray⟩ hDB'_DE
  -- Again, AB coinciding with DE,
  have hEDC' : ∠ E D C' = ∠ B' D C' := CommonNotion4.angle hB'E.symm rfl rfl
  -- the straight line AC will also coincide with DF, because the angle BAC is equal to the
  -- angle EDF;
  have hEDC'_EDF : ∠ E D C' = ∠ E D F := hEDC'.trans (hB'DC'.trans hA)
  /- On F's side of DE only one ray from D makes this angle with DE
     (`onRay_of_angle_eq` in Book Zero), so C' lies on the ray from D through F. -/
  have hC'_ray : OnRay C' D F :=
    onRay_of_angle_eq (SameSideOf.of_line hDE hD_DE hE_DE hC'_side) hEDC'_EDF
  -- hence the point C will also coincide with the point F, because AC is again equal to DF.
  have hDC'_DF : ‖D C'‖ = ‖D F‖ :=
    (len_symm D C').trans (hC'D.trans ((len_symm C A).trans hAC))
  have hC'F : C' = F := OnRay.eq_of_len_eq hC'_ray hDC'_DF
  -- But B also coincided with E;
  -- hence the base BC will coincide with the base EF.
  -- [For if, when B coincides with E and C with F, the base BC does not coincide with the base
  -- EF, two straight lines will enclose a space: which is impossible.
  -- Therefore the base BC will coincide with EF] and will be equal to it. [C.N. 4]
  /- Heiberg brackets the words from "For if" to "EF" as an early scholium. A
     finite straight line enters our Lean only through its two ends, so once B'
     is E and C' is F the base B'C' is EF, and there is no second one on those
     ends for the scholium to rule out. C.N. 4 takes the ends alone; and B'C'
     has BC's length, since the moving keeps every side. -/
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ := hB'C'.symm.trans (CommonNotion4 hB'E hC'F)
  -- Thus the whole triangle ABC will coincide with the whole triangle DEF,
  have hcoincide : △ D B' C' = △ D E F := CommonNotion4.triangle rfl hB'E hC'F
  -- and will be equal to it.
  /- Being moved does not change the triangle: DB'C' has the same sides and
     angles as ABC, so the same area (System E, Metric 9). -/
  have hmoved : △ A B C = △ D B' C' :=
    area_congruent hDB'.symm hB'C'.symm hC'D.symm
      ((angle_symm hBA.symm hCB).trans (hC'B'D.symm.trans (angle_symm hB'C''.symm hB'D.symm)))
      ((angle_symm hCB.symm hCA.symm).trans (hDC'B'.symm.trans (angle_symm hC'D'.symm hB'C'')))
      ((angle_symm hCA hBA).trans (hB'DC'.symm.trans (angle_symm hB'D hC'D')))
  have harea : △ A B C = △ D E F := hmoved.trans hcoincide
  -- And the remaining angles will also coincide with the remaining angles and will be equal to
  -- them,
  -- the angle ABC to the angle DEF,
  have hB : ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F :=
    (angle_symm hBA.symm hCB).trans
      (hC'B'D.symm.trans ((CommonNotion4.angle hC'F hB'E rfl).trans (angle_symm hFE hDE)))
  -- and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.
  have hC : ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E := hDC'B'.symm.trans (CommonNotion4.angle rfl hC'F hB'E)
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hBC, harea, hB, hC⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to prove.

helper_signatures.Elements.CommonNotion4:
/-- **Common Notion 4.** Things which coincide with one another are equal to one
another: if the ends of two finite straight lines coincide, so do the lines. -/
theorem CommonNotion4 {A B C D : Point} (hA : A = C) (hB : B = D) : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖
helper_signatures.Elements.CommonNotion4.angle:
/-- **Common Notion 4**, for angles. -/
theorem CommonNotion4.angle {A B C D E F : Point} (hA : A = D) (hB : B = E) (hC : C = F) :
    ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F
helper_signatures.Elements.CommonNotion4.triangle:
/-- **Common Notion 4**, for triangles. -/
theorem CommonNotion4.triangle {A B C D E F : Point} (hA : A = D) (hB : B = E) (hC : C = F) :
    △ A B C = △ D E F
helper_signatures.Elements.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.OnRay:
/-- `P` lies on the straight line from `A` through `B`, on `B`'s side of `A`
(it may be `B` itself, or nearer, or beyond). -/
def OnRay (P A B : Point) : Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.OnRay.eq_of_len_eq:
/-- On a ray, only one point lies at a given distance from its start: a point P
on the ray from A through B, as far from A as B is, is B itself.

This is Sir Henry Savile's argument, which Heath reports on I.4 (vol. 1,
p. 250): otherwise P falls short of B or beyond it, and either way the less
would be equal to the greater. -/
theorem OnRay.eq_of_len_eq (hP : OnRay P A B) (h : ‖A P‖ = ‖A B‖) : P = B
helper_signatures.Elements.OnRay.symm:
/-- P is on the ray from A through B exactly when B is on the ray from A
through P: they are one and the same ray. -/
theorem OnRay.symm (h : OnRay P A B) : OnRay B A P
helper_signatures.Elements.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
helper_signatures.Elements.Postulate1:
/-- **Postulate 1.** To draw a straight line from any point to any point. -/
axiom Postulate1 (A B : Point) (h : A ≠ B) : ∃ L : Line, OnLine A L ∧ OnLine B L
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf.of_line:
/-- Two points on the same side of a straight line L through A and B are on
the same side of the straight line AB, however that line is named: two points
fix one straight line. -/
theorem SameSideOf.of_line (hAB : A ≠ B) (hA : OnLine A L) (hB : OnLine B L)
    (h : SameSide P Q L) : SameSideOf P Q A B
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf.symm:
/-- If P is on the same side of AB as Q, then Q is on the same side as P. -/
theorem SameSideOf.symm (h : SameSideOf P Q A B) : SameSideOf Q P A B
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf.trans:
/-- Points on the same side as a third are on the same side as each other. -/
theorem SameSideOf.trans (h₁ : SameSideOf P Q A B) (h₂ : SameSideOf Q R A B) :
    SameSideOf P R A B
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.angle_symm:
/-- The angle ABC is the angle CBA. (Metric 4) -/
axiom angle_symm (hAB : A ≠ B) (hCB : C ≠ B) : ∠ A B C = ∠ C B A
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.area_congruent:
/-- Triangles equal in all their sides and angles are equal in area. Euclid
uses this without comment once he has shown two triangles congruent.
(Metric 9) -/
axiom area_congruent (h₁ : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (h₂ : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖) (h₃ : ‖C A‖ = ‖F D‖)
    (h₄ : ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F) (h₅ : ∠ B C A = ∠ E F D) (h₆ : ∠ C A B = ∠ F D E) :
    △ A B C = △ D E F
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.len_symm:
/-- The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3) -/
axiom len_symm (A B : Point) : ‖A B‖ = ‖B A‖
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.superposition:
/-- **Superposition.** The triangle ABC can be applied to the straight line L
with A on D, B on the ray from D through G, and C on the side of L
where H is, without changing any side or angle. -/
axiom superposition {A B C D G H : Point} {L : Line} (hABC : Triangle A B C)
    (hD : OnLine D L) (hG : OnLine G L) (hDG : D ≠ G) (hH : ¬ OnLine H L) :
    ∃ B' C' : Point, OnLine B' L ∧ ¬ Between B' D G ∧ SameSide C' H L ∧
      ‖D B'‖ = ‖A B‖ ∧ ‖B' C'‖ = ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖C' D‖ = ‖C A‖ ∧
      ∠ B' D C' = ∠ B A C ∧ ∠ D C' B' = ∠ A C B ∧ ∠ C' B' D = ∠ C B A
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle:
/-- **Definition 19.** A trilateral figure: three points not on one straight
line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₁₂:
/-- The corners of a triangle are different points. -/
theorem Triangle.ne₁₂ (h : Triangle A B C) : A ≠ B
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₁₃:
/-- The corners of a triangle are different points. -/
theorem Triangle.ne₁₃ (h : Triangle A B C) : A ≠ C
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₂₃:
/-- The corners of a triangle are different points. -/
theorem Triangle.ne₂₃ (h : Triangle A B C) : B ≠ C
helper_signatures.Elements.ne_of_len_eq:
/-- If a finite straight line AB has the length of one with different ends,
its own ends are different. -/
theorem ne_of_len_eq (h : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖) (hCD : C ≠ D) : A ≠ B
helper_signatures.Elements.onRay_of_angle_eq:
/-- On one side of a straight line, only one ray from a point of it makes a given
angle with it. If P and F are on the same side of the straight line DE, and
the angle EDP is equal to the angle EDF, then P lies on the ray from D
through F.

Otherwise either P would lie within the angle EDF, or F within the angle
EDP (System E, Triple incidence 2 says which), and either way an angle would be
a part of an angle equal to it (Diagram-angle 1 and 2, with C.N. 5). Pasch 3
puts P on F's side of D rather than behind it. -/
theorem onRay_of_angle_eq {D E F P : Point} (hPF : SameSideOf P F D E)
    (h : ∠ E D P = ∠ E D F) : OnRay P D F

definitions.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Length:
/-- A length (of a finite straight line). -/
abbrev Length := Magnitude .length
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.OnRay:
/-- `P` lies on the straight line from `A` through `B`, on `B`'s side of `A`
(it may be `B` itself, or nearer, or beyond). -/
def OnRay (P A B : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ P ≠ A ∧ Collinear A B P ∧ ¬ Between P A B
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.SameSide:
/-- `SameSide A B L`: the points `A` and `B` lie on the same side of the
straight line `L`. (Neither of them is on `L`.) -/
opaque SameSide : Point → Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Triangle:

line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop := ¬ Collinear A B C
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area
definitions.len:
/-- The length of the finite straight line from `A` to `B`. Written `‖A B‖`. -/
noncomputable opaque len : Point → Point → Length

question.instructions:
Does every proposition called by the proof unit in `lean_proof` do work towards its conclusion or a substantive intermediate step of Euclid's argument? Also check for artificial hypothesis uses. Judge this unit's uses of the supplied helper signatures; helper bodies are outside this question. Heath's sentences stand as `--` lines and `cited` gives exact enunciations. In Lean, `have h : T := p` proves T by p and calls the result h; `obtain ⟨…⟩ := p` takes p apart into named pieces; `rw [h34, h37, …]` rewrites the goal by the equalities named. Follow uses through helper calls and tactics as well as explicit names. An anonymous binding or an unused hypothesis alone does not establish a defect. If both defects occur, choose `a dummy citation`.

docs/FORMALIZATION.md, section 5:
A checked intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid is legitimate, even if the
  final proof term could do without it.

criteria.a dummy citation: Some proposition call does no substantive work: its result neither supports the argument nor establishes a substantive intermediate fact, and merely supplies a citation while the step is done another way.
criteria.an artificial hypothesis use: No dummy citation is established, but a hypothesis is mentioned only so that it looks used, and does no substantive work.
criteria.cannot tell: What is given here is not enough to decide.
criteria.all do work: Every proposition call supports a later step or the conclusion, or establishes a substantive intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid. No hypothesis is mentioned merely to look used. With no proposition calls the citation part alone is vacuous; hypothesis use must still be inspected.

state.commentary:
Euclid proves side–angle–side by picking up the triangle ABC and laying it down on DEF, and Heath thinks he did it unwillingly: "Euclid obviously used the method of superposition with reluctance" (vol. 1, p. 249). Jacques Peletier saw the danger in 1557. If superposition were allowed as a proof, Heath reports, it "could equally well have been used in I. 2, 3 (thus in I. 2 we could simply have supposed the line taken up and *placed* at the point)" (vol. 1, p. 249). So we let it in as one named rule, [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean), in LeanEuclid's form of System E §3.7, and Peletier's danger is real for it. A proof may build on the corners it places, so as a construction principle it is stronger than System E's rule, and only our policy keeps it to I.4 and I.8.

**Why must B land on E?** Heath points to something "most editors seem to have failed to observe": Euclid assumes that "if A be placed on D, and AB on DE, the point B will coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE. That is, the *converse* of *Common Notion* 4 is assumed for straight lines" (vol. 1, p. 250). Henry Savile saw the difficulty and met it with this argument: "let B fall somewhere short of E or beyond E; and in either case it will follow that the less is equal to the greater, which is impossible" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 250). His argument assumes that B falls on DE or DE produced, which Heath says needs Postulates 1 and 2 together. Our superposition rule supplies this by putting B on the ray from D through E. [Book Zero](../../Elements/Figure) has his argument, step for step, as `OnRay.eq_of_len_eq`.

AC falls along DF "because the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF", which assumes that on one side of DE only one ray from D makes that angle; Book Zero proves it as `onRay_of_angle_eq`, since otherwise one of two equal angles would be part of the other. The moving keeps every side and angle but says nothing of area, so that the triangle laid down is equal to ABC takes a rule of its own, [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean) (System E, Metric 9). The bases need no rule: Euclid's text says that otherwise "two straight lines will enclose a space", but J. L. Heiberg brackets the passage, since an-Nairīzī gives it after the Q. E. D., so it is "a *scholium* only" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 249). Once B lands on E and C on F, our base is EF.

**The modern way.** Superposition is a rigid motion: in the complex plane, $z \mapsto az + b$ or $z \mapsto a\bar{z} + b$ with $|a| = 1$, carrying A to D, B to E and C to F. What it carries is fixed by the two sides and the angle: the law of cosines, $\mathrm{BC}^2 = \mathrm{AB}^2 + \mathrm{AC}^2 - 2 \thinspace \mathrm{AB} \thinspace \mathrm{AC} \cos \mathrm{A}$, gives the base, and $\frac{1}{2} \thinspace \mathrm{AB} \thinspace \mathrm{AC} \sin \mathrm{A}$ the area.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB to DE and AC to DF, and the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF.

I say that the base BC is also equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC will be equal to the triangle DEF, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend, that is, the angle ABC to the angle DEF, and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.

For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF,

and if the point A be placed on the point D

and the straight line AB on DE,

then the point B will also coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE.

Again, AB coinciding with DE,

the straight line AC will also coincide with DF, because the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF;

hence the point C will also coincide with the point F, because AC is again equal to DF.

But B also coincided with E;

hence the base BC will coincide with the base EF.

<!-- The square brackets from "[For if" to "EF]" are printed in the 1908 text (Heiberg's brackets marking an interpolated passage). -->

[For if, when B coincides with E and C with F, the base BC does not coincide with the base EF, two straight lines will enclose a space: which is impossible.

Therefore the base BC will coincide with EF] and will be equal to it. [C.N. 4]

Thus the whole triangle ABC will coincide with the whole triangle DEF,

and will be equal to it.

And the remaining angles will also coincide with the remaining angles and will be equal to them,

the angle ABC to the angle DEF,

and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.

Therefore etc.

(Being) what it was required to prove.
state.lean_proof:
/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles
contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the
triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining
angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend. -/
theorem Prop4 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hA : ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F) :
    ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ ∧ △ A B C = △ D E F ∧ ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F ∧ ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF
  -- respectively, namely AB to DE and AC to DF, and the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF.
  have hBA : B ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₂.symm
  have hCA : C ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₃.symm
  have hCB : C ≠ B := hABC.ne₂₃.symm
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hDEF.ne₁₂
  have hFE : F ≠ E := hDEF.ne₂₃.symm
  -- I say that the base BC is also equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC will be equal to the
  -- triangle DEF, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively,
  -- namely those which the equal sides subtend, that is, the angle ABC to the angle DEF, and
  -- the angle ACB to the angle DFE.
  -- For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF,
  /- Euclid lays the triangle along the straight line DE, on the side where F
     is. Our superposition rule takes that line by name, and F off it. -/
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE⟩ := Postulate1 D E hDE
  have hF_DE : ¬ OnLine F DE := fun hF => hDEF ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE, hF⟩
  -- and if the point A be placed on the point D
  -- and the straight line AB on DE,
  /- This is superposition, the one rule that moves a figure (System E §3.7, in
     LeanEuclid's form). The triangle ABC, laid down with A on D, becomes the
     triangle DB'C': B' is on the ray from D through E, C' is on the same side
     of DE as F, and every side and angle is kept. -/
  obtain ⟨B', C', hB'_DE, hB'_ray, hC'_side, hDB', hB'C', hC'D, hB'DC', hDC'B', hC'B'D⟩ :=
    superposition hABC hD_DE hE_DE hDE hF_DE
  have hB'D : B' ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq ((len_symm B' D).trans hDB') hBA.symm
  have hC'D' : C' ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq hC'D hCA
  have hB'C'' : B' ≠ C' := ne_of_len_eq hB'C' hCB.symm
  -- then the point B will also coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE.
  /- The converse of C.N. 4 that Heath points out: on the ray from D through E,
     the one point as far from D as E is, is E itself. This is Savile's argument,
     `OnRay.eq_of_len_eq` in Book Zero. -/
  have hDB'_DE : ‖D B'‖ = ‖D E‖ := hDB'.trans hAB
  have hB'E : B' = E :=
    OnRay.eq_of_len_eq ⟨hDE, hB'D, ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE, hB'_DE⟩, hB'_ray⟩ hDB'_DE
  -- Again, AB coinciding with DE,
  have hEDC' : ∠ E D C' = ∠ B' D C' := CommonNotion4.angle hB'E.symm rfl rfl
  -- the straight line AC will also coincide with DF, because the angle BAC is equal to the
  -- angle EDF;
  have hEDC'_EDF : ∠ E D C' = ∠ E D F := hEDC'.trans (hB'DC'.trans hA)
  /- On F's side of DE only one ray from D makes this angle with DE
     (`onRay_of_angle_eq` in Book Zero), so C' lies on the ray from D through F. -/
  have hC'_ray : OnRay C' D F :=
    onRay_of_angle_eq (SameSideOf.of_line hDE hD_DE hE_DE hC'_side) hEDC'_EDF
  -- hence the point C will also coincide with the point F, because AC is again equal to DF.
  have hDC'_DF : ‖D C'‖ = ‖D F‖ :=
    (len_symm D C').trans (hC'D.trans ((len_symm C A).trans hAC))
  have hC'F : C' = F := OnRay.eq_of_len_eq hC'_ray hDC'_DF
  -- But B also coincided with E;
  -- hence the base BC will coincide with the base EF.
  -- [For if, when B coincides with E and C with F, the base BC does not coincide with the base
  -- EF, two straight lines will enclose a space: which is impossible.
  -- Therefore the base BC will coincide with EF] and will be equal to it. [C.N. 4]
  /- Heiberg brackets the words from "For if" to "EF" as an early scholium. A
     finite straight line enters our Lean only through its two ends, so once B'
     is E and C' is F the base B'C' is EF, and there is no second one on those
     ends for the scholium to rule out. C.N. 4 takes the ends alone; and B'C'
     has BC's length, since the moving keeps every side. -/
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ := hB'C'.symm.trans (CommonNotion4 hB'E hC'F)
  -- Thus the whole triangle ABC will coincide with the whole triangle DEF,
  have hcoincide : △ D B' C' = △ D E F := CommonNotion4.triangle rfl hB'E hC'F
  -- and will be equal to it.
  /- Being moved does not change the triangle: DB'C' has the same sides and
     angles as ABC, so the same area (System E, Metric 9). -/
  have hmoved : △ A B C = △ D B' C' :=
    area_congruent hDB'.symm hB'C'.symm hC'D.symm
      ((angle_symm hBA.symm hCB).trans (hC'B'D.symm.trans (angle_symm hB'C''.symm hB'D.symm)))
      ((angle_symm hCB.symm hCA.symm).trans (hDC'B'.symm.trans (angle_symm hC'D'.symm hB'C'')))
      ((angle_symm hCA hBA).trans (hB'DC'.symm.trans (angle_symm hB'D hC'D')))
  have harea : △ A B C = △ D E F := hmoved.trans hcoincide
  -- And the remaining angles will also coincide with the remaining angles and will be equal to
  -- them,
  -- the angle ABC to the angle DEF,
  have hB : ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F :=
    (angle_symm hBA.symm hCB).trans
      (hC'B'D.symm.trans ((CommonNotion4.angle hC'F hB'E rfl).trans (angle_symm hFE hDE)))
  -- and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.
  have hC : ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E := hDC'B'.symm.trans (CommonNotion4.angle rfl hC'F hB'E)
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hBC, harea, hB, hC⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to prove.

state.enunciation: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB to DE and AC to DF, and the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF.

I say that the base BC is also equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC will be equal to the triangle DEF, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend, that is, the angle ABC to the angle DEF, and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.

For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF,

and if the point A be placed on the point D

and the straight line AB on DE,

then the point B will also coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE.

Again, AB coinciding with DE,

the straight line AC will also coincide with DF, because the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF;

hence the point C will also coincide with the point F, because AC is again equal to DF.

But B also coincided with E;

hence the base BC will coincide with the base EF.

<!-- The square brackets from "[For if" to "EF]" are printed in the 1908 text (Heiberg's brackets marking an interpolated passage). -->

[For if, when B coincides with E and C with F, the base BC does not coincide with the base EF, two straight lines will enclose a space: which is impossible.

Therefore the base BC will coincide with EF] and will be equal to it. [C.N. 4]

Thus the whole triangle ABC will coincide with the whole triangle DEF,

and will be equal to it.

And the remaining angles will also coincide with the remaining angles and will be equal to them,

the angle ABC to the angle DEF,

and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.

Therefore etc.

(Being) what it was required to prove.

state.enunciation: In isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABC be an isosceles triangle having the side AB equal to the side AC;

and let the straight lines BD, CE be produced further in a straight line with AB, AC. [Post. 2]

I say that the angle ABC is equal to the angle ACB, and the angle CBD to the angle BCE.

Let a point F be taken at random on BD;

from AE the greater let AG be cut off equal to AF the less; [I. 3]

and let the straight lines FC, GB be joined. [Post. 1]

Then, since AF is equal to AG and AB to AC,

the two sides FA, AC are equal to the two sides GA, AB, respectively;

and they contain a common angle, the angle FAG.

Therefore the base FC is equal to the base GB,

and the triangle AFC is equal to the triangle AGB,

and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend,

that is, the angle ACF to the angle ABG,

and the angle AFC to the angle AGB. [I. 4]

And, since the whole AF is equal to the whole AG,

and in these AB is equal to AC,

the remainder BF is equal to the remainder CG.

But FC was also proved equal to GB;

therefore the two sides BF, FC are equal to the two sides CG, GB respectively;

and the angle BFC is equal to the angle CGB,

while the base BC is common to them;

therefore the triangle BFC is also equal to the triangle CGB,

and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend;

therefore the angle FBC is equal to the angle GCB,

and the angle BCF to the angle CBG.

Accordingly, since the whole angle ABG was proved equal to the angle ACF,

and in these the angle CBG is equal to the angle BCF,

the remaining angle ABC is equal to the remaining angle ACB;

and they are at the base of the triangle ABC.

But the angle FBC was also proved equal to the angle GCB;

and they are under the base.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

state.lean_proof:
/-- In isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal
straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop5 {A B C D E : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖)
    (hD : Between A B D) (hE : Between A C E) :
    ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B ∧ ∠ C B D = ∠ B C E := by
  -- Let ABC be an isosceles triangle having the side AB equal to the side AC;
  have hA_B : A ≠ B := hABC.ne₁₂
  have hB_C : B ≠ C := hABC.ne₂₃
  have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
  -- and let the straight lines BD, CE be produced further in a straight line with AB,
  -- AC. [Post. 2]
  /- The statement hands us D and E already produced, so our proof does not use
     Postulate 2. It does name the straight lines AB and AC themselves, with D and E
     on them, and use the fact that ABC is a triangle: C is off AB, and B is off AC. -/
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hA_B
  obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hA_C
  have hC_AB : ¬ OnLine C AB := fun h => hABC ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB, h⟩
  have hB_AC : ¬ OnLine B AC := fun h => hABC ⟨AC, hA_AC, h, hC_AC⟩
  have hE_AC : OnLine E AC := on_line_of_between hE hA_AC hC_AC
  -- I say that the angle ABC is equal to the angle ACB, and the angle CBD to the angle BCE.
  -- Let a point F be taken at random on BD;
  /- At random, but not too far out, for in the next breath AE is "the greater" and
     AF "the less". AB, being equal to AC, is less than AE, so F can be taken nearer
     to A than E is (`exists_between_nearer` in Book Zero, with a circle about A
     through E). Then F lies beyond B on the straight line AB. -/
  have hAB_AE : ‖A B‖ < ‖A E‖ := by
    rw [hAB]
    exact len_lt_of_between hE
  obtain ⟨F, hBFD, hAF_AE⟩ :=
    exists_between_nearer (ne_of_between (between_symm hD)).symm (Or.inr hD) hAB_AE
  have hABF : Between A B F := between_cut hD hBFD
  have hF_AB : OnLine F AB := on_line_of_between hABF hA_AB hB_AB
  have hA_F : A ≠ F := ne_of_between_ends hABF
  -- from AE the greater let AG be cut off equal to AF the less; [I. 3]
  obtain ⟨G, hAGE, hAG_AF⟩ := Prop3 hA_F hAF_AE
  have hG_AC : OnLine G AC := on_line_of_between_ends hAGE hA_AC hE_AC
  have hA_G : A ≠ G := ne_of_between hAGE
  -- and let the straight lines FC, GB be joined. [Post. 1]
  have hF_C : F ≠ C := fun h => hC_AB (h ▸ hF_AB)
  have hG_B : G ≠ B := fun h => hB_AC (h ▸ hG_AC)
  obtain ⟨FC, hF_FC, hC_FC⟩ := Postulate1 F C hF_C
  obtain ⟨GB, hG_GB, hB_GB⟩ := Postulate1 G B hG_B
  -- Then, since AF is equal to AG and AB to AC,
  have hAF_AG : ‖A F‖ = ‖A G‖ := hAG_AF.symm
  -- the two sides FA, AC are equal to the two sides GA, AB, respectively;
  have hAC_AB : ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ := hAB.symm
  -- and they contain a common angle, the angle FAG.
  /- Common, because B lies on AF and C lies on AG. For C that takes a word Euclid
     does not say: AG, being equal to AF, is greater than AB, that is, than AC; so G
     lies beyond C. -/
  have hAB_AF : ‖A B‖ < ‖A F‖ := by
    rw [← len_add_of_between hABF]
    exact CommonNotion5 (len_pos (ne_of_between hBFD))
  have hACG : Between A C G :=
    (OnRay.of_between hE).between_of_len_lt (OnRay.of_between hAGE)
      (by rw [hAC_AB, ← hAF_AG]; exact hAB_AF)
  have hFAC_GAB : ∠ F A C = ∠ G A B := by
    rw [angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond hABF) hA_C.symm, angle_symm hA_B.symm hA_C.symm,
      angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond hACG) hA_B.symm]
  -- Therefore the base FC is equal to the base GB,
  have hAFC : Triangle A F C := Triangle.of_line hA_AB hF_AB hA_F hC_AB
  have hAGB : Triangle A G B := Triangle.of_line hA_AC hG_AC hA_G hB_AC
  have hI4 := Prop4 hAFC hAGB hAF_AG hAC_AB hFAC_GAB
  have hFC_GB : ‖F C‖ = ‖G B‖ := hI4.1
  -- and the triangle AFC is equal to the triangle AGB,
  have : △ A F C = △ A G B := hI4.2.1
  -- and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those
  -- which the equal sides subtend,
  -- that is, the angle ACF to the angle ABG,
  have hACF_ABG : ∠ A C F = ∠ A B G := hI4.2.2.2
  -- and the angle AFC to the angle AGB. [I. 4]
  have hAFC_AGB : ∠ A F C = ∠ A G B := hI4.2.2.1
  -- And, since the whole AF is equal to the whole AG,
  have hAB_BF : ‖A B‖ + ‖B F‖ = ‖A F‖ := len_add_of_between hABF
  have hAC_CG : ‖A C‖ + ‖C G‖ = ‖A G‖ := len_add_of_between hACG
  -- and in these AB is equal to AC,
  -- the remainder BF is equal to the remainder CG.
  have hBF_CG : ‖B F‖ = ‖C G‖ := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ‖A B‖) (d := ‖A C‖) _ hAB
    rw [add_comm, hAB_BF, hAF_AG, ← hAC_CG, add_comm]
  -- But FC was also proved equal to GB;
  -- therefore the two sides BF, FC are equal to the two sides CG, GB respectively;
  have hFB_GC : ‖F B‖ = ‖G C‖ := by rw [len_symm F B, hBF_CG, len_symm C G]
  -- and the angle BFC is equal to the angle CGB,
  /- These are the angles AFC and AGB over again, since B lies on FA and C on GA. -/
  have hBFC_CGB : ∠ B F C = ∠ C G B := by
    rw [← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond (between_symm hABF)) hF_C.symm,
      ← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond (between_symm hACG)) hG_B.symm]
    exact hAFC_AGB
  -- while the base BC is common to them;
  /- Euclid is quoting I.4 ahead of time, as Heath explains: the bases are equal
     because they are one and the same base. -/
  -- therefore the triangle BFC is also equal to the triangle CGB,
  have hFBC : Triangle F B C :=
    Triangle.of_line hF_AB hB_AB (ne_of_between (between_symm hABF)) hC_AB
  have hGCB : Triangle G C B :=
    Triangle.of_line hG_AC hC_AC (ne_of_between (between_symm hACG)) hB_AC
  have hI4' := Prop4 hFBC hGCB hFB_GC hFC_GB hBFC_CGB
  have : △ B F C = △ C G B := by
    rw [← area_rotate F C B, ← area_swap F B C, hI4'.2.1, area_swap G C B, area_rotate G B C]
  -- and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those
  -- which the equal sides subtend;
  -- therefore the angle FBC is equal to the angle GCB,
  have hFBC_GCB : ∠ F B C = ∠ G C B := hI4'.2.2.1
  -- and the angle BCF to the angle CBG.
  have hBCF_CBG : ∠ B C F = ∠ C B G := by
    rw [angle_symm hB_C hF_C, angle_symm hB_C.symm hG_B]
    exact hI4'.2.2.2
  -- Accordingly, since the whole angle ABG was proved equal to the angle ACF,
  /- Whole, because C lies between A and G, so that BC falls within the angle ABG;
     likewise B lies between A and F, so that CB falls within the angle ACF. -/
  have hABG : ∠ A B G = ∠ A B C + ∠ C B G :=
    angle_add_of_between hAGB hACG
  have hACF : ∠ A C F = ∠ A C B + ∠ B C F :=
    angle_add_of_between hAFC hABF
  -- and in these the angle CBG is equal to the angle BCF,
  -- the remaining angle ABC is equal to the remaining angle ACB;
  have hbase : ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ∠ C B G) (d := ∠ B C F) _ hBCF_CBG.symm
    rw [← hABG, ← hACF, hACF_ABG]
  -- and they are at the base of the triangle ABC.
  -- But the angle FBC was also proved equal to the angle GCB;
  -- and they are under the base.
  /- Under the base: the angle CBD is the angle CBF, since F lies on BD, and the angle
     BCE is the angle BCG, since G lies between C and E. -/
  have hCGE : Between C G E := between_inner hACG hAGE
  have hunder : ∠ C B D = ∠ B C E := by
    rw [angle_symm hB_C.symm (ne_of_between (between_symm hD)),
      angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond hBFD) hB_C.symm, hFBC_GCB,
      ← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond hCGE) hB_C,
      angle_symm (ne_of_between (between_symm hE)) hB_C]
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hbase, hunder⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop3:
/-- Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the
less. -/
theorem Prop3 {A B C₁ C₂ : Point} (hC : C₁ ≠ C₂) (h : ‖C₁ C₂‖ < ‖A B‖) :
    ∃ E : Point, Between A E B ∧ ‖A E‖ = ‖C₁ C₂‖
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop4:
/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles
contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the
triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining
angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend. -/
theorem Prop4 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hA : ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F) :
    ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ ∧ △ A B C = △ D E F ∧ ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F ∧ ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E
helper_signatures.Elements.CommonNotion3:
/-- **Common Notion 3.** If equals be subtracted from equals, the remainders
are equal. (From `a + c = b + d` and `c = d`, conclude `a = b`.) -/
theorem CommonNotion3 {a b c d : Magnitude k} (h₁ : a + c = b + d) (h₂ : c = d) :
    a = b
helper_signatures.Elements.CommonNotion5:
/-- **Common Notion 5.** The whole is greater than the part: if `b` is something
(not nothing), then `a + b` is greater than `a`. -/
theorem CommonNotion5 {a b : Magnitude k} (h : 0 < b) : a < a + b

/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/

helper_signatures.Elements.OnRay.between_of_len_lt:
/-- Of two points on a ray, the one nearer the start lies between the start and
the other. -/
theorem OnRay.between_of_len_lt (hP : OnRay P A B) (hQ : OnRay Q A B) (h : ‖A P‖ < ‖A Q‖) :
    Between A P Q
helper_signatures.Elements.OnRay.of_between:
/-- A point between A and B is on the ray from A through B. -/
theorem OnRay.of_between (h : Between A P B) : OnRay P A B
helper_signatures.Elements.OnRay.of_beyond:
/-- A point beyond B, on the straight line from A through B produced, is on
the ray from A through B. -/
theorem OnRay.of_beyond (h : Between A B P) : OnRay P A B

/-- P is on the ray from A through B exactly when B is on the ray from A
through P: they are one and the same ray. -/

/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/

(Diagram-segment 1) -/

helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.ne_of_between_ends:
/-- The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1) -/
axiom ne_of_between_ends (h : Between A B C) : A ≠ C
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.on_line_of_between:

through C. (Between 2) -/

    OnLine C L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.on_line_of_between_ends:
/-- A straight line through A and C passes through every point between them.
(Between 3) -/
axiom on_line_of_between_ends (h : Between A B C) (hA : OnLine A L) (hC : OnLine C L) :
    OnLine B L
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle:
/-- **Definition 19.** A trilateral figure: three points not on one straight
line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₁₂:
/-- The corners of a triangle are different points. -/
theorem Triangle.ne₁₂ (h : Triangle A B C) : A ≠ B
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₁₃:
/-- The corners of a triangle are different points. -/
theorem Triangle.ne₁₃ (h : Triangle A B C) : A ≠ C
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₂₃:
/-- The corners of a triangle are different points. -/
theorem Triangle.ne₂₃ (h : Triangle A B C) : B ≠ C
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.of_line:
/-- Two different points of a straight line, and a third point off it, make a
triangle. -/
theorem Triangle.of_line {P Q R : Point} (hP : OnLine P L) (hQ : OnLine Q L) (hPQ : P ≠ Q)
    (hR : ¬ OnLine R L) : Triangle P Q R
helper_signatures.Elements.angle_add_of_between:
/-- If R lies between P and Q, and V is off the straight line PQ, then VR
falls within the angle PVQ, and that angle is made up of the angles PVR and
RVQ. (System E, Pasch 2 and Diagram-angle 2) -/
theorem angle_add_of_between {V P Q R : Point} (hPQV : Triangle P Q V) (h : Between P R Q) :
    ∠ P V Q = ∠ P V R + ∠ R V Q
helper_signatures.Elements.angle_onRay_left:
/-- One arm traced through another point of its ray: if B' is on the ray from A
through B, the angle B'AC is the angle BAC. (System E, Diagram-angle 4) -/
theorem angle_onRay_left {B' : Point} (hB : OnRay B' A B) (hCA : C ≠ A) :
    ∠ B' A C = ∠ B A C
helper_signatures.Elements.between_cut:
/-- Cutting off beyond a point: if B is between A and C, and D between B and
C, then B is between A and D. This is the step after "let CE be made equal to
CD [I. 3]" on a straight line produced: what is cut off from BC still lies beyond
B. -/
theorem between_cut (h₁ : Between A B C) (h₂ : Between B D C) : Between A B D
helper_signatures.Elements.between_inner:
/-- Order on a straight line: if B is between A and C, and C is between A
and D, then C is between B and D. -/
theorem between_inner (h₁ : Between A B C) (h₂ : Between A C D) : Between B C D
helper_signatures.Elements.exists_between_nearer:
/-- A chance point, but not too far out. If P is nearer to O than C is, and Q
lies beyond P as seen from O (or O is P itself), there is a point F between
P and Q that is nearer to O than C is, too. Euclid takes a point "at random" on
a straight line and in the next breath needs it near enough (I.5, I.9). A circle about
O through C keeps it in: P is inside that circle; if Q is not outside it, any
point between P and Q will do; if Q is outside, take a point between P and the
place X where PQ leaves the circle (Intersections 4). Either way F lies between
O and a point no farther from O than C is, Q or X, so OF is the less, as
the part is less than the whole. The order of the points does it, not System E's
Circle 2, which contains III.2; so I.5 and I.9 do not rest on that rule. -/
theorem exists_between_nearer {O P Q C : Point} (hPQ : P ≠ Q)
    (hO : O = P ∨ Between O P Q) (h : ‖O P‖ < ‖O C‖) :
    ∃ F : Point, Between P F Q ∧ ‖O F‖ < ‖O C‖
helper_signatures.Elements.len_lt_of_between:
/-- The part is less than the whole: if B lies between A and C, then AB is
less than AC, for AC is AB and BC together. (System E, Diagram-segment 1,
and C.N. 5) -/
theorem len_lt_of_between (h : Between A B C) : ‖A B‖ < ‖A C‖
helper_signatures.Elements.len_pos:
/-- A finite straight line with different ends has some length. -/
theorem len_pos (h : A ≠ B) : 0 < ‖A B‖

I.4.enunciation: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend.

definitions.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Length:
/-- A length (of a finite straight line). -/
abbrev Length := Magnitude .length
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.OnRay:
/-- `P` lies on the straight line from `A` through `B`, on `B`'s side of `A`
(it may be `B` itself, or nearer, or beyond). -/
def OnRay (P A B : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ P ≠ A ∧ Collinear A B P ∧ ¬ Between P A B
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.Triangle:
/-- **Definition 19.** A trilateral figure: three points not on one straight
line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop := ¬ Collinear A B C
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area
definitions.len:
/-- The length of the finite straight line from `A` to `B`. Written `‖A B‖`. -/
noncomputable opaque len : Point → Point → Length

question.instructions:
Does every proposition called by the proof unit in `lean_proof` do work towards its conclusion or a substantive intermediate step of Euclid's argument? Also check for artificial hypothesis uses. Judge this unit's uses of the supplied helper signatures; helper bodies are outside this question. Heath's sentences stand as `--` lines and `cited` gives exact enunciations. In Lean, `have h : T := p` proves T by p and calls the result h; `obtain ⟨…⟩ := p` takes p apart into named pieces; `rw [h34, h37, …]` rewrites the goal by the equalities named. Follow uses through helper calls and tactics as well as explicit names. An anonymous binding or an unused hypothesis alone does not establish a defect. If both defects occur, choose `a dummy citation`.

docs/FORMALIZATION.md, section 5:
A checked intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid is legitimate, even if the
  final proof term could do without it.

criteria.a dummy citation: Some proposition call does no substantive work: its result neither supports the argument nor establishes a substantive intermediate fact, and merely supplies a citation while the step is done another way.
criteria.an artificial hypothesis use: No dummy citation is established, but a hypothesis is mentioned only so that it looks used, and does no substantive work.
criteria.cannot tell: What is given here is not enough to decide.
criteria.all do work: Every proposition call supports a later step or the conclusion, or establishes a substantive intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid. No hypothesis is mentioned merely to look used. With no proposition calls the citation part alone is vacuous; hypothesis use must still be inspected.

state.lean_statement:
theorem Prop5 {A B C D E : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖)
    (hD : Between A B D) (hE : Between A C E) :
    ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B ∧ ∠ C B D = ∠ B C E

statement.note: Both clauses are stated with the equal sides already produced to D and E, as Euclid produces them by Postulate 2; every isosceles triangle has such points.

representation.note: Definition I.20 distinguishes isosceles from equilateral triangles. The Lean assumes only AB = AC, so it proves both conclusions for equilateral triangles as well.

hypothesis-dropped.meaning: A hypothesis of Euclid's enunciation is left out of the statement, which so claims more than he does (III.9's point need not be within the circle).
