state.commentary:
**"At the very threshold."** Proclus credits the discovery to Thales, "who however is said to have spoken of the angles as being *similar*, and not as being *equal*" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 252). Aristotle sketches an older proof, which made the equal sides radii of a circle and reasoned with the mixed angles that straight lines make with its circumference. From that passage Heath infers that Euclid's proof was his own, "and it would thus appear that his innovations as regards order of propositions and methods of proof began at the very threshold of the subject" (vol. 1, p. 254). Generations of schoolchildren knew it as the *pons asinorum*, the bridge of asses.

Euclid takes F "at random" on BD, and the Greek, Heath notes, means "a chance point" (vol. 1, p. 252). Yet at once AE is "the greater" and AF "the less", so F must not lie too far out: [Book Zero](../../Elements/Figure)'s `exists_between_nearer` keeps it inside a circle about A through E that Euclid never draws. The rest of his figure quietly settles the order of its points, and Lean wants each of those facts said. G lies beyond C, since AG, equal to AF, is greater than AC; the angle FAG is "common" because B lies on AF and C on AG; and C lies between A and G, so the "whole angle ABG" is ABC and CBG together.

Pappus needed no construction at all. "Let us conceive this one triangle as two triangles," his proof says, as Proclus reports it: AB, AC are equal to AC, AB, the angle at A is common, and I.4 does the rest (Heath, vol. 1, p. 254). Heath thinks it "by far the best"; the editors' way, turning the triangle over onto itself, "supposes the triangle to be taken up and at the same time to remain where it is" (vol. 1, p. 254). Pappus says nothing of the angles under the base, which, in Proclus' explanation as Heath gives it, Euclid added "for the purpose of fore-arming the learner against a possible *objection*" to I.7 (vol. 1, p. 255), and our I.7 uses them just so. Euclid produces the sides by Postulate 2; we state I.5 with D and E already given, so our proof does not use it.

**The modern way.** Pappus' idea is a reflection. With A at the origin and B, C at the vectors $\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{c}$, of equal length, the reflection in the straight line along $\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c}$ exchanges $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ and fixes A, so it carries the triangle ABC onto ACB, and each angle at the base onto the other.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABC be an isosceles triangle having the side AB equal to the side AC;

and let the straight lines BD, CE be produced further in a straight line with AB, AC. [Post. 2]

I say that the angle ABC is equal to the angle ACB, and the angle CBD to the angle BCE.

Let a point F be taken at random on BD;

from AE the greater let AG be cut off equal to AF the less; [I. 3]

and let the straight lines FC, GB be joined. [Post. 1]

Then, since AF is equal to AG and AB to AC,

the two sides FA, AC are equal to the two sides GA, AB, respectively;

and they contain a common angle, the angle FAG.

Therefore the base FC is equal to the base GB,

and the triangle AFC is equal to the triangle AGB,

and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend,

that is, the angle ACF to the angle ABG,

and the angle AFC to the angle AGB. [I. 4]

And, since the whole AF is equal to the whole AG,

and in these AB is equal to AC,

the remainder BF is equal to the remainder CG.

But FC was also proved equal to GB;

therefore the two sides BF, FC are equal to the two sides CG, GB respectively;

and the angle BFC is equal to the angle CGB,

while the base BC is common to them;

therefore the triangle BFC is also equal to the triangle CGB,

and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend;

therefore the angle FBC is equal to the angle GCB,

and the angle BCF to the angle CBG.

Accordingly, since the whole angle ABG was proved equal to the angle ACF,

and in these the angle CBG is equal to the angle BCF,

the remaining angle ABC is equal to the remaining angle ACB;

and they are at the base of the triangle ABC.

But the angle FBC was also proved equal to the angle GCB;

and they are under the base.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- In isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal
straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop5 {A B C D E : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖)
    (hD : Between A B D) (hE : Between A C E) :
    ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B ∧ ∠ C B D = ∠ B C E := by
  -- Let ABC be an isosceles triangle having the side AB equal to the side AC;
  have hA_B : A ≠ B := hABC.ne₁₂
  have hB_C : B ≠ C := hABC.ne₂₃
  have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
  -- and let the straight lines BD, CE be produced further in a straight line with AB,
  -- AC. [Post. 2]
  /- The statement hands us D and E already produced, so our proof does not use
     Postulate 2. It does name the straight lines AB and AC themselves, with D and E
     on them, and use the fact that ABC is a triangle: C is off AB, and B is off AC. -/
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hA_B
  obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hA_C
  have hC_AB : ¬ OnLine C AB := fun h => hABC ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB, h⟩
  have hB_AC : ¬ OnLine B AC := fun h => hABC ⟨AC, hA_AC, h, hC_AC⟩
  have hE_AC : OnLine E AC := on_line_of_between hE hA_AC hC_AC
  -- I say that the angle ABC is equal to the angle ACB, and the angle CBD to the angle BCE.
  -- Let a point F be taken at random on BD;
  /- At random, but not too far out, for in the next breath AE is "the greater" and
     AF "the less". AB, being equal to AC, is less than AE, so F can be taken nearer
     to A than E is (`exists_between_nearer` in Book Zero, with a circle about A
     through E). Then F lies beyond B on the straight line AB. -/
  have hAB_AE : ‖A B‖ < ‖A E‖ := by
    rw [hAB]
    exact len_lt_of_between hE
  obtain ⟨F, hBFD, hAF_AE⟩ :=
    exists_between_nearer (ne_of_between (between_symm hD)).symm (Or.inr hD) hAB_AE
  have hABF : Between A B F := between_cut hD hBFD
  have hF_AB : OnLine F AB := on_line_of_between hABF hA_AB hB_AB
  have hA_F : A ≠ F := ne_of_between_ends hABF
  -- from AE the greater let AG be cut off equal to AF the less; [I. 3]
  obtain ⟨G, hAGE, hAG_AF⟩ := Prop3 hA_F hAF_AE
  have hG_AC : OnLine G AC := on_line_of_between_ends hAGE hA_AC hE_AC
  have hA_G : A ≠ G := ne_of_between hAGE
  -- and let the straight lines FC, GB be joined. [Post. 1]
  have hF_C : F ≠ C := fun h => hC_AB (h ▸ hF_AB)
  have hG_B : G ≠ B := fun h => hB_AC (h ▸ hG_AC)
  obtain ⟨FC, hF_FC, hC_FC⟩ := Postulate1 F C hF_C
  obtain ⟨GB, hG_GB, hB_GB⟩ := Postulate1 G B hG_B
  -- Then, since AF is equal to AG and AB to AC,
  have hAF_AG : ‖A F‖ = ‖A G‖ := hAG_AF.symm
  -- the two sides FA, AC are equal to the two sides GA, AB, respectively;
  have hAC_AB : ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ := hAB.symm
  -- and they contain a common angle, the angle FAG.
  /- Common, because B lies on AF and C lies on AG. For C that takes a word Euclid
     does not say: AG, being equal to AF, is greater than AB, that is, than AC; so G
     lies beyond C. -/
  have hAB_AF : ‖A B‖ < ‖A F‖ := by
    rw [← len_add_of_between hABF]
    exact CommonNotion5 (len_pos (ne_of_between hBFD))
  have hACG : Between A C G :=
    (OnRay.of_between hE).between_of_len_lt (OnRay.of_between hAGE)
      (by rw [hAC_AB, ← hAF_AG]; exact hAB_AF)
  have hFAC_GAB : ∠ F A C = ∠ G A B := by
    rw [angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond hABF) hA_C.symm, angle_symm hA_B.symm hA_C.symm,
      angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond hACG) hA_B.symm]
  -- Therefore the base FC is equal to the base GB,
  have hAFC : Triangle A F C := Triangle.of_line hA_AB hF_AB hA_F hC_AB
  have hAGB : Triangle A G B := Triangle.of_line hA_AC hG_AC hA_G hB_AC
  have hI4 := Prop4 hAFC hAGB hAF_AG hAC_AB hFAC_GAB
  have hFC_GB : ‖F C‖ = ‖G B‖ := hI4.1
  -- and the triangle AFC is equal to the triangle AGB,
  have : △ A F C = △ A G B := hI4.2.1
  -- and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those
  -- which the equal sides subtend,
  -- that is, the angle ACF to the angle ABG,
  have hACF_ABG : ∠ A C F = ∠ A B G := hI4.2.2.2
  -- and the angle AFC to the angle AGB. [I. 4]
  have hAFC_AGB : ∠ A F C = ∠ A G B := hI4.2.2.1
  -- And, since the whole AF is equal to the whole AG,
  have hAB_BF : ‖A B‖ + ‖B F‖ = ‖A F‖ := len_add_of_between hABF
  have hAC_CG : ‖A C‖ + ‖C G‖ = ‖A G‖ := len_add_of_between hACG
  -- and in these AB is equal to AC,
  -- the remainder BF is equal to the remainder CG.
  have hBF_CG : ‖B F‖ = ‖C G‖ := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ‖A B‖) (d := ‖A C‖) _ hAB
    rw [add_comm, hAB_BF, hAF_AG, ← hAC_CG, add_comm]
  -- But FC was also proved equal to GB;
  -- therefore the two sides BF, FC are equal to the two sides CG, GB respectively;
  have hFB_GC : ‖F B‖ = ‖G C‖ := by rw [len_symm F B, hBF_CG, len_symm C G]
  -- and the angle BFC is equal to the angle CGB,
  /- These are the angles AFC and AGB over again, since B lies on FA and C on GA. -/
  have hBFC_CGB : ∠ B F C = ∠ C G B := by
    rw [← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond (between_symm hABF)) hF_C.symm,
      ← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond (between_symm hACG)) hG_B.symm]
    exact hAFC_AGB
  -- while the base BC is common to them;
  /- Euclid is quoting I.4 ahead of time, as Heath explains: the bases are equal
     because they are one and the same base. -/
  -- therefore the triangle BFC is also equal to the triangle CGB,
  have hFBC : Triangle F B C :=
    Triangle.of_line hF_AB hB_AB (ne_of_between (between_symm hABF)) hC_AB
  have hGCB : Triangle G C B :=
    Triangle.of_line hG_AC hC_AC (ne_of_between (between_symm hACG)) hB_AC
  have hI4' := Prop4 hFBC hGCB hFB_GC hFC_GB hBFC_CGB
  have : △ B F C = △ C G B := by
    rw [← area_rotate F C B, ← area_swap F B C, hI4'.2.1, area_swap G C B, area_rotate G B C]
  -- and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those
  -- which the equal sides subtend;
  -- therefore the angle FBC is equal to the angle GCB,
  have hFBC_GCB : ∠ F B C = ∠ G C B := hI4'.2.2.1
  -- and the angle BCF to the angle CBG.
  have hBCF_CBG : ∠ B C F = ∠ C B G := by
    rw [angle_symm hB_C hF_C, angle_symm hB_C.symm hG_B]
    exact hI4'.2.2.2
  -- Accordingly, since the whole angle ABG was proved equal to the angle ACF,
  /- Whole, because C lies between A and G, so that BC falls within the angle ABG;
     likewise B lies between A and F, so that CB falls within the angle ACF. -/
  have hABG : ∠ A B G = ∠ A B C + ∠ C B G :=
    angle_add_of_between hAGB hACG
  have hACF : ∠ A C F = ∠ A C B + ∠ B C F :=
    angle_add_of_between hAFC hABF
  -- and in these the angle CBG is equal to the angle BCF,
  -- the remaining angle ABC is equal to the remaining angle ACB;
  have hbase : ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ∠ C B G) (d := ∠ B C F) _ hBCF_CBG.symm
    rw [← hABG, ← hACF, hACF_ABG]
  -- and they are at the base of the triangle ABC.
  -- But the angle FBC was also proved equal to the angle GCB;
  -- and they are under the base.
  /- Under the base: the angle CBD is the angle CBF, since F lies on BD, and the angle
     BCE is the angle BCG, since G lies between C and E. -/
  have hCGE : Between C G E := between_inner hACG hAGE
  have hunder : ∠ C B D = ∠ B C E := by
    rw [angle_symm hB_C.symm (ne_of_between (between_symm hD)),
      angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond hBFD) hB_C.symm, hFBC_GCB,
      ← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_beyond hCGE) hB_C,
      angle_symm (ne_of_between (between_symm hE)) hB_C]
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hbase, hunder⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

statement.note: Both clauses are stated with the equal sides already produced to D and E, as Euclid produces them by Postulate 2; every isosceles triangle has such points.

theorem Prop5 {A B C D E : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖)
    (hD : Between A B D) (hE : Between A C E) :
    ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B ∧ ∠ C B D = ∠ B C E

named_declarations.Elements.exists_between_nearer:
/-- A chance point, but not too far out. If P is nearer to O than C is, and Q
lies beyond P as seen from O (or O is P itself), there is a point F between
P and Q that is nearer to O than C is, too. Euclid takes a point "at random" on
a straight line and in the next breath needs it near enough (I.5, I.9). A circle about
O through C keeps it in: P is inside that circle; if Q is not outside it, any
point between P and Q will do; if Q is outside, take a point between P and the
place X where PQ leaves the circle (Intersections 4). Either way F lies between
O and a point no farther from O than C is, Q or X, so OF is the less, as
the part is less than the whole. The order of the points does it, not System E's
Circle 2, which contains III.2; so I.5 and I.9 do not rest on that rule. -/
theorem exists_between_nearer {O P Q C : Point} (hPQ : P ≠ Q)
    (hO : O = P ∨ Between O P Q) (h : ‖O P‖ < ‖O C‖) :
    ∃ F : Point, Between P F Q ∧ ‖O F‖ < ‖O C‖

Elements.exists_between_nearer: variable {A B C D : Point} {α : Circle}

state.heath_proof:
Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC equal to the angle ACB;

I say that the side AB is also equal to the side AC.

For, if AB is unequal to AC, one of them is greater.

Let AB be greater; and from AB the greater let DB be cut off equal to AC the less;

let DC be joined.

Then, since DB is equal to AC,

and BC is common,

the two sides DB, BC are equal to the two sides AC, CB respectively;

and the angle DBC is equal to the angle ACB;

therefore the base DC is equal to the base AB,

and the triangle DBC will be equal to the triangle ACB,

the less to the greater:

which is absurd.

Therefore AB is not unequal to AC;

it is therefore equal to it.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

state.enunciation: If in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles will also be equal to one another.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC equal to the angle ACB;

I say that the side AB is also equal to the side AC.

For, if AB is unequal to AC, one of them is greater.

Let AB be greater; and from AB the greater let DB be cut off equal to AC the less;

let DC be joined.

Then, since DB is equal to AC,

and BC is common,

the two sides DB, BC are equal to the two sides AC, CB respectively;

and the angle DBC is equal to the angle ACB;

therefore the base DC is equal to the base AB,

and the triangle DBC will be equal to the triangle ACB,

the less to the greater:

which is absurd.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- If in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles
will also be equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop6 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (h : ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖ := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC equal to the angle ACB;
  -- I say that the side AB is also equal to the side AC.
  -- For, if AB is unequal to AC, one of them is greater.
  /- That of two unequal lengths one is the greater is a tacit rule of
     magnitudes (System E §3.5), `lt_trichotomy`. -/
  have one_greater : ‖A B‖ ≠ ‖A C‖ → ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ ∨ ‖A B‖ < ‖A C‖ := by
    intro hne
    rcases lt_trichotomy ‖A B‖ ‖A C‖ with hlt | heq | hgt
    · exact Or.inr hlt
    · exact absurd heq hne
    · exact Or.inl hgt
  /- Euclid takes AB to be the greater. The other case is his argument again
     with B and C exchanged, so we give the argument for every triangle whose
     angles at B and C are equal, and use it twice below. -/
  have greater : ∀ {B C : Point}, Triangle A B C → ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B →
      ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ → False := by
    intro B C hABC h hAC_AB
    -- Let AB be greater; and from AB the greater let DB be cut off equal to AC the less;
    /- Heath prints no reference here, but cutting off is I.3, from the end B. -/
    have hAC_BA : ‖A C‖ < ‖B A‖ := by rw [len_symm B A]; exact hAC_AB
    obtain ⟨D, hBDA, hBD⟩ := Prop3 (A := B) (B := A) hABC.ne₁₃ hAC_BA
    -- let DC be joined.
    /- Our proof uses only the points D and C; the straight line DC is drawn
       for the eye. -/
    -- Then, since DB is equal to AC,
    have hDB : ‖D B‖ = ‖A C‖ := (len_symm D B).trans hBD
    -- and BC is common,
    have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := len_symm B C
    -- the two sides DB, BC are equal to the two sides AC, CB respectively;
    have hsides : ‖B D‖ = ‖C A‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ :=
      ⟨(len_symm B D).trans (hDB.trans (len_symm A C)), hBC⟩
    -- and the angle DBC is equal to the angle ACB;
    /- The angle DBC is the angle ABC itself, since D lies on the ray from B
       through A (`angle_onRay_left` in Book Zero, from System E's Diagram-angle
       4), and ABC is equal to ACB by hypothesis. -/
    have hDBC : ∠ D B C = ∠ A C B :=
      (angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between hBDA) hABC.ne₂₃.symm).trans h
    -- therefore the base DC is equal to the base AB,
    /- This is I.4, applied to the triangles DBC and ACB; that DBC is a
       triangle at all is `Prop6.figure`. -/
    obtain ⟨hDC_AB, hBDC_CAB, -, -⟩ :=
      Prop4 (Prop6.figure hABC hBDA) hABC.cab hsides.1 hsides.2 hDBC
    -- and the triangle DBC will be equal to the triangle ACB,
    have hequal : △ D B C = △ A C B := by
      rw [area_swap D B C, area_rotate D C B, hBDC_CAB, ← area_rotate A B C, area_swap A B C]
    -- the less to the greater:
    /- Heath: "Euclid assumes that, because D is between A and B, the
       triangle DBC is less than the triangle ABC." We prove it, with areas:
       the whole triangle is greater than its part (`Prop6.less`). -/
    have hless : △ D B C < △ A C B := Prop6.less hABC hBDA
    -- which is absurd.
    rw [hequal] at hless
    exact lt_irrefl _ hless
  -- Therefore AB is not unequal to AC;
  have hnot : ¬ ‖A B‖ ≠ ‖A C‖ := fun hne =>
    (one_greater hne).elim (greater hABC h) (greater hABC.acb h.symm)
  -- it is therefore equal to it.
  /- Reductio ad absurdum: a length not unequal to another is equal to it. -/
  exact Classical.byContradiction hnot
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.

question.instructions:
Does every proposition called by the proof unit in `lean_proof` do work towards its conclusion or a substantive intermediate step of Euclid's argument? Also check for artificial hypothesis uses. Judge this unit's uses of the supplied helper signatures; helper bodies are outside this question. Heath's sentences stand as `--` lines and `cited` gives exact enunciations. In Lean, `have h : T := p` proves T by p and calls the result h; `obtain ⟨…⟩ := p` takes p apart into named pieces; `rw [h34, h37, …]` rewrites the goal by the equalities named. Follow uses through helper calls and tactics as well as explicit names. An anonymous binding or an unused hypothesis alone does not establish a defect. If both defects occur, choose `a dummy citation`.

docs/FORMALIZATION.md, section 5:
A checked intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid is legitimate, even if the
  final proof term could do without it.

criteria.an artificial hypothesis use: No dummy citation is established, but a hypothesis is mentioned only so that it looks used, and does no substantive work.
criteria.cannot tell: What is given here is not enough to decide.
criteria.all do work: Every proposition call supports a later step or the conclusion, or establishes a substantive intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid. No hypothesis is mentioned merely to look used. With no proposition calls the citation part alone is vacuous; hypothesis use must still be inspected.
criteria.a dummy citation: Some proposition call does no substantive work: its result neither supports the argument nor establishes a substantive intermediate fact, and merely supplies a citation while the step is done another way.

state.commentary:
**"Which is absurd."** Were AB the greater, cutting off DB equal to AC would make the triangle DBC equal, by I.4, to the whole ACB, "the less to the greater". "We have here used, for the first time in the *Elements*, the method of *reductio ad absurdum*," Heath notes (vol. 1, p. 256). The absurdity rests on a step Euclid does not argue: "Euclid assumes that, because D is between A and B, the triangle DBC is less than the triangle ABC. Some postulate is necessary to justify this tacit assumption" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 256). Heath sketches one, seeing the angle at C as "a cluster of rays issuing from C", each meeting AB in one point. We prove it by another road, with areas: the whole triangle is greater than its part (`Prop6.less`).

I.6 turns the first part of I.5 round, hypothesis and conclusion changing places exactly: the kind of converse Proclus calls leading. Yet Heath explains that "I. 6 is the geometrical, but not the logical, converse of I. 5" (vol. 1, p. 256), for logic alone gives only that some triangles with two equal angles are isosceles. As Augustus De Morgan points out, I.6 is all the same "a purely *logical* deduction from I. 5 and I. 18 taken together" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 256); Heath gives the general argument under I.19, where we meet it again. "Why, asks Proclus, did not Euclid convert the *second* part of I. 5 as well?" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 257). Because, he answers, that converse is not wanted even to meet an objection, and it follows from I.6 at any time after I.13. Isaac Todhunter adds that "I. 6, not being wanted till II. 4, could be postponed till later and proved by means of I. 26" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 258).

**The modern way.** Put $\mathrm{B} = (-1, 0)$, $\mathrm{C} = (1, 0)$ and $\mathrm{A} = (x, y)$, with $y \neq 0$. Equal angles at B and C make the slopes of BA and CA, $y/(x + 1)$ and $y/(x - 1)$, equal and opposite, so $x + 1 = 1 - x$ and $x = 0$. A lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC, and $\mathrm{AB} = \mathrm{AC} = \sqrt{1 + y^2}$.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC equal to the angle ACB;

I say that the side AB is also equal to the side AC.

For, if AB is unequal to AC, one of them is greater.

Let AB be greater; and from AB the greater let DB be cut off equal to AC the less;

let DC be joined.

Then, since DB is equal to AC,

and BC is common,

the two sides DB, BC are equal to the two sides AC, CB respectively;

and the angle DBC is equal to the angle ACB;

therefore the base DC is equal to the base AB,

and the triangle DBC will be equal to the triangle ACB,

the less to the greater:

which is absurd.

Therefore AB is not unequal to AC;

it is therefore equal to it.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- If in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles
will also be equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop6 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (h : ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖ := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC equal to the angle ACB;
  -- I say that the side AB is also equal to the side AC.
  -- For, if AB is unequal to AC, one of them is greater.
  /- That of two unequal lengths one is the greater is a tacit rule of
     magnitudes (System E §3.5), `lt_trichotomy`. -/
  have one_greater : ‖A B‖ ≠ ‖A C‖ → ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ ∨ ‖A B‖ < ‖A C‖ := by
    intro hne
    rcases lt_trichotomy ‖A B‖ ‖A C‖ with hlt | heq | hgt
    · exact Or.inr hlt
    · exact absurd heq hne
    · exact Or.inl hgt
  /- Euclid takes AB to be the greater. The other case is his argument again
     with B and C exchanged, so we give the argument for every triangle whose
     angles at B and C are equal, and use it twice below. -/
  have greater : ∀ {B C : Point}, Triangle A B C → ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B →
      ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ → False := by
    intro B C hABC h hAC_AB
    -- Let AB be greater; and from AB the greater let DB be cut off equal to AC the less;
    /- Heath prints no reference here, but cutting off is I.3, from the end B. -/
    have hAC_BA : ‖A C‖ < ‖B A‖ := by rw [len_symm B A]; exact hAC_AB
    obtain ⟨D, hBDA, hBD⟩ := Prop3 (A := B) (B := A) hABC.ne₁₃ hAC_BA
    -- let DC be joined.
    /- Our proof uses only the points D and C; the straight line DC is drawn
       for the eye. -/
    -- Then, since DB is equal to AC,
    have hDB : ‖D B‖ = ‖A C‖ := (len_symm D B).trans hBD
    -- and BC is common,
    have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := len_symm B C
    -- the two sides DB, BC are equal to the two sides AC, CB respectively;
    have hsides : ‖B D‖ = ‖C A‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ :=
      ⟨(len_symm B D).trans (hDB.trans (len_symm A C)), hBC⟩
    -- and the angle DBC is equal to the angle ACB;
    /- The angle DBC is the angle ABC itself, since D lies on the ray from B
       through A (`angle_onRay_left` in Book Zero, from System E's Diagram-angle
       4), and ABC is equal to ACB by hypothesis. -/
    have hDBC : ∠ D B C = ∠ A C B :=
      (angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between hBDA) hABC.ne₂₃.symm).trans h
    -- therefore the base DC is equal to the base AB,
    /- This is I.4, applied to the triangles DBC and ACB; that DBC is a
       triangle at all is `Prop6.figure`. -/
    obtain ⟨hDC_AB, hBDC_CAB, -, -⟩ :=
      Prop4 (Prop6.figure hABC hBDA) hABC.cab hsides.1 hsides.2 hDBC
    -- and the triangle DBC will be equal to the triangle ACB,
    have hequal : △ D B C = △ A C B := by
      rw [area_swap D B C, area_rotate D C B, hBDC_CAB, ← area_rotate A B C, area_swap A B C]
    -- the less to the greater:
    /- Heath: "Euclid assumes that, because D is between A and B, the
       triangle DBC is less than the triangle ABC." We prove it, with areas:
       the whole triangle is greater than its part (`Prop6.less`). -/
    have hless : △ D B C < △ A C B := Prop6.less hABC hBDA
    -- which is absurd.
    rw [hequal] at hless
    exact lt_irrefl _ hless
  -- Therefore AB is not unequal to AC;
  have hnot : ¬ ‖A B‖ ≠ ‖A C‖ := fun hne =>
    (one_greater hne).elim (greater hABC h) (greater hABC.acb h.symm)
  -- it is therefore equal to it.
  /- Reductio ad absurdum: a length not unequal to another is equal to it. -/
  exact Classical.byContradiction hnot
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.

state.lean_proof:
/-- Given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and meeting in a
point, there cannot be constructed on the same straight line (from its extremities), and on the
same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another point and equal to the former two
respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it. -/
theorem Prop7 {A B C D : Point} (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖D A‖)
    (hCB : ‖C B‖ = ‖D B‖) :
    C = D := by
  -- For, if possible, given two straight lines AC, CB constructed on the straight line AB and
  -- meeting at the point C, let two other straight lines AD, DB be constructed on the same
  -- straight line AB, on the same side of it, meeting in another point D and equal to the
  -- former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it, so that
  -- CA is equal to DA which has the same extremity A with it, and CB to DB which has the same
  -- extremity B with it; and let CD be joined.
  apply Classical.byContradiction
  intro hne
  /- Euclid draws one figure, in which the straight lines AD and CB cross. Three others are
     possible (`Prop7.cases`). If AC and DB cross instead, it is Euclid's figure with the
     letters C and D exchanged, so we exchange them. If D falls within the triangle ABC, or C
     within the triangle ABD, Euclid's argument does not apply as it stands: that is the case
     Proclus answers with the second part of I. 5, proved in `Prop7.within`. From here on, C
     and D are named as in Euclid's figure, and X is the point where AD and CB cross.
     Our proof draws no straight line CD here: `Prop7.figure` draws its own. -/
  obtain ⟨C, D, hCD, hCA, hCB, hne, X, hAXD, hBXC⟩ :
      ∃ C D : Point, SameSideOf C D A B ∧ ‖C A‖ = ‖D A‖ ∧ ‖C B‖ = ‖D B‖ ∧ C ≠ D ∧
        ∃ X : Point, Between A X D ∧ Between B X C := by
    rcases Prop7.cases hCD hCA hCB hne with h | h | h | h
    · exact (Prop7.within hCD hCA hCB hne h).elim
    · exact (Prop7.within (SameSideOf.symm hCD) hCA.symm hCB.symm (Ne.symm hne) h).elim
    · exact ⟨C, D, hCD, hCA, hCB, hne, h⟩
    · exact ⟨D, C, SameSideOf.symm hCD, hCA.symm, hCB.symm, Ne.symm hne, h⟩
  have hACD : Triangle A C D := Prop7.triangle hCD hCA hne
  have hBCD : Triangle B C D := Prop7.triangle (SameSideOf.swap hCD) hCB hne
  -- Then, since AC is equal to AD,
  have hAC_AD : ‖A C‖ = ‖A D‖ := by rw [len_symm A C, hCA, len_symm D A]
  -- the angle ACD is also equal to the angle ADC; [I. 5]
  /- I.5 is stated with the equal sides produced, so `Prop5.base` produces AC, AD
     [Post. 2] and keeps only the angles at the base. -/
  have hACD_ADC : ∠ A C D = ∠ A D C := Prop5.base hACD hAC_AD
  -- therefore the angle ADC is greater than the angle DCB;
  /- Heath: "It would be natural to insert here the step 'but the angle ACD is greater than
     the angle BCD. [C. N. 5.]'" It rests on what the figure shows: CB falls within the
     angle ACD, so the angle ACD is made up of the angles ACB, BCD. -/
  obtain ⟨hACD_sum, hCDB_sum, hACB, hADB⟩ := Prop7.figure hCD hCA hCB hne hAXD hBXC
  have hDCB_ADC : ∠ D C B < ∠ A D C := by
    rw [← hACD_ADC, hACD_sum, angle_symm (Ne.symm hne) hBCD.ne₁₂, add_comm]
    exact CommonNotion5 hACB
  -- therefore the angle CDB is much greater than the angle DCB.
  /- DA falls within the angle CDB, so the angle CDB is greater than the angle CDA. [C.N. 5] -/
  have hDCB_CDB : ∠ D C B < ∠ C D B := by
    refine lt_trans hDCB_ADC ?_
    rw [hCDB_sum, angle_symm hACD.ne₁₃ hne]
    exact CommonNotion5 hADB
  -- Again, since CB is equal to DB,
  have hBC_BD : ‖B C‖ = ‖B D‖ := by rw [len_symm B C, hCB, len_symm D B]
  -- the angle CDB is also equal to the angle DCB.
  have hCDB_DCB : ∠ C D B = ∠ D C B := by
    rw [angle_symm hne hBCD.ne₁₃, ← Prop5.base hBCD hBC_BD, angle_symm hBCD.ne₁₂ (Ne.symm hne)]
  -- But it was also proved much greater than it:
  rw [hCDB_DCB] at hDCB_CDB
  -- which is impossible.
  exact lt_irrefl _ hDCB_CDB
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.

made up of two angles, and neither part is nothing. -/
theorem Prop7.figure {A B C D X : Point} (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖D A‖)
    (hCB : ‖C B‖ = ‖D B‖) (hne : C ≠ D) (hAXD : Between A X D) (hBXC : Between B X C) :
    ∠ A C D = ∠ A C B + ∠ B C D ∧ ∠ C D B = ∠ C D A + ∠ A D B ∧
      0 < ∠ A C B ∧ 0 < ∠ A D B
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop7.triangle:
/-- D is a different point from C, on the same side of AB and as far from A. Then
D is not on the straight line AC, so ACD really is a triangle. (Heath: "The case in
which D falls on AC or BC does not require proof.") On the ray from A through C, the
point D would make one length equal to itself with something added; on the other ray, the
straight line AB would separate C from D. -/
theorem Prop7.triangle {A B C D : Point} (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖D A‖)
    (hne : C ≠ D) : Triangle A C D
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop7.within:
/-- The case Euclid leaves out, answered as Proclus answers it (Heath, vol. 1, p. 260). If
D falls within the triangle ABC, produce AC, AD to E, F. Since AC is equal to
AD, the angles ECD, FDC under the base of the triangle ACD are equal [I. 5]. But the
angle ECD is greater than the angle BCD, so the angle BDC is greater by far than the
angle BCD; and, since DB is equal to CB, it is also equal to it [I. 5]. -/
theorem Prop7.within {A B C D : Point} (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖D A‖)
    (hCB : ‖C B‖ = ‖D B‖) (hne : C ≠ D) (hD : InsideTriangle D A B C) : False
helper_signatures.Elements.CommonNotion5:
/-- **Common Notion 5.** The whole is greater than the part: if `b` is something
(not nothing), then `a + b` is greater than `a`. -/
theorem CommonNotion5 {a b : Magnitude k} (h : 0 < b) : a < a + b
helper_signatures.Elements.InsideTriangle:
/-- `D` lies within the triangle `ABC`. -/
def InsideTriangle (D A B C : Point) : Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
helper_signatures.Elements.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
helper_signatures.Elements.Postulate1:
/-- **Postulate 1.** To draw a straight line from any point to any point. -/
axiom Postulate1 (A B : Point) (h : A ≠ B) : ∃ L : Line, OnLine A L ∧ OnLine B L
helper_signatures.Elements.Postulate2:
/-- **Postulate 2.** To produce a finite straight line continuously in a straight
line.

The finite straight line `BC`, lying on `L`, is produced beyond `C` to a new
point `A`. Because it can be produced as far as we please, we may also ask that
`A` avoid any finitely many points already in the figure (the list `avoid`):
System E §3.3, Points rule 4. -/
axiom Postulate2 {B C : Point} {L : Line} (hB : OnLine B L) (hC : OnLine C L) (hBC : B ≠ C)
    (avoid : List Point) : ∃ A : Point, OnLine A L ∧ Between B C A ∧ A ∉ avoid
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSide:
/-- `SameSide A B L`: the points `A` and `B` lie on the same side of the
straight line `L`. (Neither of them is on `L`.) -/
opaque SameSide : Point → Point → Line → Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf:
/-- `P` and `Q` lie on the same side of the straight line `AB`. -/
def SameSideOf (P Q A B : Point) : Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf.swap:
/-- "On the same side of AB" is the same as "on the same side of BA". -/
theorem SameSideOf.swap (h : SameSideOf P Q A B) : SameSideOf P Q B A
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf.symm:
/-- If P is on the same side of AB as Q, then Q is on the same side as P. -/
theorem SameSideOf.symm (h : SameSideOf P Q A B) : SameSideOf Q P A B
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.add_comm:
/-- The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5) -/
axiom add_comm (a b : Magnitude k) : a + b = b + a
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.angle_add_of_inside:
/-- If D lies within the angle BAC, then BAC is made up of BAD and DAC.
(Diagram-angle 2) -/
axiom angle_add_of_inside (hAL : OnLine A L) (hAM : OnLine A M) (hB : OnLine B L)
    (hC : OnLine C M) (hAB : A ≠ B) (hAC : A ≠ C) (hDL : ¬ OnLine D L) (hDM : ¬ OnLine D M)
    (hLM : L ≠ M) (hBD : SameSide B D M) (hCD : SameSide C D L) :
    ∠ B A C = ∠ B A D + ∠ D A C
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.angle_symm:
/-- The angle ABC is the angle CBA. (Metric 4) -/
axiom angle_symm (hAB : A ≠ B) (hCB : C ≠ B) : ∠ A B C = ∠ C B A
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.between_cases:
/-- Of three different points on a straight line, one is between the other two.
(Between 6) -/
axiom between_cases (hAB : A ≠ B) (hBC : B ≠ C) (hAC : A ≠ C) (hA : OnLine A L)
    (hB : OnLine B L) (hC : OnLine C L) : Between A B C ∨ Between B A C ∨ Between A C B
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.between_symm:
/-- If B is between A and C, it is between C and A. (Between 1) -/
axiom between_symm (h : Between A B C) : Between C B A
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.len_add_of_between:
/-- If B is between A and C, then AB and BC together make up AC.
(Diagram-segment 1) -/
axiom len_add_of_between (h : Between A B C) : ‖A B‖ + ‖B C‖ = ‖A C‖
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.len_symm:
/-- The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3) -/

helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.line_unique:
/-- Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1) -/

    (hBM : OnLine B M) : L = M
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.lines_meet_of_opposite_si:
/-- A straight line joining points on opposite sides of L crosses L.
(Intersection 1) -/
axiom lines_meet_of_opposite_sides (h : OppositeSides A B L) (hAM : OnLine A M)
    (hBM : OnLine B M) : LinesMeet L M
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.lt_irrefl:
/-- No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5) -/
axiom lt_irrefl (a : Magnitude k) : ¬ a < a
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.lt_trans:
/-- What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5) -/
axiom lt_trans {a b c : Magnitude k} : a < b → b < c → a < c
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.ne_of_between:
/-- A point between two others differs from the first. (Between 1) -/
axiom ne_of_between (h : Between A B C) : A ≠ B
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.not_on_line_of_same_side:
/-- Points on one side of a straight line are not on it. (Same side 3) -/
axiom not_on_line_of_same_side (h : SameSide A B L) : ¬ OnLine A L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.on_line_of_between_ends:
/-- A straight line through A and C passes through every point between them.
(Between 3) -/
axiom on_line_of_between_ends (h : Between A B C) (hA : OnLine A L) (hC : OnLine C L) :
    OnLine B L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.pasch2:
/-- If B is between A and C, A is on L and B is off it, then B and C are
on the same side of L: a straight line that leaves L at A does not cross it
again. (Pasch 2) -/
axiom pasch2 (h : Between A B C) (hA : OnLine A L) (hB : ¬ OnLine B L) : SameSide B C L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.pasch3:
/-- A straight line through a point between A and C separates them. (Pasch 3) -/
axiom pasch3 (h : Between A B C) (hB : OnLine B L) : ¬ SameSide A C L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.pasch4:
/-- If two different straight lines L and M meet at B, and A and C are points
of M, different from each other and from B, that are not on the same side of
L, then B is between A and C. (Pasch 4) -/
axiom pasch4 (hLM : L ≠ M) (hBL : OnLine B L) (hBM : OnLine B M) (hAM : OnLine A M)
    (hCM : OnLine C M) (hAC : A ≠ C) (hAB : A ≠ B) (hCB : C ≠ B) (h : ¬ SameSide A C L) :
    Between A B C
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.same_side_symm:
/-- If A is on the same side of a straight line as B, then B is on the same side
as A. (Same side 2) -/
axiom same_side_symm (h : SameSide A B L) : SameSide B A L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.same_side_trans:
/-- Two points on the same side of a straight line as a third point are on the same
side as each other. (Same side 4) -/
axiom same_side_trans (h₁ : SameSide A B L) (h₂ : SameSide A C L) : SameSide B C L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.triple_incidence1:
/-- Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A. If C
lies within the angle BAD (on D's side of L and on B's side of N), then B
and D are not on the same side of M: the straight line AC separates them.
(Triple incidence 1) -/
axiom triple_incidence1 (hAL : OnLine A L) (hAM : OnLine A M) (hAN : OnLine A N)
    (hB : OnLine B L) (hC : OnLine C M) (hD : OnLine D N) (hCD : SameSide C D L)
    (hBC : SameSide B C N) : ¬ SameSide B D M

/-- **Definition 19.** A trilateral figure: three points not on one straight
line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.angle_pos:
/-- An angle of a triangle is something, not nothing: in the triangle ABC, were
the angle ABC nothing, C would lie on the straight line BA (System E,

helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₁₃:
/-- The corners of a triangle are different points. -/
theorem Triangle.ne₁₃ (h : Triangle A B C) : A ≠ C
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.of_line:
/-- Two different points of a straight line, and a third point off it, make a

question.instructions:
Does every proposition called by the proof unit in `lean_proof` do work towards its conclusion or a substantive intermediate step of Euclid's argument? Also check for artificial hypothesis uses. Judge this unit's uses of the supplied helper signatures; helper bodies are outside this question. Heath's sentences stand as `--` lines and `cited` gives exact enunciations. In Lean, `have h : T := p` proves T by p and calls the result h; `obtain ⟨…⟩ := p` takes p apart into named pieces; `rw [h34, h37, …]` rewrites the goal by the equalities named. Follow uses through helper calls and tactics as well as explicit names. An anonymous binding or an unused hypothesis alone does not establish a defect. If both defects occur, choose `a dummy citation`.

docs/FORMALIZATION.md, section 5:
A checked intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid is legitimate, even if the
  final proof term could do without it.

criteria.an artificial hypothesis use: No dummy citation is established, but a hypothesis is mentioned only so that it looks used, and does no substantive work.
criteria.cannot tell: What is given here is not enough to decide.
criteria.all do work: Every proposition call supports a later step or the conclusion, or establishes a substantive intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid. No hypothesis is mentioned merely to look used. With no proposition calls the citation part alone is vacuous; hypothesis use must still be inspected.
criteria.a dummy citation: Some proposition call does no substantive work: its result neither supports the argument nor establishes a substantive intermediate fact, and merely supplies a citation while the step is done another way.

state.commentary:
Euclid's enunciation is hard going, and the words in parentheses are Heath's, put in "in order to make it intelligible" (vol. 1, p. 259). Euclid could write so, Heath explains, because "the phraseology was traditional and therefore, vague as it was, had a conventional meaning which the contemporary geometer well understood" (vol. 1, p. 259). The meaning is plain enough: given the base and the two sides, "only one triangle satisfying these conditions can be constructed on one and the same side of the given base" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 261). I.1 and I.22 build such a triangle, and I.7 says there is just one on each side.

Some editors used I.7 only to prove I.8, and some dropped it for Philo's proof of I.8. Charles Dodgson saw more in it, and Heath quotes him: "of all plane figures that can be made by hingeing rods together, the *three*-sided ones (and these only) are *rigid*" (vol. 1, p. 261). Proclus has a story too, as Heath tells it: "It was said that astronomers used it to prove that three successive eclipses could not occur at equal intervals of time" (vol. 1, p. 261).

Euclid draws one figure, with AD crossing CB. The second case that Robert Simson and the textbooks add "is not in the original text", Heath explains (vol. 1, p. 260): as under I.2, Euclid gives one case and leaves the rest to the reader. Proclus answered that case with the angles under the base, which I.5 proved for just this purpose.

**Four places for D.** Lean has no reader to leave cases to, and we find D in four places. AD may cross CB, as in Euclid's figure, or AC may cross DB, his figure with C and D exchanged; or D or C falls within the triangle the other makes with AB, and that we answer as Proclus does. Our proof must also show that there is no fifth (`Prop7.cases`). Where BC separates D from A, AD crosses BC on C's side of AB, either within CB, as in Euclid's figure, or beyond C, and then C lies within the triangle ABD; where AC separates D from B, the same holds with A and B exchanged; where neither does, D lies within the triangle ABC. Euclid had no call to count the places. His figure shows a D that cannot exist, drawn to be refuted, and he refutes it where he draws it; a reader who drew it elsewhere had that case to answer, as Proclus answered one. For Euclid's figure Heath asks for "Postulates which shall satisfy us as to the relative positions" of the straight lines at C and at D (vol. 1, p. 260). The point where AD and CB cross does that work: it puts CB within the angle ACD, and DA within the angle CDB, so that each angle is made up of two.

**The modern way.** Put $\mathrm{A} = (0, 0)$ and $\mathrm{B} = (c, 0)$. A point $(x, y)$ at distance $b$ from A and $a$ from B has $x^2 + y^2 = b^2$ and $(x - c)^2 + y^2 = a^2$, so $x = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2)/(2c)$ and $y = \pm\sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$: two answers, mirror images in AB, one on each side.
state.heath_proof:
For, if possible, given two straight lines AC, CB constructed on the straight line AB and meeting at the point C, let two other straight lines AD, DB be constructed on the same straight line AB, on the same side of it, meeting in another point D and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it, so that CA is equal to DA which has the same extremity A with it, and CB to DB which has the same extremity B with it; and let CD be joined.

Then, since AC is equal to AD,

the angle ACD is also equal to the angle ADC; [I. 5]

therefore the angle ADC is greater than the angle DCB;

therefore the angle CDB is much greater than the angle DCB.

Again, since CB is equal to DB,

the angle CDB is also equal to the angle DCB.

But it was also proved much greater than it:

which is impossible.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- Given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and meeting in a
point, there cannot be constructed on the same straight line (from its extremities), and on the
same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another point and equal to the former two
respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it. -/
theorem Prop7 {A B C D : Point} (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖D A‖)
    (hCB : ‖C B‖ = ‖D B‖) :
    C = D := by
  -- For, if possible, given two straight lines AC, CB constructed on the straight line AB and
  -- meeting at the point C, let two other straight lines AD, DB be constructed on the same
  -- straight line AB, on the same side of it, meeting in another point D and equal to the
  -- former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it, so that
  -- CA is equal to DA which has the same extremity A with it, and CB to DB which has the same
  -- extremity B with it; and let CD be joined.
  apply Classical.byContradiction
  intro hne
  /- Euclid draws one figure, in which the straight lines AD and CB cross. Three others are
     possible (`Prop7.cases`). If AC and DB cross instead, it is Euclid's figure with the
     letters C and D exchanged, so we exchange them. If D falls within the triangle ABC, or C
     within the triangle ABD, Euclid's argument does not apply as it stands: that is the case
     Proclus answers with the second part of I. 5, proved in `Prop7.within`. From here on, C
     and D are named as in Euclid's figure, and X is the point where AD and CB cross.
     Our proof draws no straight line CD here: `Prop7.figure` draws its own. -/
  obtain ⟨C, D, hCD, hCA, hCB, hne, X, hAXD, hBXC⟩ :
      ∃ C D : Point, SameSideOf C D A B ∧ ‖C A‖ = ‖D A‖ ∧ ‖C B‖ = ‖D B‖ ∧ C ≠ D ∧
        ∃ X : Point, Between A X D ∧ Between B X C := by
    rcases Prop7.cases hCD hCA hCB hne with h | h | h | h
    · exact (Prop7.within hCD hCA hCB hne h).elim
    · exact (Prop7.within (SameSideOf.symm hCD) hCA.symm hCB.symm (Ne.symm hne) h).elim
    · exact ⟨C, D, hCD, hCA, hCB, hne, h⟩
    · exact ⟨D, C, SameSideOf.symm hCD, hCA.symm, hCB.symm, Ne.symm hne, h⟩
  have hACD : Triangle A C D := Prop7.triangle hCD hCA hne
  have hBCD : Triangle B C D := Prop7.triangle (SameSideOf.swap hCD) hCB hne
  -- Then, since AC is equal to AD,
  have hAC_AD : ‖A C‖ = ‖A D‖ := by rw [len_symm A C, hCA, len_symm D A]
  -- the angle ACD is also equal to the angle ADC; [I. 5]
  /- I.5 is stated with the equal sides produced, so `Prop5.base` produces AC, AD
     [Post. 2] and keeps only the angles at the base. -/
  have hACD_ADC : ∠ A C D = ∠ A D C := Prop5.base hACD hAC_AD
  -- therefore the angle ADC is greater than the angle DCB;
  /- Heath: "It would be natural to insert here the step 'but the angle ACD is greater than
     the angle BCD. [C. N. 5.]'" It rests on what the figure shows: CB falls within the
     angle ACD, so the angle ACD is made up of the angles ACB, BCD. -/
  obtain ⟨hACD_sum, hCDB_sum, hACB, hADB⟩ := Prop7.figure hCD hCA hCB hne hAXD hBXC
  have hDCB_ADC : ∠ D C B < ∠ A D C := by
    rw [← hACD_ADC, hACD_sum, angle_symm (Ne.symm hne) hBCD.ne₁₂, add_comm]
    exact CommonNotion5 hACB
  -- therefore the angle CDB is much greater than the angle DCB.
  /- DA falls within the angle CDB, so the angle CDB is greater than the angle CDA. [C.N. 5] -/
  have hDCB_CDB : ∠ D C B < ∠ C D B := by
    refine lt_trans hDCB_ADC ?_
    rw [hCDB_sum, angle_symm hACD.ne₁₃ hne]
    exact CommonNotion5 hADB
  -- Again, since CB is equal to DB,
  have hBC_BD : ‖B C‖ = ‖B D‖ := by rw [len_symm B C, hCB, len_symm D B]
  -- the angle CDB is also equal to the angle DCB.
  have hCDB_DCB : ∠ C D B = ∠ D C B := by
    rw [angle_symm hne hBCD.ne₁₃, ← Prop5.base hBCD hBC_BD, angle_symm hBCD.ne₁₂ (Ne.symm hne)]
  -- But it was also proved much greater than it:
  rw [hCDB_DCB] at hDCB_CDB
  -- which is impossible.
  exact lt_irrefl _ hDCB_CDB
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.

which is impossible.

state.lean_proof:
/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base
equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal
straight lines. -/
theorem Prop8 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖) :
    ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF
  -- respectively, namely AB to DE, and AC to DF; and let them have the base BC equal to the
  -- base EF;
  -- I say that the angle BAC is also equal to the angle EDF.
  -- For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF, and if the point B be placed on
  -- the point E and the straight line BC on EF,
  /- To lay BC along EF we need the straight line EF itself (Postulate 1). The
     rule of superposition then sets B on E, sends C along the ray from E through
     F, and lets us choose the side of EF on which A comes down: D's side, so
     that the two triangles lie over one another, as Euclid's word "applied"
     means. The copy of ABC is `G E C'`: C lands at C' and A at G. -/
  have hEF : E ≠ F := hDEF.ne₂₃
  obtain ⟨EF, hE_EF, hF_EF⟩ := Postulate1 E F hEF
  have hD_EF : ¬ OnLine D EF := fun hD => hDEF ⟨EF, hD, hE_EF, hF_EF⟩
  obtain ⟨C', G, hC'_EF, hC'_ray, hGD_EF, hEC', hC'G, hGE, -, hEGC', -⟩ :=
    superposition hABC.bca hE_EF hF_EF hEF hD_EF
  -- the point C will also coincide with F,
  -- because BC is equal to EF.
  /- C lands on the ray from E through F, as far from E as F is; on a ray only one
     point is at that distance (`OnRay.eq_of_len_eq` in Book Zero). -/
  have hEC'_EF : ‖E C'‖ = ‖E F‖ := hEC'.trans hBC
  have hC'F : C' = F :=
    OnRay.eq_of_len_eq ⟨hEF, (ne_of_len_eq hEC'_EF hEF).symm, ⟨EF, hE_EF, hF_EF, hC'_EF⟩, hC'_ray⟩
      hEC'_EF
  -- Then, BC coinciding with EF,
  -- BA, AC will also coincide with ED, DF;
  /- The sides BA, AC have been carried to GE, GF, and they are equal to ED, DF. -/
  have hGE_DE : ‖G E‖ = ‖D E‖ := hGE.trans hAB
  have hGF_DF : ‖G F‖ = ‖D F‖ :=
    calc ‖G F‖ = ‖F G‖ := len_symm G F
      _ = ‖C' G‖ := by rw [hC'F]
      _ = ‖C A‖ := hC'G
      _ = ‖A C‖ := len_symm C A
      _ = ‖D F‖ := hAC
  -- for, if the base BC coincides with the base EF, and the sides BA, AC do not coincide with
  -- ED, DF but fall beside them as EG, GF,
  -- then, given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and
  -- meeting in a point, there will have been constructed on the same straight line (from its
  -- extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another
  -- point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same
  -- extremity with it.
  /- G and D are on the same side of EF: superposition put G there. And since
     two points fix one straight line, that is the same side of "the straight
     line EF" however it is named (`SameSideOf.of_line` in Book Zero). -/
  have hGD_side : SameSideOf G D E F := SameSideOf.of_line hEF hE_EF hF_EF hGD_EF
  -- But they cannot be so constructed. [I. 7]
  -- Therefore it is not possible that, if the base BC be applied to the base EF, the sides BA,
  -- AC should not coincide with ED, DF;
  -- they will therefore coincide,
  /- Our I.7 is stated positively: two such points are one and the same point.
     So Euclid's reduction to the impossible is a single step here. -/
  have hGD : G = D := Prop7 hGD_side hGE_DE hGF_DF
  -- so that the angle BAC will also coincide with the angle EDF, and will be equal to it.
  /- The angle BAC was carried to the angle EGC', and G is D, C' is F. -/
  have hEGC'_EDF : ∠ E G C' = ∠ E D F := CommonNotion4.angle rfl hGD hC'F
  exact hEGC'.symm.trans hEGC'_EDF
  -- If therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.

state.commentary:
Heath calls I.8 "a *partial* converse of I. 4" (vol. 1, p. 262): the equal bases, which I.4 proves, are given here, and the angle is proved instead. Euclid goes no further than the angles at the vertices A and D, because, as Heath explains after Proclus and Henry Savile, "when once the vertical angles are proved equal, the rest follows from I. 4, and there is no object in proving again what has been proved already" (vol. 1, p. 262).

For the second time Euclid picks up a triangle and lays it on another, and the moving is again our rule [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean), which only I.4 and I.8 call on. It hands us a copy of ABC with B on E, C on the ray from E through F, and A on whichever side of EF we ask for. Euclid never says which side A comes down on, but I.7 needs to know, since D and its mirror image in EF are each as far from E and from F as the other; so we ask for D's side, which is what "applied" means. C lands on F "because BC is equal to EF", and because BC was laid along EF, as in I.4. Then Euclid's reduction to the impossible, in which BA, AC "fall beside" ED, DF, becomes one citation of `Prop7`: G, where A comes down, is D. The Greek verb, Heath notes, means "to pass by without touching," "to miss" or "to deviate" (vol. 1, p. 262).

I.8 may once have said more. Aristotle, speaking of the rainbow, concludes that "*the triangles are equal*", and J. L. Heiberg took this for a trace of an older I.8: "we see here therefore, in a clear example, how the stones of the ancient fabric were recut for the rigid structure of his *Elements*" (Heath, vol. 1, pp. 262–263). Heath doubts the inference is safe. Proclus also preserves a proof by Philo that lays ABC on the far side of EF and uses I.5 in place of I.7, and Heath finds that "it is elegant; but it is inconvenient in one respect, since three cases have to be distinguished" (vol. 1, p. 263). David Hilbert, who made side, angle, side an axiom, proves side, side, side from it with no moving of figures.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB to DE, and AC to DF; and let them have the base BC equal to the base EF;

I say that the angle BAC is also equal to the angle EDF.

For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF, and if the point B be placed on the point E and the straight line BC on EF,

the point C will also coincide with F,

because BC is equal to EF.

Then, BC coinciding with EF,

BA, AC will also coincide with ED, DF;

for, if the base BC coincides with the base EF, and the sides BA, AC do not coincide with ED, DF but fall beside them as EG, GF,

then, given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and meeting in a point, there will have been constructed on the same straight line (from its extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it.

But they cannot be so constructed. [I. 7]

Therefore it is not possible that, if the base BC be applied to the base EF, the sides BA, AC should not coincide with ED, DF;

they will therefore coincide,

so that the angle BAC will also coincide with the angle EDF, and will be equal to it.

If therefore etc.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base
equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal
straight lines. -/
theorem Prop8 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖) :
    ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF
  -- respectively, namely AB to DE, and AC to DF; and let them have the base BC equal to the
  -- base EF;
  -- I say that the angle BAC is also equal to the angle EDF.
  -- For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF, and if the point B be placed on
  -- the point E and the straight line BC on EF,
  /- To lay BC along EF we need the straight line EF itself (Postulate 1). The
     rule of superposition then sets B on E, sends C along the ray from E through
     F, and lets us choose the side of EF on which A comes down: D's side, so
     that the two triangles lie over one another, as Euclid's word "applied"
     means. The copy of ABC is `G E C'`: C lands at C' and A at G. -/
  have hEF : E ≠ F := hDEF.ne₂₃
  obtain ⟨EF, hE_EF, hF_EF⟩ := Postulate1 E F hEF
  have hD_EF : ¬ OnLine D EF := fun hD => hDEF ⟨EF, hD, hE_EF, hF_EF⟩
  obtain ⟨C', G, hC'_EF, hC'_ray, hGD_EF, hEC', hC'G, hGE, -, hEGC', -⟩ :=
    superposition hABC.bca hE_EF hF_EF hEF hD_EF
  -- the point C will also coincide with F,
  -- because BC is equal to EF.
  /- C lands on the ray from E through F, as far from E as F is; on a ray only one
     point is at that distance (`OnRay.eq_of_len_eq` in Book Zero). -/
  have hEC'_EF : ‖E C'‖ = ‖E F‖ := hEC'.trans hBC
  have hC'F : C' = F :=
    OnRay.eq_of_len_eq ⟨hEF, (ne_of_len_eq hEC'_EF hEF).symm, ⟨EF, hE_EF, hF_EF, hC'_EF⟩, hC'_ray⟩
      hEC'_EF
  -- Then, BC coinciding with EF,
  -- BA, AC will also coincide with ED, DF;
  /- The sides BA, AC have been carried to GE, GF, and they are equal to ED, DF. -/
  have hGE_DE : ‖G E‖ = ‖D E‖ := hGE.trans hAB
  have hGF_DF : ‖G F‖ = ‖D F‖ :=
    calc ‖G F‖ = ‖F G‖ := len_symm G F
      _ = ‖C' G‖ := by rw [hC'F]
      _ = ‖C A‖ := hC'G
      _ = ‖A C‖ := len_symm C A
      _ = ‖D F‖ := hAC
  -- for, if the base BC coincides with the base EF, and the sides BA, AC do not coincide with
  -- ED, DF but fall beside them as EG, GF,
  -- then, given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and
  -- meeting in a point, there will have been constructed on the same straight line (from its
  -- extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another
  -- point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same
  -- extremity with it.
  /- G and D are on the same side of EF: superposition put G there. And since
     two points fix one straight line, that is the same side of "the straight
     line EF" however it is named (`SameSideOf.of_line` in Book Zero). -/
  have hGD_side : SameSideOf G D E F := SameSideOf.of_line hEF hE_EF hF_EF hGD_EF
  -- But they cannot be so constructed. [I. 7]
  -- Therefore it is not possible that, if the base BC be applied to the base EF, the sides BA,
  -- AC should not coincide with ED, DF;
  -- they will therefore coincide,
  /- Our I.7 is stated positively: two such points are one and the same point.
     So Euclid's reduction to the impossible is a single step here. -/
  have hGD : G = D := Prop7 hGD_side hGE_DE hGF_DF
  -- so that the angle BAC will also coincide with the angle EDF, and will be equal to it.
  /- The angle BAC was carried to the angle EGC', and G is D, C' is F. -/
  have hEGC'_EDF : ∠ E G C' = ∠ E D F := CommonNotion4.angle rfl hGD hC'F
  exact hEGC'.symm.trans hEGC'_EDF
  -- If therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.

theorem Prop8 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖) :

/-- Given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and meeting in a
