Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is greater than either of
the interior and opposite angles. -/
theorem Prop16 {A B C D : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hBCD : Between B C D) :
    ∠ C B A < ∠ A C D ∧ ∠ B A C < ∠ A C D := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle, and let one side of it BC be produced to D;
  -- I say that the exterior angle ACD is greater than either of the interior and opposite
  -- angles CBA, BAC.
  /- Euclid proves the angle BAC less, and then says "similarly" for CBA. So we give
     his argument for every triangle with a side produced, in his letters, and use it
     twice below. It also hands back the point G on AC produced, which the "similarly"
     needs. -/
  have greater : ∀ {A B C D : Point}, Triangle A B C → Between B C D →
      ∃ G : Point, Between A C G ∧ ∠ B A C < ∠ A C D := by
    intro A B C D hABC hBCD
    have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
    have hB_A : B ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₂.symm
    have hD_C : D ≠ C := ne_of_between (between_symm hBCD)
    obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hA_C
    have hB_AC : ¬ OnLine B AC := hABC.acb.off_line hA_AC hC_AC
    -- Let AC be bisected at E [I. 10], and let BE be joined and produced in a straight line to
    -- F;
    obtain ⟨E, hAEC, hAE_EC⟩ := Prop10 hA_C
    have hE_AC : OnLine E AC := on_line_of_between_ends hAEC hA_AC hC_AC
    have hB_E : B ≠ E := fun h => hB_AC (h ▸ hE_AC)
    obtain ⟨BE, hB_BE, hE_BE⟩ := Postulate1 B E hB_E
    /- Produced beyond E to a point X, far enough for I.3 to cut EF off from EX
       (`produce_longer`, as in I.11). -/
    obtain ⟨X, hBEX, hEB_EX⟩ := produce_longer hB_E hB_E.symm
    -- let EF be made equal to BE [I. 3], let FC be joined [Post. 1], and let AC be drawn through
    -- to G [Post. 2].
    obtain ⟨F, hEFX, hEF_BE⟩ :=
      Prop3 (A := E) (B := X) hB_E (by rw [len_symm B E]; exact hEB_EX)
    /- F lies between E and X, so E lies between B and F: BE produced reaches F
       (`between_cut`). -/
    have hBEF : Between B E F := between_cut hBEX hEFX
    have hF_BE : OnLine F BE := on_line_of_between hBEF hB_BE hE_BE
    have hE_F : E ≠ F := (ne_of_between (between_symm hBEF)).symm
    have hF_AC : ¬ OnLine F AC := fun h =>
      hB_AC ((line_unique hE_F hE_BE hF_BE hE_AC h) ▸ hB_BE)
    have hF_C : F ≠ C := fun h => hF_AC (h ▸ hC_AC)
    obtain ⟨FC, hF_FC, hC_FC⟩ := Postulate1 F C hF_C
    obtain ⟨G, -, hACG, -⟩ := Postulate2 hA_AC hC_AC hA_C []
    -- Then, since AE is equal to EC, and BE to EF,
    have hBE_EF : ‖B E‖ = ‖E F‖ := hEF_BE.symm
    -- the two sides AE, EB are equal to the two sides CE, EF respectively;
    have hEA_EC : ‖E A‖ = ‖E C‖ := (len_symm E A).trans hAE_EC
    have hEB_EF : ‖E B‖ = ‖E F‖ := (len_symm E B).trans hBE_EF
    -- and the angle AEB is equal to the angle FEC,
    -- for they are vertical angles. [I. 15]
    /- AC and BF cut one another at E, and B is off AC. -/
    have hAEB_FEC : ∠ A E B = ∠ F E C := (Prop15 hAEC hBEF hABC.acb).1
    -- Therefore the base AB is equal to the base FC,
    /- I.4, applied to the triangles EAB and ECF: E and A, and E and C, lie on AC,
       with B and F off it. -/
    have hE_A : E ≠ A := (ne_of_between hAEC).symm
    have hE_C : E ≠ C := (ne_of_between (between_symm hAEC)).symm
    have hEAB : Triangle E A B := Triangle.of_line hE_AC hA_AC hE_A hB_AC
    have hECF : Triangle E C F := Triangle.of_line hE_AC hC_AC hE_C hF_AC
    have hAEB_CEF : ∠ A E B = ∠ C E F := hAEB_FEC.trans (angle_symm hE_F.symm hE_C.symm)
    obtain ⟨hAB_CF, hEAB_ECF, hEAB_ECF', hEBA_EFC⟩ := Prop4 hEAB hECF hEA_EC hEB_EF hAEB_CEF
    have hAB_FC : ‖A B‖ = ‖F C‖ := hAB_CF.trans (len_symm C F)
    -- and the triangle ABE is equal to the triangle CFE,
    have : △ A B E = △ C F E := by
      rw [area_rotate A B E, area_rotate C F E]
      exact hEAB_ECF
    -- and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those
    -- which the equal sides subtend; [I. 4]
    have : ∠ E B A = ∠ E F C := hEBA_EFC
    -- therefore the angle BAE is equal to the angle ECF.
    have hBAE_ECF : ∠ B A E = ∠ E C F := (angle_symm hB_A hE_A).trans hEAB_ECF'
    -- But the angle ECD is greater than the angle ECF; [C.N. 5]
    /- Heath's figure shows F within the angle ECD (`Prop16.within`), so that the
       angle ECD is made up of the angles ECF and FCD (`angle_add_of_within`), and
       FCD, an angle of the triangle FCD, is something (`Triangle.angle_pos`). The
       whole is greater than the part. -/
    obtain ⟨hFD, hFE⟩ := Prop16.within hABC hBCD hAEC hBEF
    have hECF_ECD : ∠ E C F < ∠ E C D := by
      rw [angle_add_of_within hFD hFE]
      exact CommonNotion5 hFE.triangle.cab.angle_pos
    -- therefore the angle ACD is greater than the angle BAE.
    /- The angle ECD is the angle ACD, since E lies on the ray from C through A
       (`angle_onRay_left`). -/
    have hBAE_ACD : ∠ B A E < ∠ A C D := by
      rw [hBAE_ECF, ← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between (between_symm hAEC)) hD_C]
      exact hECF_ECD
    /- And the angle BAE is the angle BAC, since E lies on the ray from A through C. -/
    have hBAE_BAC : ∠ B A E = ∠ B A C := angle_onRay_right (OnRay.of_between hAEC) hB_A
    exact ⟨G, hACG, hBAE_BAC ▸ hBAE_ACD⟩
  /- Euclid's argument, in his own figure: the angle ACD is greater than the angle BAC,
     and AC is drawn through to G. -/
  obtain ⟨G, hACG, hBAC_ACD⟩ := greater hABC hBCD
  -- Similarly also, if BC be bisected, the angle BCG, that is, the angle ACD [I. 15], can be
  -- proved greater than the angle ABC as well.
  /- The same argument for the triangle BAC, with AC produced to G: now BC is bisected,
     and the exterior angle is BCG. -/
  obtain ⟨-, -, hABC_BCG⟩ := greater hABC.bac hACG
  /- AG and BD cut one another at C, and B is off AG: the vertical angles BCG and
     ACD are equal. [I. 15] -/
  obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hABC.ne₁₃
  have hAGB : Triangle A G B :=
    Triangle.of_line hA_AC (on_line_of_between hACG hA_AC hC_AC) (ne_of_between_ends hACG)
      (hABC.acb.off_line hA_AC hC_AC)
  have hBCG_ACD : ∠ B C G = ∠ A C D := (Prop15 hACG hBCD hAGB).2
  have hCBA_ACD : ∠ C B A < ∠ A C D := by
    rw [angle_symm hABC.ne₂₃.symm hABC.ne₁₂, ← hBCG_ACD]
    exact hABC_BCG
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hCBA_ACD, hBAC_ACD⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

helper_signatures.Elements.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop10:
/-- To bisect a given finite straight line. -/
theorem Prop10 {A B : Point} (hAB : A ≠ B) :
    ∃ D : Point, Between A D B ∧ ‖A D‖ = ‖D B‖
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop15:
/-- If two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop15 {A B C D E : Point} (hAEB : Between A E B) (hCED : Between C E D)
    (hC : ¬ Collinear A B C) :
    ∠ A E C = ∠ D E B ∧ ∠ C E B = ∠ A E D
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop16.within:
/-- What Euclid sees in his figure: F lies within the angle ECD, on D's side of AC
and on E's side of BC (System E, Pasch 2 and 3, Same side 5). -/
theorem Prop16.within {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hBCD : Between B C D)
    (hAEC : Between A E C) (hBEF : Between B E F) :
    SameSideOf F D C E ∧ SameSideOf F E C D
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop3:
/-- Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the
less. -/
theorem Prop3 {A B C₁ C₂ : Point} (hC : C₁ ≠ C₂) (h : ‖C₁ C₂‖ < ‖A B‖) :
    ∃ E : Point, Between A E B ∧ ‖A E‖ = ‖C₁ C₂‖
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop4:
/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles
contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the
triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining
angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend. -/
theorem Prop4 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hA : ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F) :
    ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ ∧ △ A B C = △ D E F ∧ ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F ∧ ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E
helper_signatures.Elements.CommonNotion5:
/-- **Common Notion 5.** The whole is greater than the part: if `b` is something
(not nothing), then `a + b` is greater than `a`. -/
theorem CommonNotion5 {a b : Magnitude k} (h : 0 < b) : a < a + b
helper_signatures.Elements.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.OnRay.of_between:
/-- A point between A and B is on the ray from A through B. -/
theorem OnRay.of_between (h : Between A P B) : OnRay P A B
helper_signatures.Elements.OnRay.symm:
/-- P is on the ray from A through B exactly when B is on the ray from A
through P: they are one and the same ray. -/
theorem OnRay.symm (h : OnRay P A B) : OnRay B A P
helper_signatures.Elements.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
helper_signatures.Elements.Postulate1:
/-- **Postulate 1.** To draw a straight line from any point to any point. -/
axiom Postulate1 (A B : Point) (h : A ≠ B) : ∃ L : Line, OnLine A L ∧ OnLine B L
helper_signatures.Elements.Postulate2:
/-- **Postulate 2.** To produce a finite straight line continuously in a straight
line.

The finite straight line `BC`, lying on `L`, is produced beyond `C` to a new
point `A`. Because it can be produced as far as we please, we may also ask that
`A` avoid any finitely many points already in the figure (the list `avoid`):
System E §3.3, Points rule 4. -/
axiom Postulate2 {B C : Point} {L : Line} (hB : OnLine B L) (hC : OnLine C L) (hBC : B ≠ C)
    (avoid : List Point) : ∃ A : Point, OnLine A L ∧ Between B C A ∧ A ∉ avoid
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSide:
/-- `SameSide A B L`: the points `A` and `B` lie on the same side of the
straight line `L`. (Neither of them is on `L`.) -/
opaque SameSide : Point → Point → Line → Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf:
/-- `P` and `Q` lie on the same side of the straight line `AB`. -/
def SameSideOf (P Q A B : Point) : Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf.of_line:
/-- Two points on the same side of a straight line L through A and B are on
the same side of the straight line AB, however that line is named: two points
fix one straight line. -/
theorem SameSideOf.of_line (hAB : A ≠ B) (hA : OnLine A L) (hB : OnLine B L)
    (h : SameSide P Q L) : SameSideOf P Q A B
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf.symm:
/-- If P is on the same side of AB as Q, then Q is on the same side as P. -/
theorem SameSideOf.symm (h : SameSideOf P Q A B) : SameSideOf Q P A B
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf.trans:
/-- Points on the same side as a third are on the same side as each other. -/
theorem SameSideOf.trans (h₁ : SameSideOf P Q A B) (h₂ : SameSideOf Q R A B) :
    SameSideOf P R A B
helper_signatures.Elements.SameSideOf.triangle:
/-- A point on one side of the straight line AB is not on it, so ABP is a
triangle. -/
theorem SameSideOf.triangle (h : SameSideOf P Q A B) : Triangle A B P
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.angle_symm:
/-- The angle ABC is the angle CBA. (Metric 4) -/
axiom angle_symm (hAB : A ≠ B) (hCB : C ≠ B) : ∠ A B C = ∠ C B A
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.area_rotate:
/-- The triangle ABC is the triangle CAB. (Metric 8) -/
axiom area_rotate (A B C : Point) : △ A B C = △ C A B
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.between_symm:
/-- If B is between A and C, it is between C and A. (Between 1) -/
axiom between_symm (h : Between A B C) : Between C B A
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.len_symm:
/-- The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3) -/
axiom len_symm (A B : Point) : ‖A B‖ = ‖B A‖
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.line_unique:
/-- Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1) -/
axiom line_unique (hAB : A ≠ B) (hAL : OnLine A L) (hBL : OnLine B L) (hAM : OnLine A M)
    (hBM : OnLine B M) : L = M
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.ne_of_between:
/-- A point between two others differs from the first. (Between 1) -/
axiom ne_of_between (h : Between A B C) : A ≠ B
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.ne_of_between_ends:
/-- The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1) -/
axiom ne_of_between_ends (h : Between A B C) : A ≠ C
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.on_line_of_between:
/-- A straight line through A and B, with B between A and C, passes
through C. (Between 2) -/
axiom on_line_of_between (h : Between A B C) (hA : OnLine A L) (hB : OnLine B L) :
    OnLine C L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.on_line_of_between_ends:
/-- A straight line through A and C passes through every point between them.
(Between 3) -/
axiom on_line_of_between_ends (h : Between A B C) (hA : OnLine A L) (hC : OnLine C L) :
    OnLine B L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.pasch2:
/-- If B is between A and C, A is on L and B is off it, then B and C are
on the same side of L: a straight line that leaves L at A does not cross it
again. (Pasch 2) -/
axiom pasch2 (h : Between A B C) (hA : OnLine A L) (hB : ¬ OnLine B L) : SameSide B C L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.pasch3:
/-- A straight line through a point between A and C separates them. (Pasch 3) -/
axiom pasch3 (h : Between A B C) (hB : OnLine B L) : ¬ SameSide A C L
helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.same_side_symm:
/-- If A is on the same side of a straight line as B, then B is on the same side
as A. (Same side 2) -/
axiom same_side_symm (h : SameSide A B L) : SameSide B A L
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle:
/-- **Definition 19.** A trilateral figure: three points not on one straight
line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.acb:
/-- The triangle ABC, named the other way round, as ACB. -/
theorem Triangle.acb (h : Triangle A B C) : Triangle A C B
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.angle_pos:
/-- An angle of a triangle is something, not nothing: in the triangle ABC, were
the angle ABC nothing, C would lie on the straight line BA (System E,
Diagram-angle 1), and A, B, C would be on one straight line. -/
theorem Triangle.angle_pos (h : Triangle A B C) : 0 < ∠ A B C
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.bac:
/-- The triangle ABC, named the other way round, as BAC. -/
theorem Triangle.bac (h : Triangle A B C) : Triangle B A C
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.bca:
/-- The triangle ABC, named from B, as BCA. -/
theorem Triangle.bca (h : Triangle A B C) : Triangle B C A
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.cab:
/-- The triangle ABC, named from C, as CAB. -/
theorem Triangle.cab (h : Triangle A B C) : Triangle C A B
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₁₂:
/-- The corners of a triangle are different points. -/
theorem Triangle.ne₁₂ (h : Triangle A B C) : A ≠ B
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₁₃:
/-- The corners of a triangle are different points. -/
theorem Triangle.ne₁₃ (h : Triangle A B C) : A ≠ C
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₂₃:
/-- The corners of a triangle are different points. -/
theorem Triangle.ne₂₃ (h : Triangle A B C) : B ≠ C
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.of_line:
/-- Two different points of a straight line, and a third point off it, make a
triangle. -/
theorem Triangle.of_line {P Q R : Point} (hP : OnLine P L) (hQ : OnLine Q L) (hPQ : P ≠ Q)
    (hR : ¬ OnLine R L) : Triangle P Q R
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.off_line:
/-- In the triangle ABC, the corner C is off every straight line through A
and B. -/
theorem Triangle.off_line (h : Triangle A B C) (hA : OnLine A L) (hB : OnLine B L) :
    ¬ OnLine C L
helper_signatures.Elements.angle_add_of_within:
/-- A straight line drawn from the corner of an angle through a point within it
cuts the angle into two. If R lies within the angle PVQ, on Q's side of VP
and on P's side of VQ, then the angle PVQ is made up of the angles PVR and
RVQ. This is System E's Diagram-angle 2, said of "the straight lines VP, VQ"
rather than of lines drawn and named. -/
theorem angle_add_of_within {V P Q R : Point} (hRQ : SameSideOf R Q V P)
    (hRP : SameSideOf R P V Q) : ∠ P V Q = ∠ P V R + ∠ R V Q
helper_signatures.Elements.angle_onRay_left:
/-- One arm traced through another point of its ray: if B' is on the ray from A
through B, the angle B'AC is the angle BAC. (System E, Diagram-angle 4) -/
theorem angle_onRay_left {B' : Point} (hB : OnRay B' A B) (hCA : C ≠ A) :
    ∠ B' A C = ∠ B A C
helper_signatures.Elements.angle_onRay_right:
/-- The other arm traced through another point of its ray: if C' is on the ray
from A through C, the angle BAC' is the angle BAC. (System E,
Diagram-angle 4) -/
theorem angle_onRay_right {C' : Point} (hC : OnRay C' A C) (hBA : B ≠ A) :
    ∠ B A C' = ∠ B A C
helper_signatures.Elements.between_cut:
/-- Cutting off beyond a point: if B is between A and C, and D between B and
C, then B is between A and D. This is the step after "let CE be made equal to
CD [I. 3]" on a straight line produced: what is cut off from BC still lies beyond
B. -/
theorem between_cut (h₁ : Between A B C) (h₂ : Between B D C) : Between A B D
helper_signatures.Elements.produce_longer:
/-- Room to cut off. A finite straight line AB can be produced beyond B further
than a given straight line BC from B. Postulate 2 produces a straight line but
never says how far, and I.3 cuts off only from a *greater* straight line; so Euclid's
"let CE be made equal to CD [I. 3]", on a straight line produced, needs this first
(I.11, I.16, I.20, I.22). Describe the circle with centre B and distance BC
[Post. 3]; the straight line AB, produced beyond the centre, cuts it at some Y
(System E, Intersections 5); and BY, produced a little further still to X
[Post. 2], is greater than BY, that is, than BC [Def. 15, C.N. 5]. -/
theorem produce_longer (hAB : A ≠ B) (hBC : B ≠ C) :
    ∃ X : Point, Between A B X ∧ ‖B C‖ < ‖B X‖
helper_signatures.Elements.same_side_of_opposite_sides:
/-- A straight line has only two sides: two points, each on the other side of the
straight line L from C, are on the same side of L as each other. (System E,
Same side 5) -/
theorem same_side_of_opposite_sides {C D E : Point} (h₁ : OppositeSides C D L)
    (h₂ : OppositeSides C E L) : SameSide D E L

definitions.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Length:
/-- A length (of a finite straight line). -/
abbrev Length := Magnitude .length
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.OnRay:
/-- `P` lies on the straight line from `A` through `B`, on `B`'s side of `A`
(it may be `B` itself, or nearer, or beyond). -/
def OnRay (P A B : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ P ≠ A ∧ Collinear A B P ∧ ¬ Between P A B
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.SameSide:
/-- `SameSide A B L`: the points `A` and `B` lie on the same side of the
straight line `L`. (Neither of them is on `L`.) -/
opaque SameSide : Point → Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Triangle:
/-- **Definition 19.** A trilateral figure: three points not on one straight
line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop := ¬ Collinear A B C
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area
definitions.len:
/-- The length of the finite straight line from `A` to `B`. Written `‖A B‖`. -/
noncomputable opaque len : Point → Point → Length

question.instructions:
Does every proposition called by the proof unit in `lean_proof` do work towards its conclusion or a substantive intermediate step of Euclid's argument? Also check for artificial hypothesis uses. Judge this unit's uses of the supplied helper signatures; helper bodies are outside this question. Heath's sentences stand as `--` lines and `cited` gives exact enunciations. In Lean, `have h : T := p` proves T by p and calls the result h; `obtain ⟨…⟩ := p` takes p apart into named pieces; `rw [h34, h37, …]` rewrites the goal by the equalities named. Follow uses through helper calls and tactics as well as explicit names. An anonymous binding or an unused hypothesis alone does not establish a defect. If both defects occur, choose `a dummy citation`.

docs/FORMALIZATION.md, section 5:
A checked intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid is legitimate, even if the
  final proof term could do without it.

criteria.cannot tell: What is given here is not enough to decide.
criteria.all do work: Every proposition call supports a later step or the conclusion, or establishes a substantive intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid. No hypothesis is mentioned merely to look used. With no proposition calls the citation part alone is vacuous; hypothesis use must still be inspected.
criteria.a dummy citation: Some proposition call does no substantive work: its result neither supports the argument nor establishes a substantive intermediate fact, and merely supplies a citation while the step is done another way.
criteria.an artificial hypothesis use: No dummy citation is established, but a hypothesis is mentioned only so that it looks used, and does no substantive work.

state.commentary:
I.17, I.18 and I.21 lean on I.16, and I.27 draws its parallels with it. Its proof rests on one step that only the figure supports: "the angle ECD is greater than the angle ECF", by Common Notion 5, the whole greater than the part. For that, Heath says, "it is necessary that CF should always fall within the angle ACD" (vol. 1, p. 280). It need not: "As is well known, this proposition is not universally true under the Riemann hypothesis of a space endless in extent but not infinite in size. On this hypothesis a straight line is a 'closed series' and returns on itself; and two straight lines which have one point of intersection have another point of intersection also" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 280). In that sphere-like geometry, which we met under I.12, a long enough BE brings F round onto CD, making the exterior angle equal to the interior one, and a longer BE carries F past, making it less.

In the plane, the rules of order and sides keep F inside, the very rules that a space whose straight lines return on themselves must give up, and we prove where F falls with them (`Prop16.within`). AC separates B from F, since E lies between them, and B from D, since C does; a straight line has only two sides, so F lies on D's side of AC. And BF, setting out from B on BC, passes through E, off BC, before it reaches F, so F lies on E's side of BC.

Proclus puts the proposition to work at once: "The present proposition enables Proclus to prove what he did not succeed in establishing conclusively in his note on I. 12, namely that *from one point there cannot be drawn to the same straight line three straight lines equal in length*" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 280). Were there three, I.5 in the two isosceles triangles they make would give a triangle an exterior angle equal to an interior and opposite one.

**The modern way.** Put $\mathrm{C} = 0$ and $\mathrm{B} = -1$ in the complex plane, with A at $a$ above them, so that D lies along the positive real axis. The exterior angle ACD is $\arg a$, and the angles at B and A are $\arg(a + 1)$ and $\arg(a/(a + 1))$, all between $0$ and $\pi$. Since $a = (a + 1) \frac{a}{a + 1}$, the first is the sum of the other two. That is I.32, which is not Euclid's route here and does not hold in the hyperbolic plane, where the parallel postulate fails; I.16 is the part of it that holds there too.

therefore the angle BAE is equal to the angle ECF.

therefore the angle ACD is greater than the angle BAE.

/-- In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is greater than either of
the interior and opposite angles. -/
theorem Prop16 {A B C D : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hBCD : Between B C D) :
    ∠ C B A < ∠ A C D ∧ ∠ B A C < ∠ A C D := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle, and let one side of it BC be produced to D;
  -- I say that the exterior angle ACD is greater than either of the interior and opposite
  -- angles CBA, BAC.
  /- Euclid proves the angle BAC less, and then says "similarly" for CBA. So we give
     his argument for every triangle with a side produced, in his letters, and use it
     twice below. It also hands back the point G on AC produced, which the "similarly"
     needs. -/
  have greater : ∀ {A B C D : Point}, Triangle A B C → Between B C D →
      ∃ G : Point, Between A C G ∧ ∠ B A C < ∠ A C D := by
    intro A B C D hABC hBCD
    have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
    have hB_A : B ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₂.symm
    have hD_C : D ≠ C := ne_of_between (between_symm hBCD)
    obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hA_C
    have hB_AC : ¬ OnLine B AC := hABC.acb.off_line hA_AC hC_AC
    -- Let AC be bisected at E [I. 10], and let BE be joined and produced in a straight line to
    -- F;
    obtain ⟨E, hAEC, hAE_EC⟩ := Prop10 hA_C
    have hE_AC : OnLine E AC := on_line_of_between_ends hAEC hA_AC hC_AC
    have hB_E : B ≠ E := fun h => hB_AC (h ▸ hE_AC)
    obtain ⟨BE, hB_BE, hE_BE⟩ := Postulate1 B E hB_E
    /- Produced beyond E to a point X, far enough for I.3 to cut EF off from EX
       (`produce_longer`, as in I.11). -/
    obtain ⟨X, hBEX, hEB_EX⟩ := produce_longer hB_E hB_E.symm
    -- let EF be made equal to BE [I. 3], let FC be joined [Post. 1], and let AC be drawn through
    -- to G [Post. 2].
    obtain ⟨F, hEFX, hEF_BE⟩ :=
      Prop3 (A := E) (B := X) hB_E (by rw [len_symm B E]; exact hEB_EX)
    /- F lies between E and X, so E lies between B and F: BE produced reaches F
       (`between_cut`). -/
    have hBEF : Between B E F := between_cut hBEX hEFX
    have hF_BE : OnLine F BE := on_line_of_between hBEF hB_BE hE_BE
    have hE_F : E ≠ F := (ne_of_between (between_symm hBEF)).symm
    have hF_AC : ¬ OnLine F AC := fun h =>
      hB_AC ((line_unique hE_F hE_BE hF_BE hE_AC h) ▸ hB_BE)
    have hF_C : F ≠ C := fun h => hF_AC (h ▸ hC_AC)
    obtain ⟨FC, hF_FC, hC_FC⟩ := Postulate1 F C hF_C
    obtain ⟨G, -, hACG, -⟩ := Postulate2 hA_AC hC_AC hA_C []
    -- Then, since AE is equal to EC, and BE to EF,
    have hBE_EF : ‖B E‖ = ‖E F‖ := hEF_BE.symm
    -- the two sides AE, EB are equal to the two sides CE, EF respectively;
    have hEA_EC : ‖E A‖ = ‖E C‖ := (len_symm E A).trans hAE_EC
    have hEB_EF : ‖E B‖ = ‖E F‖ := (len_symm E B).trans hBE_EF
    -- and the angle AEB is equal to the angle FEC,
    -- for they are vertical angles. [I. 15]
    /- AC and BF cut one another at E, and B is off AC. -/
    have hAEB_FEC : ∠ A E B = ∠ F E C := (Prop15 hAEC hBEF hABC.acb).1
    -- Therefore the base AB is equal to the base FC,
    /- I.4, applied to the triangles EAB and ECF: E and A, and E and C, lie on AC,
       with B and F off it. -/
    have hE_A : E ≠ A := (ne_of_between hAEC).symm
    have hE_C : E ≠ C := (ne_of_between (between_symm hAEC)).symm
    have hEAB : Triangle E A B := Triangle.of_line hE_AC hA_AC hE_A hB_AC
    have hECF : Triangle E C F := Triangle.of_line hE_AC hC_AC hE_C hF_AC
    have hAEB_CEF : ∠ A E B = ∠ C E F := hAEB_FEC.trans (angle_symm hE_F.symm hE_C.symm)
    obtain ⟨hAB_CF, hEAB_ECF, hEAB_ECF', hEBA_EFC⟩ := Prop4 hEAB hECF hEA_EC hEB_EF hAEB_CEF
    have hAB_FC : ‖A B‖ = ‖F C‖ := hAB_CF.trans (len_symm C F)
    -- and the triangle ABE is equal to the triangle CFE,
    have : △ A B E = △ C F E := by
      rw [area_rotate A B E, area_rotate C F E]
      exact hEAB_ECF
    -- and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those
    -- which the equal sides subtend; [I. 4]
    have : ∠ E B A = ∠ E F C := hEBA_EFC
    -- therefore the angle BAE is equal to the angle ECF.
    have hBAE_ECF : ∠ B A E = ∠ E C F := (angle_symm hB_A hE_A).trans hEAB_ECF'
    -- But the angle ECD is greater than the angle ECF; [C.N. 5]
    /- Heath's figure shows F within the angle ECD (`Prop16.within`), so that the
       angle ECD is made up of the angles ECF and FCD (`angle_add_of_within`), and
       FCD, an angle of the triangle FCD, is something (`Triangle.angle_pos`). The
       whole is greater than the part. -/
    obtain ⟨hFD, hFE⟩ := Prop16.within hABC hBCD hAEC hBEF
    have hECF_ECD : ∠ E C F < ∠ E C D := by
      rw [angle_add_of_within hFD hFE]
      exact CommonNotion5 hFE.triangle.cab.angle_pos
    -- therefore the angle ACD is greater than the angle BAE.
    /- The angle ECD is the angle ACD, since E lies on the ray from C through A
       (`angle_onRay_left`). -/
    have hBAE_ACD : ∠ B A E < ∠ A C D := by
      rw [hBAE_ECF, ← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between (between_symm hAEC)) hD_C]
      exact hECF_ECD
    /- And the angle BAE is the angle BAC, since E lies on the ray from A through C. -/
    have hBAE_BAC : ∠ B A E = ∠ B A C := angle_onRay_right (OnRay.of_between hAEC) hB_A
    exact ⟨G, hACG, hBAE_BAC ▸ hBAE_ACD⟩
  /- Euclid's argument, in his own figure: the angle ACD is greater than the angle BAC,
     and AC is drawn through to G. -/
  obtain ⟨G, hACG, hBAC_ACD⟩ := greater hABC hBCD
  -- Similarly also, if BC be bisected, the angle BCG, that is, the angle ACD [I. 15], can be
  -- proved greater than the angle ABC as well.
  /- The same argument for the triangle BAC, with AC produced to G: now BC is bisected,
     and the exterior angle is BCG. -/
  obtain ⟨-, -, hABC_BCG⟩ := greater hABC.bac hACG
  /- AG and BD cut one another at C, and B is off AG: the vertical angles BCG and
     ACD are equal. [I. 15] -/
  obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hABC.ne₁₃
  have hAGB : Triangle A G B :=
    Triangle.of_line hA_AC (on_line_of_between hACG hA_AC hC_AC) (ne_of_between_ends hACG)
      (hABC.acb.off_line hA_AC hC_AC)
  have hBCG_ACD : ∠ B C G = ∠ A C D := (Prop15 hACG hBCD hAGB).2
  have hCBA_ACD : ∠ C B A < ∠ A C D := by
    rw [angle_symm hABC.ne₂₃.symm hABC.ne₁₂, ← hBCG_ACD]
    exact hABC_BCG
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hCBA_ACD, hBAC_ACD⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

/-- In any triangle two angles taken together in any manner are less than two right angles. -/
theorem Prop17 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) :
    ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∟ + ∟ ∧ ∠ B A C + ∠ A C B < ∟ + ∟ ∧ ∠ C A B + ∠ A B C < ∟ + ∟ := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle;
  -- I say that two angles of the triangle ABC taken together in any manner are less than two
  -- right angles.
  /- "In any manner": any two of the three angles, so three sums. Euclid's argument is
     for the angles ABC, BCA; we give it for every triangle, in his letters, and use
     it for each pair below. -/
  have less : ∀ {A B C : Point}, Triangle A B C → ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∟ + ∟ := by
    intro A B C hABC
    have hA_B : A ≠ B := hABC.ne₁₂
    have hB_C : B ≠ C := hABC.ne₂₃
    have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
    -- For let BC be produced to D. [Post. 2]
    obtain ⟨BC, hB_BC, hC_BC⟩ := Postulate1 B C hB_C
    obtain ⟨D, hD_BC, hBCD, -⟩ := Postulate2 hB_BC hC_BC hB_C []
    -- Then, since the angle ACD is an exterior angle of the triangle ABC,
    -- it is greater than the interior and opposite angle ABC. [I. 16]
    /- I.16 names the interior angle from C, as CBA; it is the angle ABC read the
       other way round (`angle_symm`). -/
    have hABC_ACD : ∠ A B C < ∠ A C D := by
      rw [angle_symm hA_B hB_C.symm]
      exact (Prop16 hABC hBCD).1
    -- Let the angle ACB be added to each;
    /- The same angle added to a greater and a less leaves the first sum greater: no
       Common Notion says so, but a tacit rule of magnitudes does (`add_lt_add_right`,
       System E §3.5). -/
    have hadded : ∠ A B C + ∠ A C B < ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B := add_lt_add_right (∠ A C B) hABC_ACD
    -- therefore the angles ACD, ACB are greater than the angles ABC, BCA.
    /- The angle ACB, added to ABC, is the angle BCA read the other way round. -/
    have hgreater : ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B := by
      rw [angle_symm hB_C hA_C]
      exact hadded
    -- But the angles ACD, ACB are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]
    /- AC stands on BD, which is BC produced; A is off it, since ABC is a triangle
       (`Triangle.off_line`, `Triangle.of_line`). I.13 names the two angles BCA, ACD. -/
    have hA_BC : ¬ OnLine A BC := hABC.bca.off_line hB_BC hC_BC
    have hBDA : Triangle B D A := Triangle.of_line hB_BC hD_BC (ne_of_between_ends hBCD) hA_BC
    have htwo : ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B = ∟ + ∟ := by
      rw [add_comm (∠ A C D), angle_symm hA_C hB_C]
      exact Prop13 hBCD hBDA
    -- Therefore the angles ABC, BCA are less than two right angles.
    rw [← htwo]
    exact hgreater
  /- This is Euclid's own figure, with the angles ABC, BCA. -/
  have hABC_BCA : ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∟ + ∟ := less hABC
  -- Similarly we can prove that the angles BAC, ACB are also less than two right angles, and
  -- so are the angles CAB, ABC as well.
  /- The same argument in the triangle BAC: AC is produced, and the exterior angle at C
     is greater than the angle BAC. And in the triangle CAB: AB is produced, and the
     exterior angle at B is greater than the angle CAB. -/
  have hBAC_ACB : ∠ B A C + ∠ A C B < ∟ + ∟ := less hABC.bac

state.commentary:
Behind Euclid's "taken together in any manner", Heath notes, is the Greek "πάντῃ μεταλαμβανόμεναι, i.e. any pair added together" (vol. 1, p. 282). So our statement names all three pairs, in Euclid's letters. Euclid argues for the first pair and says "similarly" for the others, so we prove his case for any triangle and call on it three times, producing BC, AC and AB in turn. Proclus draws from I.17 at once that there cannot be two perpendiculars from one point to a straight line: they would make a triangle with two right angles (Heath, vol. 1, p. 282).

Heath gives no reference for "Let the angle ACB be added to each", and no Common Notion fits: Common Notion 2 adds equals to equals, not to unequals. The manuscripts and editions add "*If equals be added to unequals, the wholes are unequal*", which J. L. Heiberg prints in brackets and Heath rejects: "(a) stands self-condemned because 'unequal' tells us nothing. It is easy to see what is wanted if we refer to I. 17, where the same angle is added to a *greater* and a *less*, and it is inferred that the first sum is greater than the second" (vol. 1, p. 223). Our proof cites instead the tacit rule from which our Common Notions 3 and 5 are proved, `add_lt_add_right` (System E §3.5): adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than".

Postulate 5 says that straight lines making angles less than two right angles with a third will meet; I.17, that straight lines which meet make such angles. Proclus held this against the postulate: "This ought even to be struck out of the Postulates altogether; for it is a theorem involving many difficulties … And the converse of it is actually proved by Euclid himself as a theorem" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 202). But I.17 is proved without Postulate 5, and holds in the geometry of János Bolyai and Nikolai Lobachevsky, where the postulate fails. In Bernhard Riemann's (see I.16) even I.17 fails: a triangle with a corner at the pole of a straight line and the other two on it has two right angles.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABC be a triangle;

I say that two angles of the triangle ABC taken together in any manner are less than two right angles.

For let BC be produced to D. [Post. 2]

Then, since the angle ACD is an exterior angle of the triangle ABC,

it is greater than the interior and opposite angle ABC. [I. 16]

Let the angle ACB be added to each;

therefore the angles ACD, ACB are greater than the angles ABC, BCA.

But the angles ACD, ACB are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]

Therefore the angles ABC, BCA are less than two right angles.

Similarly we can prove that the angles BAC, ACB are also less than two right angles, and so are the angles CAB, ABC as well.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- In any triangle two angles taken together in any manner are less than two right angles. -/
theorem Prop17 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) :
    ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∟ + ∟ ∧ ∠ B A C + ∠ A C B < ∟ + ∟ ∧ ∠ C A B + ∠ A B C < ∟ + ∟ := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle;
  -- I say that two angles of the triangle ABC taken together in any manner are less than two
  -- right angles.
  /- "In any manner": any two of the three angles, so three sums. Euclid's argument is
     for the angles ABC, BCA; we give it for every triangle, in his letters, and use
     it for each pair below. -/
  have less : ∀ {A B C : Point}, Triangle A B C → ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∟ + ∟ := by
    intro A B C hABC
    have hA_B : A ≠ B := hABC.ne₁₂
    have hB_C : B ≠ C := hABC.ne₂₃
    have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
    -- For let BC be produced to D. [Post. 2]
    obtain ⟨BC, hB_BC, hC_BC⟩ := Postulate1 B C hB_C
    obtain ⟨D, hD_BC, hBCD, -⟩ := Postulate2 hB_BC hC_BC hB_C []
    -- Then, since the angle ACD is an exterior angle of the triangle ABC,
    -- it is greater than the interior and opposite angle ABC. [I. 16]
    /- I.16 names the interior angle from C, as CBA; it is the angle ABC read the
       other way round (`angle_symm`). -/
    have hABC_ACD : ∠ A B C < ∠ A C D := by
      rw [angle_symm hA_B hB_C.symm]
      exact (Prop16 hABC hBCD).1
    -- Let the angle ACB be added to each;
    /- The same angle added to a greater and a less leaves the first sum greater: no
       Common Notion says so, but a tacit rule of magnitudes does (`add_lt_add_right`,
       System E §3.5). -/
    have hadded : ∠ A B C + ∠ A C B < ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B := add_lt_add_right (∠ A C B) hABC_ACD
    -- therefore the angles ACD, ACB are greater than the angles ABC, BCA.
    /- The angle ACB, added to ABC, is the angle BCA read the other way round. -/
    have hgreater : ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B := by
      rw [angle_symm hB_C hA_C]
      exact hadded
    -- But the angles ACD, ACB are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]
    /- AC stands on BD, which is BC produced; A is off it, since ABC is a triangle
       (`Triangle.off_line`, `Triangle.of_line`). I.13 names the two angles BCA, ACD. -/
    have hA_BC : ¬ OnLine A BC := hABC.bca.off_line hB_BC hC_BC
    have hBDA : Triangle B D A := Triangle.of_line hB_BC hD_BC (ne_of_between_ends hBCD) hA_BC
    have htwo : ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B = ∟ + ∟ := by
      rw [add_comm (∠ A C D), angle_symm hA_C hB_C]
      exact Prop13 hBCD hBDA
    -- Therefore the angles ABC, BCA are less than two right angles.
    rw [← htwo]
    exact hgreater
  /- This is Euclid's own figure, with the angles ABC, BCA. -/
  have hABC_BCA : ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∟ + ∟ := less hABC
  -- Similarly we can prove that the angles BAC, ACB are also less than two right angles, and
  -- so are the angles CAB, ABC as well.
  /- The same argument in the triangle BAC: AC is produced, and the exterior angle at C
     is greater than the angle BAC. And in the triangle CAB: AB is produced, and the
     exterior angle at B is greater than the angle CAB. -/
  have hBAC_ACB : ∠ B A C + ∠ A C B < ∟ + ∟ := less hABC.bac
  have hCAB_ABC : ∠ C A B + ∠ A B C < ∟ + ∟ := less hABC.cab
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hABC_BCA, hBAC_ACB, hCAB_ABC⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

  /- I.3 cuts off from AC, beginning at A, a straight line AD equal to AB; D lies
     between A and C. Joining BD is Postulate 1; our proof uses only the points. -/
  obtain ⟨D, hADC, hAD_AB⟩ := Prop3 hA_B h
  have hD_AC : OnLine D AC := on_line_of_between_ends hADC hA_AC hC_AC
  have hD_C : D ≠ C := (ne_of_between (between_symm hADC)).symm
  have hA_D : A ≠ D := ne_of_between hADC
  -- Then, since the angle ADB is an exterior angle of the triangle BCD,
  /- BCD is a triangle, since B is off the straight line AC on which C and D lie;
     and its side CD is produced to A, since D lies between C and A. -/
  have hBCD : Triangle B C D := (Triangle.of_line hC_AC hD_AC hD_C.symm hB_AC).cab
  have hCDA : Between C D A := between_symm hADC
  -- it is greater than the interior and opposite angle DCB. [I. 16]
  have hDCB_BDA : ∠ D C B < ∠ B D A := (Prop16 hBCD hCDA).1
  /- I.16 names the exterior angle BDA; read from the other arm, it is ADB. -/
  have hB_D : B ≠ D := fun e => hB_AC (e ▸ hD_AC)
  have hDCB_ADB : ∠ D C B < ∠ A D B := by
    rw [angle_symm hB_D hA_D] at hDCB_BDA
    exact hDCB_BDA
  -- But the angle ADB is equal to the angle ABD,
  -- since the side AB is equal to AD;
  /- This is I.5 (`Prop5.base`), for the isosceles triangle ABD. -/
  have hABD : Triangle A B D := (Triangle.of_line hA_AC hD_AC hA_D hB_AC).acb
  have hAB_AD : ‖A B‖ = ‖A D‖ := hAD_AB.symm
  have hABD_ADB : ∠ A B D = ∠ A D B := Prop5.base hABD hAB_AD
  -- therefore the angle ABD is also greater than the angle ACB;
  /- The angle DCB is the angle ACB, since D lies on the ray from C through A. -/
  have hDCB_ACB : ∠ D C B = ∠ A C B := angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between hCDA) hB_C
  have hACB_ABD : ∠ A C B < ∠ A B D := by
    rw [← hDCB_ACB, hABD_ADB]
    exact hDCB_ADB
  -- therefore the angle ABC is much greater than the angle ACB.
  /- The angle ABC is made up of ABD and DBC (`angle_add_of_between`), and DBC,
     an angle of the triangle DBC, is something (`Triangle.angle_pos`): the whole
     is greater than the part [C.N. 5]. -/
  have hABD_ABC : ∠ A B D < ∠ A B C := by
    rw [angle_add_of_between hABC.acb hADC]
    exact CommonNotion5 hBCD.cab.angle_pos
  have hACB_ABC : ∠ A C B < ∠ A B C := lt_trans hACB_ABD hABD_ABC
  -- Therefore etc.
  /- The angle ACB is the angle BCA, named from the other arm. -/
  rw [angle_symm hB_C hA_C]
  exact hACB_ABC
  -- Q. E. D.

state.commentary:
I.18 and I.19 say almost the same words in a different order, and Heath gives the rule that tells them apart: "the *datum* comes first and the *quaesitum* second, the *datum* being in this proposition the greater *side* and in the next the greater *angle*" (vol. 1, p. 283), the given before the sought. Aristotle already quotes the result of I.19 "using the exact wording" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 283). To help the student remember which of the two is proved directly, Isaac Todhunter observes that "the order is similar to that in I. 5 and I. 6" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 283): I.18, like I.5, is direct; I.19, like I.6, is a *reductio*.

**"Much greater."** Euclid's two words carry two steps, and his figure hides both. BD falls within the angle ABC, because I.3 put D between A and C, so the angle ABD is only a part of ABC; and what is greater than the greater is greater still, a tacit rule of magnitudes. We prove both. The figure also spares us a step: CD runs on to A, so the angle DCB that I.16 gives is the triangle's own angle ACB. Porphyry's proof, which Heath gives from Proclus, "starts by supposing a length equal to AB cut off from the other end of AC; that is, CD and not AD is made equal to AB" (vol. 1, p. 283), and it too ends by going from greater to greater still, which Heath marks *a fortiori*.

**The modern way.** Name the sides $a = \mathrm{BC}$, $b = \mathrm{CA}$ and $c = \mathrm{AB}$. The law of cosines gives $\cos \mathrm{C} - \cos \mathrm{B} = (b - c)(b + c - a)(a + b + c)/(2abc)$, and $b + c$ is greater than $a$ (that is I.20), so when $b \gt c$, $\cos \mathrm{B} \lt \cos \mathrm{C}$ and the angle B is the greater.
state.heath_proof:
For let ABC be a triangle having the side AC greater than AB;

I say that the angle ABC is also greater than the angle BCA.

For, since AC is greater than AB, let AD be made equal to AB [I. 3], and let BD be joined.

Then, since the angle ADB is an exterior angle of the triangle BCD,

it is greater than the interior and opposite angle DCB. [I. 16]

But the angle ADB is equal to the angle ABD,

since the side AB is equal to AD;

therefore the angle ABD is also greater than the angle ACB;

therefore the angle ABC is much greater than the angle ACB.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

  -- For let ABC be a triangle having the side AC greater than AB;
  have hA_B : A ≠ B := hABC.ne₁₂
  have hB_C : B ≠ C := hABC.ne₂₃
  have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
  obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hA_C
  have hB_AC : ¬ OnLine B AC := hABC.acb.off_line hA_AC hC_AC
  -- I say that the angle ABC is also greater than the angle BCA.
  -- For, since AC is greater than AB, let AD be made equal to AB [I. 3], and let BD be joined.
  /- I.3 cuts off from AC, beginning at A, a straight line AD equal to AB; D lies
     between A and C. Joining BD is Postulate 1; our proof uses only the points. -/
  obtain ⟨D, hADC, hAD_AB⟩ := Prop3 hA_B h
  have hD_AC : OnLine D AC := on_line_of_between_ends hADC hA_AC hC_AC
  have hD_C : D ≠ C := (ne_of_between (between_symm hADC)).symm
  have hA_D : A ≠ D := ne_of_between hADC
  -- Then, since the angle ADB is an exterior angle of the triangle BCD,
  /- BCD is a triangle, since B is off the straight line AC on which C and D lie;
     and its side CD is produced to A, since D lies between C and A. -/
  have hBCD : Triangle B C D := (Triangle.of_line hC_AC hD_AC hD_C.symm hB_AC).cab
  have hCDA : Between C D A := between_symm hADC
  -- it is greater than the interior and opposite angle DCB. [I. 16]
  have hDCB_BDA : ∠ D C B < ∠ B D A := (Prop16 hBCD hCDA).1
  /- I.16 names the exterior angle BDA; read from the other arm, it is ADB. -/
  have hB_D : B ≠ D := fun e => hB_AC (e ▸ hD_AC)
  have hDCB_ADB : ∠ D C B < ∠ A D B := by
    rw [angle_symm hB_D hA_D] at hDCB_BDA
    exact hDCB_BDA
  -- But the angle ADB is equal to the angle ABD,
  -- since the side AB is equal to AD;
  /- This is I.5 (`Prop5.base`), for the isosceles triangle ABD. -/
  have hABD : Triangle A B D := (Triangle.of_line hA_AC hD_AC hA_D hB_AC).acb
  have hAB_AD : ‖A B‖ = ‖A D‖ := hAD_AB.symm
  have hABD_ADB : ∠ A B D = ∠ A D B := Prop5.base hABD hAB_AD
  -- therefore the angle ABD is also greater than the angle ACB;
  /- The angle DCB is the angle ACB, since D lies on the ray from C through A. -/
  have hDCB_ACB : ∠ D C B = ∠ A C B := angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between hCDA) hB_C
  have hACB_ABD : ∠ A C B < ∠ A B D := by
    rw [← hDCB_ACB, hABD_ADB]
    exact hDCB_ADB
  -- therefore the angle ABC is much greater than the angle ACB.
  /- The angle ABC is made up of ABD and DBC (`angle_add_of_between`), and DBC,
     an angle of the triangle DBC, is something (`Triangle.angle_pos`): the whole
     is greater than the part [C.N. 5]. -/
  have hABD_ABC : ∠ A B D < ∠ A B C := by
    rw [angle_add_of_between hABC.acb hADC]
    exact CommonNotion5 hBCD.cab.angle_pos
  have hACB_ABC : ∠ A C B < ∠ A B C := lt_trans hACB_ABD hABD_ABC
  -- Therefore etc.
  /- The angle ACB is the angle BCA, named from the other arm. -/
  rw [angle_symm hB_C hA_C]
  exact hACB_ABC

state.lean_proof:
/-- In any triangle the greater angle is subtended by the greater side. -/
theorem Prop19 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (h : ∠ B C A < ∠ A B C) :
    ‖A B‖ < ‖A C‖ := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC greater than the angle BCA;
  /- Euclid names the less angle BCA here and ACB below. They are one angle,
     read from either arm (`angle_symm`, System E's Metric 4). -/
  have hBCA_ACB : ∠ B C A = ∠ A C B := angle_symm hABC.ne₂₃ hABC.ne₁₃
  have hACB_ABC : ∠ A C B < ∠ A B C := hBCA_ACB ▸ h
  -- I say that the side AC is also greater than the side AB.
  -- For, if not, AC is either equal to AB or less.
  /- That a length not greater than another is equal to it or less is the tacit
     rule of magnitudes `lt_trichotomy` (System E §3.5). -/
  have either : ¬ ‖A B‖ < ‖A C‖ → ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ ∨ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ := by
    intro hnot
    rcases lt_trichotomy ‖A C‖ ‖A B‖ with hlt | heq | hgt
    · exact Or.inr hlt
    · exact Or.inl heq
    · exact absurd hgt hnot
  -- Now AC is not equal to AB;
  have not_equal : ‖A C‖ ≠ ‖A B‖ := by
    intro hAC_AB
    -- for then the angle ABC would also have been equal to the angle ACB; [I. 5]
    have hABC_ACB : ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B := Prop5.base hABC hAC_AB.symm
    -- but it is not;
    /- It is greater: the hypothesis, with BCA read as ACB. -/
    have hne : ∠ A B C ≠ ∠ A C B := fun heq => Magnitude.ne_of_lt hACB_ABC heq.symm
    -- therefore AC is not equal to AB.
    exact hne hABC_ACB
  -- Neither is AC less than AB,
  have not_less : ¬ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ := by
    intro hAC_AB
    -- for then the angle ABC would also have been less than the angle ACB; [I. 18]
    /- This is I.18 for the triangle ACB, whose side AB is the greater. It hands
       back the angle CBA, which is the angle ABC read from the other arm. -/
    have hABC_ACB : ∠ A B C < ∠ A C B := by
      have hI18 : ∠ C B A < ∠ A C B := Prop18 hABC.acb hAC_AB
      rw [angle_symm hABC.ne₂₃.symm hABC.ne₁₂] at hI18
      exact hI18
    -- but it is not;
    /- It is greater, and a magnitude cannot be both less and greater than
       another (`lt_trans`, `lt_irrefl`). -/
    have hnot : ¬ ∠ A B C < ∠ A C B := fun hlt => lt_irrefl _ (lt_trans hlt hACB_ABC)
    -- therefore AC is not less than AB.
    exact hnot hABC_ACB
  -- And it was proved that it is not equal either.
  /- Both ways out are closed; Euclid's division is complete. -/
  have neither : ¬ (‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ ∨ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖) := fun hor =>
    hor.elim not_equal not_less
  -- Therefore AC is greater than AB.
  /- Reductio ad absurdum: were AC not greater, the division above would make it
     equal or less, and it is neither. -/
  exact Classical.byContradiction fun hnot => neither (either hnot)
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.

state.commentary:
I.19 turns I.18 round, as I.6 turns I.5 round. "Here, says Proclus (p. 318, 16–23), Euclid proves the impossibility 'by means of *division*' (ἐκ διαιρέσεως). This means simply the separation of different hypotheses, each of which is inconsistent with the truth of the theorem to be proved, and which therefore must be successively shown to be impossible" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 285). If AC is not greater than AB, it is equal to it or less; I.5 shuts the first way out and I.18 the second. The division is itself a tacit rule of magnitudes, which our proof cites (`lt_trichotomy`): of two lengths, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. And where Euclid's hypothesis calls the less angle BCA and his argument calls it ACB, our proof says that they are one angle (`angle_symm`).

Could logic alone do it? Augustus De Morgan thought so: I.19, "like I. 6, can be proved by merely *logical* deduction from I. 5 and I. 18 taken together" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 284). Of three assertions X, Y, Z, "one or the other must be true, *and one only*", and so too of three more, P, Q, R. If X brings P, Y brings Q and Z brings R, then "it follows that, when P is true, X is true, when Q is true, Y is true, when R is true, Z is true" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 284). Here X, Y, Z compare AC with AB, P, Q, R the angles at B and C, and I.5 and I.18 are the links. Proclus also has a direct proof, which an-Nairīzī attributes to Heron, built on a lemma about the bisector of an angle; Heath finds it "open to the slight objection of separating a theorem from its converse. But the lemma and proof are worth giving" (vol. 1, p. 285).

**The modern way.** Put $\mathrm{B} = (0, 0)$, $\mathrm{C} = (a, 0)$ and $\mathrm{A} = (x, y)$ with $a \gt 0$ and $y \gt 0$. Then $\cot \mathrm{B} = x/y$ and $\cot \mathrm{C} = (a - x)/y$, so the angle at B is the greater exactly when $x \lt a/2$; and $\mathrm{AC}^2 - \mathrm{AB}^2 = a(a - 2x)$, so AC is the greater exactly then too: I.18 and I.19 in one line.

state.heath_proof:
Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC greater than the angle BCA;

I say that the side AC is also greater than the side AB.

For, if not, AC is either equal to AB or less.

Now AC is not equal to AB;

for then the angle ABC would also have been equal to the angle ACB; [I. 5]

but it is not;

therefore AC is not equal to AB.

Neither is AC less than AB,

for then the angle ABC would also have been less than the angle ACB; [I. 18]

but it is not;

therefore AC is not less than AB.

And it was proved that it is not equal either.

Therefore AC is greater than AB.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

state.heath_proof:
For let ABC be a triangle;

I say that in the triangle ABC two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one, namely

BA, AC greater than BC,

AB, BC greater than AC,

BC, CA greater than AB.

For let BA be drawn through to the point D,

let DA be made equal to CA, and let DC be joined.

Then, since DA is equal to AC,

the angle ADC is also equal to the angle ACD; [I. 5]

therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC. [C.N. 5]

And, since DCB is a triangle having the angle BCD greater than the angle BDC,

and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]

therefore DB is greater than BC.

But DA is equal to AC;

therefore BA, AC are greater than BC.

Similarly we can prove that AB, BC are also greater than CA, and BC, CA than AB.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

state.heath_proof:

the angle ADC is also equal to the angle ACD; [I. 5]

therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC. [C.N. 5]

And, since DCB is a triangle having the angle BCD greater than the angle BDC,

and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]

therefore DB is greater than BC.

state.lean_proof:
/-- In any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one. -/
theorem Prop20 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) :
    ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ + ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖A B‖ < ‖B C‖ + ‖C A‖ := by
  -- For let ABC be a triangle;
  -- I say that in the triangle ABC two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the
  -- remaining one, namely
  -- BA, AC greater than BC,
  -- AB, BC greater than AC,
  -- BC, CA greater than AB.
  /- Euclid proves the first, and says "similarly" for the other two. So we give his
     argument for every triangle, in his letters, and use it three times below. -/
  have greater : ∀ {A B C : Point}, Triangle A B C → ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := by
    intro A B C hABC
    have hB_A : B ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₂.symm
    have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
    obtain ⟨BA, hB_BA, hA_BA⟩ := Postulate1 B A hB_A
    have hC_BA : ¬ OnLine C BA := hABC.bac.off_line hB_BA hA_BA
    -- For let BA be drawn through to the point D,
    /- Drawn through beyond A to a point X, far enough for I.3 to cut AD off from AX
       (`produce_longer`, as in I.11). -/
    obtain ⟨X, hBAX, hAC_AX⟩ := produce_longer hB_A hA_C
    -- let DA be made equal to CA, and let DC be joined.
    /- Heath gives no bracket here, but "let DA be made equal" is I.3's work, as in
       I.11 and I.16: cut off AD from AX. Then D lies between A and X, and so A lies
       between B and D (`between_cut`): BA drawn through reaches D. -/
    obtain ⟨D, hADX, hAD_CA⟩ := Prop3 (A := A) (B := X) hA_C.symm
      (by rw [len_symm C A]; exact hAC_AX)
    have hBAD : Between B A D := between_cut hBAX hADX
    have hD_BA : OnLine D BA := on_line_of_between hBAD hB_BA hA_BA
    have hA_D : A ≠ D := ne_of_between hADX
    have hD_C : D ≠ C := fun e => hC_BA (e ▸ hD_BA)
    obtain ⟨DC, hD_DC, hC_DC⟩ := Postulate1 D C hD_C
    -- Then, since DA is equal to AC,
    have hDA_AC : ‖D A‖ = ‖A C‖ := by rw [len_symm D A, hAD_CA, len_symm C A]
    -- the angle ADC is also equal to the angle ACD; [I. 5]
    have hADC : Triangle A D C := Triangle.of_line hA_BA hD_BA hA_D hC_BA
    have hADC_ACD : ∠ A D C = ∠ A C D :=
      Prop5.base hADC (by rw [← len_symm D A]; exact hDA_AC)
    -- therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC. [C.N. 5]
    /- Greater than the angle ACD, which is equal to it: CA falls within the angle
       BCD, since A lies between B and D, so that the angle BCD is made up of the
       angles BCA and ACD (`angle_add_of_between`); the angle BCA, an angle of the
       triangle ABC, is something (`Triangle.angle_pos`); and the whole is greater
       than the part. -/
    have hBDC : Triangle B D C :=
      Triangle.of_line hB_BA hD_BA (ne_of_between_ends hBAD) hC_BA
    have hADC_BCD : ∠ A D C < ∠ B C D := by
      rw [hADC_ACD, angle_add_of_between hBDC hBAD, add_comm]
      exact CommonNotion5 hABC.bca.angle_pos
    -- And, since DCB is a triangle having the angle BCD greater than the angle BDC,
    /- The angle BDC is the angle ADC, since A lies on the ray from D through B
       (`angle_onRay_left`). -/
    have hDCB : Triangle D C B := hBDC.bca
    have hBDC_BCD : ∠ B D C < ∠ B C D := by
      rw [← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between (between_symm hBAD)) hD_C.symm]
      exact hADC_BCD
    -- and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]
    /- I.19 for the triangle BCD, named from B: the angle at C is greater than the
       angle at D, so the side BD, opposite C, is greater than the side BC, opposite
       D. -/
    have hBC_BD : ‖B C‖ < ‖B D‖ :=
      Prop19 hDCB.cba (by rw [angle_symm hD_C.symm (ne_of_between_ends hBAD)]; exact hBDC_BCD)
    -- therefore DB is greater than BC.
    have hBC_DB : ‖B C‖ < ‖D B‖ := by rw [len_symm D B]; exact hBC_BD
    -- But DA is equal to AC;
    /- And DB is BA and AD together, since A lies between B and D (System E,
       Diagram-segment 1); so DB is BA and AC together. -/
    have hDB : ‖D B‖ = ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := by
      rw [← hDA_AC, len_symm D A, len_add_of_between hBAD, len_symm D B]
    -- therefore BA, AC are greater than BC.
    rw [← hDB]
    exact hBC_DB
  /- Euclid's argument, in his own figure: BA, AC are greater than BC. -/
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := greater hABC
  -- Similarly we can prove that AB, BC are also greater than CA, and BC, CA than AB.
  /- The same argument for the triangle BAC, with AB drawn through beyond B, and for
     the triangle CBA, with BC drawn through beyond C. -/
  have hAC : ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ + ‖B C‖ := greater hABC.bac
  have hAB : ‖A B‖ < ‖B C‖ + ‖C A‖ := by
    rw [len_symm A B]
    exact greater hABC.cba
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hBC, hAC, hAB⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop3:
/-- Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the
less. -/
theorem Prop3 {A B C₁ C₂ : Point} (hC : C₁ ≠ C₂) (h : ‖C₁ C₂‖ < ‖A B‖) :
    ∃ E : Point, Between A E B ∧ ‖A E‖ = ‖C₁ C₂‖
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop5:
/-- In isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal
straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop5 {A B C D E : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖)
    (hD : Between A B D) (hE : Between A C E) :
    ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B ∧ ∠ C B D = ∠ B C E
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop5.base:
/-- The angles at the base, and only those. Our I.5 is stated as Euclid states it,
with the equal sides produced and the angles under the base as well, so a proof that
cites it must first produce AB and AC (Post. 2). When only the angles at the base are
wanted, as in I.7, I.9, I.18, I.19, I.20 and I.24, any points beyond B and C
will do, and this produces them once. [I. 5] -/
theorem Prop5.base {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (h : ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖) :
    ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B
helper_signatures.Elements.CommonNotion5:
/-- **Common Notion 5.** The whole is greater than the part: if `b` is something
(not nothing), then `a + b` is greater than `a`. -/
theorem CommonNotion5 {a b : Magnitude k} (h : 0 < b) : a < a + b

theorem OnRay.of_between (h : Between A P B) : OnRay P A B
helper_signatures.Elements.OnRay.symm:

theorem Triangle.cba (h : Triangle A B C) : Triangle C B A

theorem Triangle.ne₁₂ (h : Triangle A B C) : A ≠ B
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.ne₁₃:

theorem Triangle.ne₁₃ (h : Triangle A B C) : A ≠ C
helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.of_line:

theorem Triangle.of_line {P Q R : Point} (hP : OnLine P L) (hQ : OnLine Q L) (hPQ : P ≠ Q)

helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.off_line:

helper_signatures.Elements.angle_add_of_between:

falls within the angle PVQ, and that angle is made up of the angles PVR and
RVQ. (System E, Pasch 2 and Diagram-angle 2) -/
theorem angle_add_of_between {V P Q R : Point} (hPQV : Triangle P Q V) (h : Between P R Q) :
    ∠ P V Q = ∠ P V R + ∠ R V Q
helper_signatures.Elements.angle_onRay_left:
/-- One arm traced through another point of its ray: if B' is on the ray from A
through B, the angle B'AC is the angle BAC. (System E, Diagram-angle 4) -/
theorem angle_onRay_left {B' : Point} (hB : OnRay B' A B) (hCA : C ≠ A) :
    ∠ B' A C = ∠ B A C
helper_signatures.Elements.between_cut:
/-- Cutting off beyond a point: if B is between A and C, and D between B and
C, then B is between A and D. This is the step after "let CE be made equal to
CD [I. 3]" on a straight line produced: what is cut off from BC still lies beyond
B. -/
theorem between_cut (h₁ : Between A B C) (h₂ : Between B D C) : Between A B D
helper_signatures.Elements.produce_longer:
/-- Room to cut off. A finite straight line AB can be produced beyond B further
than a given straight line BC from B. Postulate 2 produces a straight line but
never says how far, and I.3 cuts off only from a *greater* straight line; so Euclid's
"let CE be made equal to CD [I. 3]", on a straight line produced, needs this first
(I.11, I.16, I.20, I.22). Describe the circle with centre B and distance BC
[Post. 3]; the straight line AB, produced beyond the centre, cuts it at some Y
(System E, Intersections 5); and BY, produced a little further still to X
[Post. 2], is greater than BY, that is, than BC [Def. 15, C.N. 5]. -/
theorem produce_longer (hAB : A ≠ B) (hBC : B ≠ C) :
    ∃ X : Point, Between A B X ∧ ‖B C‖ < ‖B X‖

state.commentary:
"It was the habit of the Epicureans, says Proclus (p. 322), to ridicule this theorem as being evident even to an ass and requiring no proof" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 287). Put fodder at one corner of a triangle and the ass at another, and he walks the one side between them, not the other two. Henry Savile exclaimed that they were "digni ipsi, qui cum Asino foenum essent" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 287), fit to eat hay with the ass themselves. "Proclus replies truly that a mere perception of the truth of the theorem is a different thing from a scientific proof of it and a knowledge of the reason *why* it is true. Moreover, as Simson says, the number of axioms should not be increased without necessity" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 287). We take Robert Simson's side: no tacit rule of ours states the theorem, so I.20 is proved, as Euclid proves it, from I.5 and I.19.

Heath's reference for "the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC" is Common Notion 5, the whole greater than the part: BCD is greater than ACD, which I.5 has just made equal to ADC. That needs CA to fall within the angle BCD, and we say why: A lies between B and D, where Euclid put it when he drew BA through to D. Heron and Porphyry, Heath reports from Proclus, "proved this theorem in different ways … without producing one of the sides" (vol. 1, p. 287). The first of the two Heath gives, in a figure of its own, bisects the angle BAC by AD, meeting BC at D; then AC is greater than CD, and AB than BD (I.16 and I.19), and adding gives the theorem.

**The modern way.** For vectors, $|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + 2 \thinspace \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} + |\mathbf{v}|^2$, and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \le |\mathbf{u}| \thinspace |\mathbf{v}|$ makes this at most $(|\mathbf{u}| + |\mathbf{v}|)^2$, with equality only when $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ point the same way. In the complex plane it reads $|z + w| \le |z| + |w|$, and what Euclid proves, the theory of metric spaces takes as part of the definition of distance: the triangle inequality.
state.heath_proof:
For let ABC be a triangle;

I say that in the triangle ABC two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one, namely

BA, AC greater than BC,

AB, BC greater than AC,

BC, CA greater than AB.

For let BA be drawn through to the point D,

let DA be made equal to CA, and let DC be joined.

Then, since DA is equal to AC,

the angle ADC is also equal to the angle ACD; [I. 5]

therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC. [C.N. 5]

And, since DCB is a triangle having the angle BCD greater than the angle BDC,

and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]

therefore DB is greater than BC.

But DA is equal to AC;

therefore BA, AC are greater than BC.

Similarly we can prove that AB, BC are also greater than CA, and BC, CA than AB.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- In any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one. -/
theorem Prop20 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) :
    ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ + ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖A B‖ < ‖B C‖ + ‖C A‖ := by
  -- For let ABC be a triangle;
  -- I say that in the triangle ABC two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the
  -- remaining one, namely
  -- BA, AC greater than BC,
  -- AB, BC greater than AC,
  -- BC, CA greater than AB.
  /- Euclid proves the first, and says "similarly" for the other two. So we give his
     argument for every triangle, in his letters, and use it three times below. -/
  have greater : ∀ {A B C : Point}, Triangle A B C → ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := by
    intro A B C hABC
    have hB_A : B ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₂.symm
    have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
    obtain ⟨BA, hB_BA, hA_BA⟩ := Postulate1 B A hB_A
    have hC_BA : ¬ OnLine C BA := hABC.bac.off_line hB_BA hA_BA
    -- For let BA be drawn through to the point D,
    /- Drawn through beyond A to a point X, far enough for I.3 to cut AD off from AX
       (`produce_longer`, as in I.11). -/
    obtain ⟨X, hBAX, hAC_AX⟩ := produce_longer hB_A hA_C
    -- let DA be made equal to CA, and let DC be joined.
    /- Heath gives no bracket here, but "let DA be made equal" is I.3's work, as in
       I.11 and I.16: cut off AD from AX. Then D lies between A and X, and so A lies
       between B and D (`between_cut`): BA drawn through reaches D. -/
    obtain ⟨D, hADX, hAD_CA⟩ := Prop3 (A := A) (B := X) hA_C.symm
      (by rw [len_symm C A]; exact hAC_AX)
    have hBAD : Between B A D := between_cut hBAX hADX
    have hD_BA : OnLine D BA := on_line_of_between hBAD hB_BA hA_BA
    have hA_D : A ≠ D := ne_of_between hADX
    have hD_C : D ≠ C := fun e => hC_BA (e ▸ hD_BA)
    obtain ⟨DC, hD_DC, hC_DC⟩ := Postulate1 D C hD_C
    -- Then, since DA is equal to AC,
    have hDA_AC : ‖D A‖ = ‖A C‖ := by rw [len_symm D A, hAD_CA, len_symm C A]
    -- the angle ADC is also equal to the angle ACD; [I. 5]
    have hADC : Triangle A D C := Triangle.of_line hA_BA hD_BA hA_D hC_BA
    have hADC_ACD : ∠ A D C = ∠ A C D :=
      Prop5.base hADC (by rw [← len_symm D A]; exact hDA_AC)
    -- therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC. [C.N. 5]
    /- Greater than the angle ACD, which is equal to it: CA falls within the angle
       BCD, since A lies between B and D, so that the angle BCD is made up of the
       angles BCA and ACD (`angle_add_of_between`); the angle BCA, an angle of the
       triangle ABC, is something (`Triangle.angle_pos`); and the whole is greater
       than the part. -/
    have hBDC : Triangle B D C :=
      Triangle.of_line hB_BA hD_BA (ne_of_between_ends hBAD) hC_BA
    have hADC_BCD : ∠ A D C < ∠ B C D := by
      rw [hADC_ACD, angle_add_of_between hBDC hBAD, add_comm]
      exact CommonNotion5 hABC.bca.angle_pos
    -- And, since DCB is a triangle having the angle BCD greater than the angle BDC,
    /- The angle BDC is the angle ADC, since A lies on the ray from D through B
       (`angle_onRay_left`). -/
    have hDCB : Triangle D C B := hBDC.bca
    have hBDC_BCD : ∠ B D C < ∠ B C D := by
      rw [← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between (between_symm hBAD)) hD_C.symm]
      exact hADC_BCD
    -- and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]
    /- I.19 for the triangle BCD, named from B: the angle at C is greater than the
       angle at D, so the side BD, opposite C, is greater than the side BC, opposite
       D. -/
    have hBC_BD : ‖B C‖ < ‖B D‖ :=
      Prop19 hDCB.cba (by rw [angle_symm hD_C.symm (ne_of_between_ends hBAD)]; exact hBDC_BCD)
    -- therefore DB is greater than BC.
    have hBC_DB : ‖B C‖ < ‖D B‖ := by rw [len_symm D B]; exact hBC_BD
    -- But DA is equal to AC;
    /- And DB is BA and AD together, since A lies between B and D (System E,
       Diagram-segment 1); so DB is BA and AC together. -/
    have hDB : ‖D B‖ = ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := by
      rw [← hDA_AC, len_symm D A, len_add_of_between hBAD, len_symm D B]
    -- therefore BA, AC are greater than BC.
    rw [← hDB]
    exact hBC_DB
  /- Euclid's argument, in his own figure: BA, AC are greater than BC. -/
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := greater hABC
  -- Similarly we can prove that AB, BC are also greater than CA, and BC, CA than AB.
  /- The same argument for the triangle BAC, with AB drawn through beyond B, and for
     the triangle CBA, with BC drawn through beyond C. -/
  have hAC : ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ + ‖B C‖ := greater hABC.bac
  have hAB : ‖A B‖ < ‖B C‖ + ‖C A‖ := by
    rw [len_symm A B]
    exact greater hABC.cba
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hBC, hAC, hAB⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

/-- If on one of the sides of a triangle, from its extremities, there be constructed two straight
lines meeting within the triangle, the straight lines so constructed will be less than the
remaining two sides of the triangle, but will contain a greater angle. -/
theorem Prop21 {A B C D : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hD : InsideTriangle D A B C) :
    ‖B D‖ + ‖D C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ ∧ ∠ B A C < ∠ B D C := by
  -- On BC, one of the sides of the triangle ABC, from its extremities B, C, let the two
  -- straight lines BD, DC be constructed meeting within the triangle;
  /- The statement hands us D within the triangle. -/
  -- I say that BD, DC are less than the remaining two sides of the triangle BA, AC, but
  -- contain an angle BDC greater than the angle BAC.
  -- For let BD be drawn through to E.
  /- BD produced crosses AC at E, beyond D: see `Prop21.through`. -/
  obtain ⟨E, hBDE, hAEC⟩ := Prop21.through hD
  /- B is off AC, since ABC is a triangle. And C is off BE: else BE would be BC,
     and D, which is on A's side of BC, would lie on it. -/
  obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hABC.ne₁₃
  have hE_AC : OnLine E AC := on_line_of_between_ends hAEC hA_AC hC_AC
  have hB_AC : ¬ OnLine B AC := hABC.acb.off_line hA_AC hC_AC
  have hA_E : A ≠ E := ne_of_between hAEC
  have hB_E : B ≠ E := ne_of_between_ends hBDE
  have hD_E : D ≠ E := (ne_of_between (between_symm hBDE)).symm
  obtain ⟨BE, hB_BE, hE_BE⟩ := Postulate1 B E hB_E
  have hD_BE : OnLine D BE := on_line_of_between_ends hBDE hB_BE hE_BE
  have hC_BE : ¬ OnLine C BE := by
    intro hC
    obtain ⟨BC, hB_BC, hC_BC⟩ := Postulate1 B C hABC.ne₂₃
    have hD_BC : ¬ OnLine D BC := not_on_line_of_same_side (hD.1.sameSide hB_BC hC_BC)
    exact hD_BC (line_unique hABC.ne₂₃ hB_BE hC hB_BC hC_BC ▸ hD_BE)
  /- So ABE and CED are triangles. -/
  have hAEB : Triangle A E B := Triangle.of_line hA_AC hE_AC hA_E hB_AC
  have hEDC : Triangle E D C := Triangle.of_line hE_BE hD_BE hD_E.symm hC_BE
  -- Then, since in any triangle two sides are greater than the remaining one, [I. 20]
  -- therefore, in the triangle ABE, the two sides AB, AE are greater than BE.
  have hBE_lt : ‖B E‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A E‖ := (Prop20 hAEB.acb).1
  -- Let EC be added to each;
  have hBEC : ‖B E‖ + ‖E C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A E‖ + ‖E C‖ := add_lt_add_right ‖E C‖ hBE_lt
  -- therefore BA, AC are greater than BE, EC.
  /- AE and EC together make up AC, since E lies between A and C. -/
  have hBA_AC : ‖B E‖ + ‖E C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := by
    rw [← len_add_of_between hAEC, ← add_assoc]
    exact hBEC
  -- Again, since, in the triangle CED,
  have hCED : Triangle C E D := hEDC.cab
  -- the two sides CE, ED are greater than CD,
  have hCD_lt : ‖C D‖ < ‖C E‖ + ‖E D‖ := (Prop20 hCED).2.1
  -- let DB be added to each;
  have hCDB : ‖C D‖ + ‖D B‖ < ‖C E‖ + ‖E D‖ + ‖D B‖ := add_lt_add_right ‖D B‖ hCD_lt
  -- therefore CE, EB are greater than CD, DB.
  /- ED and DB together make up EB, since D lies between E and B. -/
  have hCE_EB : ‖C D‖ + ‖D B‖ < ‖C E‖ + ‖E B‖ := by
    rw [← len_add_of_between (between_symm hBDE), ← add_assoc]
    exact hCDB
  -- But BA, AC were proved greater than BE, EC;
  have : ‖B E‖ + ‖E C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := hBA_AC
  -- therefore BA, AC are much greater than BD, DC.
  /- BD, DC are CD, DB taken the other way round, and BE, EC are CE, EB. -/
  have hsides : ‖B D‖ + ‖D C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := by
    have h₁ : ‖B D‖ + ‖D C‖ = ‖C D‖ + ‖D B‖ := by
      rw [add_comm, len_symm D C, len_symm B D]
    have h₂ : ‖C E‖ + ‖E B‖ = ‖B E‖ + ‖E C‖ := by
      rw [add_comm, len_symm C E, len_symm E B]
    rw [h₁]
    exact lt_trans (h₂ ▸ hCE_EB) hBA_AC
  -- Again, since in any triangle the exterior angle is greater than the interior and opposite
  -- angle, [I. 16]
  -- therefore, in the triangle CDE,
  /- In the triangle CDE the side ED is produced to B. -/
  have hEDB : Between E D B := between_symm hBDE
  -- the exterior angle BDC is greater than the angle CED.
  /- I.16 reads both angles the other way round, as DEC and CDB. -/
  have hCED_BDC : ∠ C E D < ∠ B D C := by
    rw [angle_symm (ne_of_between (between_symm hAEC)) hD_E,
      angle_symm (ne_of_between hBDE) hEDC.ne₂₃.symm]
    exact (Prop16 hCED hEDB).1
  -- For the same reason, moreover, in the triangle ABE also,
  /- In the triangle ABE the side AE is produced to C. -/
  have hBAE : Triangle B A E := hAEB.cab
  -- the exterior angle CEB is greater than the angle BAC.
  /- I.16 gives the angle EAB less than BEC. The angle EAB, read the other way
     round, is BAE, and that is the angle BAC, since E lies on the ray from A
     through C. -/
  have hBAC_CEB : ∠ B A C < ∠ C E B := by
    rw [← angle_onRay_right (OnRay.of_between hAEC) hABC.ne₁₂.symm,
      angle_symm hABC.ne₁₂.symm hA_E.symm,
      angle_symm (ne_of_between (between_symm hAEC)) hB_E]
    exact (Prop16 hBAE hAEC).1
  -- But the angle BDC was proved greater than the angle CEB;
  /- The angle CED is the angle CEB, since D lies on the ray from E through
     B. -/
  have hCEB_BDC : ∠ C E B < ∠ B D C := by
    rw [← angle_onRay_right (OnRay.of_between hEDB) (ne_of_between (between_symm hAEC))]
    exact hCED_BDC
  -- therefore the angle BDC is much greater than the angle BAC.
  have hangle : ∠ B A C < ∠ B D C := lt_trans hBAC_CEB hCEB_BDC
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hsides, hangle⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/

/-- In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is greater than either of

/-- In any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one. -/

    ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ + ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖A B‖ < ‖B C‖ + ‖C A‖
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop21.through:
/-- "Let BD be drawn through to E." In Euclid's figure BD, produced beyond D,
meets the side AC at a point E between A and C.

It meets it because D lies within the angle ABC (on C's side of BA and on
A's side of BC), so the ray from B through D crosses AC (`crossbar`). And
D falls short of E, rather than beyond it: E is on AC, while B and D are
on one side of AC, so E cannot lie between them (System E, Pasch 3); and B is
not between D and E, since E is on the ray from B through D. Of three points
on a straight line one is between the other two (Between 6), so it is D. -/
theorem Prop21.through {A B C D : Point} (hD : InsideTriangle D A B C) :
    ∃ E : Point, Between B D E ∧ Between A E C

triangle. -/

helper_signatures.Elements.angle_onRay_right:
/-- The other arm traced through another point of its ray: if C' is on the ray
from A through C, the angle BAC' is the angle BAC. (System E,
Diagram-angle 4) -/
theorem angle_onRay_right {C' : Point} (hC : OnRay C' A C) (hBA : B ≠ A) :
    ∠ B A C' = ∠ B A C
helper_signatures.Elements.crossbar:
/-- A straight line drawn from the corner of an angle through a point within it
crosses every finite straight line joining the two arms. If D lies within the
angle BAC (on C's side of AB and on B's side of AC), the ray from A
through D meets BC at a point X between B and C.

Euclid uses this without a word in I.10, where the bisector CD of the angle
ACB meets AB at D, and in I.21, where BD is "drawn through" to meet
AC. In Hilbert's geometry it is called the crossbar theorem. Here it follows
from System E: by Triple incidence 1 the straight line AD separates B from
C, so it crosses BC (Intersection 1, Pasch 4), and Pasch 2 and 3 put the
crossing on D's side of A. -/
theorem crossbar {D : Point} (hDC : SameSideOf D C A B) (hDB : SameSideOf D B A C) :
    ∃ X : Point, Between B X C ∧ OnRay X A D

definitions.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Length:
/-- A length (of a finite straight line). -/
abbrev Length := Magnitude .length
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.OnRay:
/-- `P` lies on the straight line from `A` through `B`, on `B`'s side of `A`
(it may be `B` itself, or nearer, or beyond). -/
def OnRay (P A B : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ P ≠ A ∧ Collinear A B P ∧ ¬ Between P A B
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.SameSide:
/-- `SameSide A B L`: the points `A` and `B` lie on the same side of the
straight line `L`. (Neither of them is on `L`.) -/
opaque SameSide : Point → Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Triangle:
/-- **Definition 19.** A trilateral figure: three points not on one straight
line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop := ¬ Collinear A B C
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area
definitions.len:
/-- The length of the finite straight line from `A` to `B`. Written `‖A B‖`. -/
noncomputable opaque len : Point → Point → Length
