state.commentary:
Euclid draws CE through C parallel to AB, and I.29 carries the angle at A across to ACE and the angle at B up to ECD. Together they fill the exterior angle ACD; add the angle ACB to each, and I.13 makes the three angles two right angles. Without Postulate 5, I.17 lets us say only that any two of them fall short of two right angles. With it, the shortfall is exactly the third.

Euclid's figure puts E inside the angle ACD, and we prove it. Our I.31 gives a point of the parallel on either side of C, and we take the one on A's side of BC. E then lies across AC from B, for otherwise the parallel would run into the triangle and cross AB; and so it lies within the angle ACD.

Eudemus, Proclus reports, credited the theorem and its proof to the Pythagoreans, who drew the parallel to BC through A (Heath, vol. 1, p. 320): its alternate angles copy those at B and C, and with the angle at A they fill two right angles. Aristotle knew Euclid's own construction, as J. L. Heiberg saw: "If then the parallel to the side had been *drawn up* (ἀνῆκτο), the fact would at once have been clear from merely looking at the figure" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 321). Heath adds that "'drawn *upwards*' applied to the parallel to a side can only indicate Euclid's" (vol. 1, p. 321).

**A straight line that turns.** Bernhard Friedrich Thibaut turned a straight line about each corner of the triangle in turn: back on the straight line it began on, it has turned through four right angles, the three exterior angles together. Heath objects that it turns about different points: "it is necessary to assume as an axiom that the two motions are independent" (vol. 1, p. 321). Heinrich Christian Schumacher tried to make it a turning about one point, and Carl Friedrich Gauss replied that he had assumed a proposition which is, "in essence, the very proposition to be proved" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 321). Euclid moves his angles with I.29, and pays with Postulate 5.

**The modern way.** Put A, B, C anticlockwise in the complex plane. The angles at A, B, C are the arguments of $\mathrm{(C - A)/(B - A)}$, $\mathrm{(A - B)/(C - B)}$ and $\mathrm{(B - C)/(A - C)}$, each between $0$ and $\pi$, and the three numbers multiply to $-1$. So the angles add up to an odd multiple of $\pi$, and as the sum lies between $0$ and $3\pi$, to $\pi$.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABC be a triangle, and let one side of it BC be produced to D;

I say that the exterior angle ACD is equal to the two interior and opposite angles CAB, ABC, and the three interior angles of the triangle ABC, BCA, CAB are equal to two right angles.

For let CE be drawn through the point C parallel to the straight line AB. [I. 31]

Then, since AB is parallel to CE,

and AC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles BAC, ACE are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Again, since AB is parallel to CE,

and the straight line BD has fallen upon them,

the exterior angle ECD is equal to the interior and opposite angle ABC. [I. 29]

But the angle ACE was also proved equal to the angle BAC;

therefore the whole angle ACD is equal to the two interior and opposite angles BAC, ABC.

Let the angle ACB be added to each;

therefore the angles ACD, ACB are equal to the three angles ABC, BCA, CAB.

But the angles ACD, ACB are equal to two right angles; [I. 13]

therefore the angles ABC, BCA, CAB are also equal to two right angles.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is equal to the two
interior and opposite angles, and the three interior angles of the triangle are equal to two
right angles. -/
theorem Prop32 {A B C D : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hBCD : Between B C D) :
    ∠ A C D = ∠ C A B + ∠ A B C ∧ ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A + ∠ C A B = ∟ + ∟ := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle, and let one side of it BC be produced to D;
  obtain ⟨BC, hB_BC, hC_BC⟩ := Postulate1 B C hABC.ne₂₃
  have hD_BC : OnLine D BC := on_line_of_between hBCD hB_BC hC_BC
  have hCD : C ≠ D := (ne_of_between (between_symm hBCD)).symm
  -- I say that the exterior angle ACD is equal to the two interior and opposite angles CAB,
  -- ABC, and the three interior angles of the triangle ABC, BCA, CAB are equal to two right
  -- angles.
  -- For let CE be drawn through the point C parallel to the straight line AB. [I. 31]
  obtain ⟨P, Q, hPCQ, hPQ⟩ := Prop31 hABC.ne₁₂ hABC
  obtain ⟨E, hCE, hEA⟩ := Prop32.choose_end hABC hPCQ hPQ
  -- Then, since AB is parallel to CE,
  have hAB : AreParallel A B C E := hCE.symm
  -- and AC has fallen upon them,
  have hBE : OppositeSidesOf B E A C := hAB.swap_left.oppositeSidesOf hEA.symm
  -- the alternate angles BAC, ACE are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hBAC_ACE : ∠ B A C = ∠ A C E := Prop29.alternate hAB.swap_left hBE
  -- Again, since AB is parallel to CE,
  have hCE_BA : AreParallel C E B A := hCE.swap_right
  -- and the straight line BD has fallen upon them,
  -- the exterior angle ECD is equal to the interior and opposite angle ABC. [I. 29]
  have hECD_ABC : ∠ E C D = ∠ A B C := by
    have h := Prop29.exterior hCE_BA hEA.swap (between_symm hBCD)
    rw [angle_symm hCD.symm hCE.1.symm, angle_symm hABC.ne₂₃.symm hABC.ne₁₂] at h
    exact h
  -- But the angle ACE was also proved equal to the angle BAC;
  have hACE_BAC : ∠ A C E = ∠ B A C := hBAC_ACE.symm
  -- therefore the whole angle ACD is equal to the two interior and opposite angles BAC, ABC.
  /- E lies within ACD: both E and D are opposite B across AC,
     and E is on A's side of the straight line CD, which is BC. -/
  have hED : SameSideOf E D C A :=
    (hBE.sameSideOf (OppositeSidesOf.of_between hABC.acb hBCD)).swap
  have hEA_CD : SameSideOf E A C D :=
    SameSideOf.of_line hCD hC_BC hD_BC (hEA.sameSide hB_BC hC_BC)
  have hACD : ∠ A C D = ∠ C A B + ∠ A B C := by
    rw [angle_add_of_within hED hEA_CD, hACE_BAC, hECD_ABC,
      angle_symm hABC.ne₁₂.symm hABC.ne₁₃.symm]
  -- Let the angle ACB be added to each;
  have hadd := CommonNotion2 hACD (Eq.refl (∠ A C B))
  -- therefore the angles ACD, ACB are equal to the three angles ABC, BCA, CAB.
  have hthree : ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B = ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A + ∠ C A B := by
    rw [hadd, angle_symm hABC.ne₁₃ hABC.ne₂₃,
      add_comm (∠ C A B), add_assoc, add_comm (∠ C A B), ← add_assoc]
  -- But the angles ACD, ACB are equal to two right angles; [I. 13]
  have hright : ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B = ∟ + ∟ := by
    rw [add_comm, angle_symm hABC.ne₁₃ hABC.ne₂₃]
    exact Prop13 hBCD (Triangle.of_line hB_BC hD_BC (ne_of_between_ends hBCD)
      (hABC.bca.off_line hB_BC hC_BC))
  -- therefore the angles ABC, BCA, CAB are also equal to two right angles.
  have hsum : ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A + ∠ C A B = ∟ + ∟ := hthree.symm.trans hright
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hACD, hsum⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

state.heath_proof:
Let AB, CD be equal and parallel, and let the straight lines AC, BD join them (at the extremities which are) in the same directions (respectively);

I say that AC, BD are also equal and parallel.

Let BC be joined.

Then, since AB is parallel to CD,

and BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

and BC is common,

and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;

therefore the base AC is equal to the base BD,

and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB,

and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend; [I. 4]

therefore the angle ACB is equal to the angle CBD.

And, since the straight line BC falling on the two straight lines AC, BD has made the alternate angles equal to one another,

state.lean_proof:
/-- The straight lines joining equal and parallel straight lines (at the extremities which are) in
the same directions (respectively) are themselves also equal and parallel. -/
theorem Prop33 {A B C D : Point} (hpar : AreParallel A B C D) (heq : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖)
    (hdir : SameSideOf B D A C) :
    ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ ∧ AreParallel A C B D := by
  -- Let AB, CD be equal and parallel, and let the straight lines AC, BD join them (at the
  -- extremities which are) in the same directions (respectively);
  have hABC : Triangle A B C := hpar.triangle
  have hCDB : Triangle C D B := hpar.symm.swap_right.triangle
  have hAC : A ≠ C := hdir.1
  have hBD : B ≠ D := hCDB.ne₂₃.symm
  -- I say that AC, BD are also equal and parallel.
  -- Let BC be joined.
  have hBC : B ≠ C := hABC.ne₂₃
  -- Then, since AB is parallel to CD,
  have hAB_CD : AreParallel A B C D := hpar
  -- and BC has fallen upon them,
  /- The ends joined in the same directions leave A and D on opposite sides
     of BC (`AreParallel.oppositeSidesOf`). -/
  have hAD : OppositeSidesOf A D B C := hAB_CD.oppositeSidesOf hdir
  -- the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hABC_BCD : ∠ A B C = ∠ B C D := Prop29.alternate hAB_CD hAD
  -- And, since AB is equal to CD,
  have hAB_CD_eq : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ := heq
  -- and BC is common,
  have hBC_CB : ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := len_symm B C
  -- the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB;
  have : ‖A B‖ = ‖D C‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ :=
    ⟨hAB_CD_eq.trans (len_symm C D), hBC_CB⟩
  -- and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;
  have hABC_DCB : ∠ A B C = ∠ D C B :=
    hABC_BCD.trans (angle_symm hBC hCDB.ne₁₂.symm)
  -- therefore the base AC is equal to the base BD,
  /- I.4 takes the corner of the given angle first: BAC and CDB pair B with C,
     A with D, and C with B. -/
  obtain ⟨hAC_DB, hBAC_CDB, hBAC_CDB', hBCA_CBD⟩ :=
    Prop4 hABC.bac hCDB ((len_symm B A).trans hAB_CD_eq) hBC_CB hABC_DCB
  have hAC_BD : ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ := hAC_DB.trans (len_symm D B)
  -- and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB,
  have : △ A B C = △ D C B := by
    rw [area_bac A B C, hBAC_CDB, area_bac C D B]
  -- and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those
  -- which the equal sides subtend; [I. 4]
  have : ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B ∧ ∠ B C A = ∠ C B D := ⟨hBAC_CDB', hBCA_CBD⟩
  -- therefore the angle ACB is equal to the angle CBD.
  have hACB_CBD : ∠ A C B = ∠ C B D := (angle_symm hAC hBC).trans hBCA_CBD
  -- And, since the straight line BC falling on the two straight lines AC, BD has made the
  -- alternate angles equal to one another,
  /- Produce AC beyond C and DB beyond B (Post. 2), so BC falls between two
     points of each straight line, as I.27 asks. Heath gives these ends no letters. -/
  obtain ⟨C₁, hACC₁⟩ := produce hAC
  obtain ⟨B₁, hDBB₁⟩ := produce hBD.symm
  -- AC is parallel to BD. [I. 27]
  have h27 : AreParallel A C₁ B₁ D :=
    Prop27 hACC₁ (between_symm hDBB₁) hAD.swap hACB_CBD
  /- Parallelism belongs to the whole straight lines, whichever two points
     name each one. Postulate 1 names those through A, C and B, D. -/
  obtain ⟨L, hA_L, hC_L⟩ := Postulate1 A C hAC
  obtain ⟨M, hB_M, hD_M⟩ := Postulate1 B D hBD
  have hC₁_L : OnLine C₁ L := on_line_of_between hACC₁ hA_L hC_L
  have hB₁_M : OnLine B₁ M := on_line_of_between hDBB₁ hD_M hB_M
  have hAC_BD_par : AreParallel A C B D :=
    AreParallel.of_parallel hAC hBD hA_L hC_L hB_M hD_M
      (h27.parallel hA_L hC₁_L hB₁_M hD_M)
  -- And it was also proved equal to it.
  have : ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ := hAC_BD
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hAC_BD, hAC_BD_par⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

parallel to CD" of any other two points P, Q of the straight line AB and R,

I.4.enunciation: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend.

I.27.enunciation: If a straight line falling on two straight lines make the alternate angles equal to one another, the straight lines will be parallel to one another.

I.29.enunciation: A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, and the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles.

state.commentary:
I.33 is, as Heath reports Proclus saying, "the connecting link between the exposition of the theory of parallels and the investigation of parallelograms", and Heath says why: it "gives, without expressing the fact, the construction or origin of the parallelogram, so that in the next proposition Euclid is able to speak of 'parallelogrammic areas' without any further explanation" (vol. 1, p. 323). Euclid joins BC, which falls on the parallels AB, CD and makes the alternate angles ABC, BCD equal (I.29); I.4 then makes AC equal to BD and the angle ACB equal to CBD, and those angles, alternate in their turn, make AC parallel to BD (I.27).

**"In the same directions."** The words in parentheses in the enunciation are Heath's own: "I have for clearness' sake inserted the words in brackets though they are not in the original Greek" (vol. 1, p. 323). Everything hangs on them. Join A to D and B to C instead, and the joining straight lines cross, so they are never parallel. Our statement gives the words their force with `SameSideOf`: B and D lie on one side of AC. The same words put A and D on opposite sides of BC, and so make the angles there alternate.

Heath writes DC, CB and DCB where the Greek has BC, CD and BCD, for "Euclid is not always careful to write in corresponding order the letters denoting corresponding points in congruent figures. On the contrary, he evidently prefers the alphabetical order, and seems to disdain to alter it for the sake of beginners or others who might be confused by it" (vol. 1, p. 323). Our I.4 has no such freedom. It pairs corners by their places, the given angle's corner first, so the triangles go in as BAC and CDB, and the angle BCA it hands back, read from the other arm, is Euclid's ACB.

**The modern way.** As vectors, AB and CD, equal, parallel and running the same way, give $\mathrm{B - A = D - C}$. Then $\mathrm{C - A = D - B}$, so AC and BD are equal and parallel too; and $\mathrm{A + D = B + C}$, so the diagonals AD and BC of the parallelogram ABDC bisect one another.
state.heath_proof:
Let AB, CD be equal and parallel, and let the straight lines AC, BD join them (at the extremities which are) in the same directions (respectively);

I say that AC, BD are also equal and parallel.

Let BC be joined.

Then, since AB is parallel to CD,

and BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

And, since AB is equal to CD,

and BC is common,

the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB;

and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;

therefore the base AC is equal to the base BD,

and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB,

and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend; [I. 4]

therefore the angle ACB is equal to the angle CBD.

And, since the straight line BC falling on the two straight lines AC, BD has made the alternate angles equal to one another,

AC is parallel to BD. [I. 27]

And it was also proved equal to it.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- The straight lines joining equal and parallel straight lines (at the extremities which are) in
the same directions (respectively) are themselves also equal and parallel. -/
theorem Prop33 {A B C D : Point} (hpar : AreParallel A B C D) (heq : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖)
    (hdir : SameSideOf B D A C) :
    ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ ∧ AreParallel A C B D := by
  -- Let AB, CD be equal and parallel, and let the straight lines AC, BD join them (at the
  -- extremities which are) in the same directions (respectively);
  have hABC : Triangle A B C := hpar.triangle
  have hCDB : Triangle C D B := hpar.symm.swap_right.triangle
  have hAC : A ≠ C := hdir.1
  have hBD : B ≠ D := hCDB.ne₂₃.symm
  -- I say that AC, BD are also equal and parallel.
  -- Let BC be joined.
  have hBC : B ≠ C := hABC.ne₂₃
  -- Then, since AB is parallel to CD,
  have hAB_CD : AreParallel A B C D := hpar
  -- and BC has fallen upon them,
  /- The ends joined in the same directions leave A and D on opposite sides
     of BC (`AreParallel.oppositeSidesOf`). -/
  have hAD : OppositeSidesOf A D B C := hAB_CD.oppositeSidesOf hdir
  -- the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hABC_BCD : ∠ A B C = ∠ B C D := Prop29.alternate hAB_CD hAD
  -- And, since AB is equal to CD,
  have hAB_CD_eq : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ := heq
  -- and BC is common,
  have hBC_CB : ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := len_symm B C
  -- the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB;
  have : ‖A B‖ = ‖D C‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ :=
    ⟨hAB_CD_eq.trans (len_symm C D), hBC_CB⟩
  -- and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;
  have hABC_DCB : ∠ A B C = ∠ D C B :=
    hABC_BCD.trans (angle_symm hBC hCDB.ne₁₂.symm)
  -- therefore the base AC is equal to the base BD,
  /- I.4 takes the corner of the given angle first: BAC and CDB pair B with C,
     A with D, and C with B. -/
  obtain ⟨hAC_DB, hBAC_CDB, hBAC_CDB', hBCA_CBD⟩ :=
    Prop4 hABC.bac hCDB ((len_symm B A).trans hAB_CD_eq) hBC_CB hABC_DCB
  have hAC_BD : ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ := hAC_DB.trans (len_symm D B)
  -- and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB,
  have : △ A B C = △ D C B := by
    rw [area_bac A B C, hBAC_CDB, area_bac C D B]
  -- and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those
  -- which the equal sides subtend; [I. 4]
  have : ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B ∧ ∠ B C A = ∠ C B D := ⟨hBAC_CDB', hBCA_CBD⟩
  -- therefore the angle ACB is equal to the angle CBD.
  have hACB_CBD : ∠ A C B = ∠ C B D := (angle_symm hAC hBC).trans hBCA_CBD
  -- And, since the straight line BC falling on the two straight lines AC, BD has made the
  -- alternate angles equal to one another,
  /- Produce AC beyond C and DB beyond B (Post. 2), so BC falls between two
     points of each straight line, as I.27 asks. Heath gives these ends no letters. -/
  obtain ⟨C₁, hACC₁⟩ := produce hAC
  obtain ⟨B₁, hDBB₁⟩ := produce hBD.symm
  -- AC is parallel to BD. [I. 27]
  have h27 : AreParallel A C₁ B₁ D :=
    Prop27 hACC₁ (between_symm hDBB₁) hAD.swap hACB_CBD
  /- Parallelism belongs to the whole straight lines, whichever two points
     name each one. Postulate 1 names those through A, C and B, D. -/
  obtain ⟨L, hA_L, hC_L⟩ := Postulate1 A C hAC
  obtain ⟨M, hB_M, hD_M⟩ := Postulate1 B D hBD
  have hC₁_L : OnLine C₁ L := on_line_of_between hACC₁ hA_L hC_L
  have hB₁_M : OnLine B₁ M := on_line_of_between hDBB₁ hD_M hB_M
  have hAC_BD_par : AreParallel A C B D :=
    AreParallel.of_parallel hAC hBD hA_L hC_L hB_M hD_M
      (h27.parallel hA_L hC₁_L hB₁_M hD_M)
  -- And it was also proved equal to it.
  have : ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ := hAC_BD
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hAC_BD, hAC_BD_par⟩
  -- Q. E. D.

statement.note: "In the same directions" is stated as B and D lying on one side of AC (`SameSideOf B D A C`).

state.heath_proof:
Let ACDB be a parallelogrammic area, and BC its diameter;

I say that the opposite sides and angles of the parallelogram ACDB are equal to one another, and the diameter BC bisects it.

For, since AB is parallel to CD,

and the straight line BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Again, since AC is parallel to BD,

and BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ACB, CBD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Therefore ABC, DCB are two triangles having the two angles ABC, BCA equal to the two angles DCB, CBD respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely that adjoining the equal angles and common to both of them, BC;

therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides respectively, and the remaining angle to the remaining angle; [I. 26]

therefore the side AB is equal to CD,

and AC to BD,

and further the angle BAC is equal to the angle CDB.

And, since the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD,

and the angle CBD to the angle ACB,

the whole angle ABD is equal to the whole angle ACD. [C.N. 2]

And the angle BAC was also proved equal to the angle CDB.

Therefore in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another.

I say, next, that the diameter also bisects the areas.

For, since AB is equal to CD,

and BC is common,

the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB respectively;

and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;

therefore the base AC is also equal to DB,

and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB. [I. 4]

Therefore the diameter BC bisects the parallelogram ACDB.

Q. E. D.

lies between A and C and between B and D. Its sides AB and DC are
parallel, so they do not cross, and `AreParallel.cross_or` leaves only the
diameters. -/

    ∃ X : Point, Between A X C ∧ Between B X D

ABCD measured by BD, as BCDA, is the same as measured by AC. -/
theorem Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea B C D A = quadArea A B C D

definitions.AreParallel:
/-- The straight lines `AB` and `CD` are parallel (Definition 23). -/
def AreParallel (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ C ≠ D ∧
    ∀ L M : Line, OnLine A L → OnLine B L → OnLine C M → OnLine D M → Parallel L M
definitions.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Length:
/-- A length (of a finite straight line). -/
abbrev Length := Magnitude .length
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Parallel:
/-- **Definition 23.** "Parallel straight lines are straight lines which, being in
the same plane and being produced indefinitely in both directions, do not meet
one another in either direction." -/
def Parallel (L M : Line) : Prop :=
  L ≠ M ∧ ¬ ∃ P : Point, OnLine P L ∧ OnLine P M
definitions.Parallelogram:
/-- The parallelogram `ABCD`, its corners taken in order: `AB` is parallel to
`CD`, and `BC` to `DA`. Euclid does not define it; he first speaks of
"parallelogrammic areas" in I.34. -/
def Parallelogram (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  AreParallel A B C D ∧ AreParallel B C D A
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area
definitions.len:
/-- The length of the finite straight line from `A` to `B`. Written `‖A B‖`. -/
noncomputable opaque len : Point → Point → Length
definitions.quadArea:
/-- The area of the four-sided figure `ABCD` (corners in order), measured as the
two triangles into which its diameter `AC` cuts it. -/
noncomputable def quadArea (A B C D : Point) : Area := △ A B C + △ A C D

state.enunciation: In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the diameter bisects the areas.
state.heath_proof:
Let ACDB be a parallelogrammic area, and BC its diameter;

I say that the opposite sides and angles of the parallelogram ACDB are equal to one another, and the diameter BC bisects it.

For, since AB is parallel to CD,

and the straight line BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Again, since AC is parallel to BD,

and BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ACB, CBD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Therefore ABC, DCB are two triangles having the two angles ABC, BCA equal to the two angles DCB, CBD respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely that adjoining the equal angles and common to both of them, BC;

therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides respectively, and the remaining angle to the remaining angle; [I. 26]

therefore the side AB is equal to CD,

and AC to BD,

and further the angle BAC is equal to the angle CDB.

And, since the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD,

and the angle CBD to the angle ACB,

the whole angle ABD is equal to the whole angle ACD. [C.N. 2]

And the angle BAC was also proved equal to the angle CDB.

Therefore in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another.

I say, next, that the diameter also bisects the areas.

For, since AB is equal to CD,

and BC is common,

the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB respectively;

and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;

therefore the base AC is also equal to DB,

and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB. [I. 4]

Therefore the diameter BC bisects the parallelogram ACDB.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the
diameter bisects the areas. -/
theorem Prop34 {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A C D B) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ ∧ ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B ∧ ∠ A B D = ∠ A C D ∧
      △ A B C = △ D C B := by
  -- Let ACDB be a parallelogrammic area, and BC its diameter;
  have hBC : B ≠ C := h.2.symm.triangle.ne₁₃
  -- I say that the opposite sides and angles of the parallelogram ACDB are equal to one
  -- another, and the diameter BC bisects it.
  -- For, since AB is parallel to CD,
  have hpar₁ : AreParallel A B C D := h.2.symm.swap_left
  -- and the straight line BC has fallen upon them,
  have hAD : OppositeSidesOf A D B C := hpar₁.oppositeSidesOf h.sameSideOf.symm
  -- the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hABC_BCD : ∠ A B C = ∠ B C D := Prop29.alternate hpar₁ hAD
  -- Again, since AC is parallel to BD,
  have hpar₂ : AreParallel A C B D := h.1.swap_right
  -- and BC has fallen upon them,
  have hAD_CB : OppositeSidesOf A D C B := hAD.swap
  -- the alternate angles ACB, CBD are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hACB_CBD : ∠ A C B = ∠ C B D := Prop29.alternate hpar₂ hAD_CB
  -- Therefore ABC, DCB are two triangles having the two angles ABC, BCA equal to the two
  -- angles DCB, CBD respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely that adjoining the
  -- equal angles and common to both of them, BC;
  have hABC : Triangle A B C := hpar₁.triangle
  have hDCB : Triangle D C B := hpar₁.symm.swap_left.swap_right.triangle
  have hDC : D ≠ C := hpar₁.2.1.symm
  have hAC : A ≠ C := hpar₂.1
  have hB : ∠ A B C = ∠ D C B := hABC_BCD.trans (angle_symm hBC hDC)
  have hC : ∠ B C A = ∠ C B D := (angle_symm hBC hAC).trans hACB_CBD
  -- therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides
  -- respectively, and the remaining angle to the remaining angle; [I. 26]
  obtain ⟨hAB_DC, hAC_DB, -, hBAC_CDB⟩ :=
    Prop26 hABC hDCB hB hC (Or.inl (len_symm B C))
  -- therefore the side AB is equal to CD,
  have hAB_CD : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ := hAB_DC.trans (len_symm D C)
  -- and AC to BD,
  have hAC_BD : ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ := hAC_DB.trans (len_symm D B)
  -- and further the angle BAC is equal to the angle CDB.
  have hBAC : ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B := hBAC_CDB
  -- And, since the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD,
  -- and the angle CBD to the angle ACB,
  -- the whole angle ABD is equal to the whole angle ACD. [C.N. 2]
  /- BC falls within both angles: C within the angle ABD, and B within the
     angle ACD, as `Parallelogram.sameSideOf` says of the parallelogram named
     from each corner. -/
  have hABD : ∠ A B D = ∠ A B C + ∠ C B D :=
    angle_add_of_within h.rotate.rotate.rotate.sameSideOf h.rotate.rotate.sameSideOf.symm.swap
  have hACD : ∠ A C D = ∠ A C B + ∠ B C D :=
    angle_add_of_within h.sameSideOf.symm.swap h.rotate.sameSideOf
  have hABD_ACD : ∠ A B D = ∠ A C D := by
    rw [hABD, hACD, add_comm (∠ A C B)]
    exact CommonNotion2 hABC_BCD hACB_CBD.symm
  -- And the angle BAC was also proved equal to the angle CDB.
  -- Therefore in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one
  -- another.
  refine ⟨hAB_CD, hAC_BD, hBAC, hABD_ACD, ?_⟩
  -- I say, next, that the diameter also bisects the areas.
  -- For, since AB is equal to CD,
  have hBA_CD : ‖B A‖ = ‖C D‖ := (len_symm B A).trans hAB_CD
  -- and BC is common,
  have hBC_CB : ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := len_symm B C
  -- the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB respectively;
  have : ‖A B‖ = ‖D C‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := ⟨hAB_DC, hBC_CB⟩
  -- and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;
  have : ∠ A B C = ∠ D C B := hB
  -- therefore the base AC is also equal to DB,
  /- I.4 takes the corner of the given angle first: BAC and CDB, as in I.33. -/
  obtain ⟨hAC_DB', hBAC_CDB_area, -, -⟩ := Prop4 hABC.bac hDCB.bac hBA_CD hBC_CB hB
  -- and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB. [I. 4]
  have harea : △ A B C = △ D C B := by
    rw [area_bac A B C, hBAC_CDB_area, area_bac C D B]
  -- Therefore the diameter BC bisects the parallelogram ACDB.
  exact harea
  -- Q. E. D.

helper_signatures.Elements.AreParallel:
/-- The straight lines `AB` and `CD` are parallel (Definition 23). -/
def AreParallel (A B C D : Point) : Prop
helper_signatures.Elements.AreParallel.oppositeSidesOf:
/-- Joining two parallels. If AB is parallel to CD, and B and D lie on the
same side of AC (the two "in the same directions", as I.33 says), then A and D
lie on opposite sides of BC: the angles ABC, BCD are alternate.

Were D on A's side of BC, it would lie within the angle ACB, and the straight
line CD, drawn within that angle, would cross AB (`crossbar`); but parallels do
not meet. -/
theorem AreParallel.oppositeSidesOf (h : AreParallel A B C D) (hBD : SameSideOf B D A C) :
    OppositeSidesOf A D B C
helper_signatures.Elements.AreParallel.sameSideOf:
/-- The ends of one parallel lie on one side of the other: if AB is parallel to
CD, then A and B are on the same side of CD (`Parallel.sameSide`). -/
theorem AreParallel.sameSideOf (h : AreParallel A B C D) : SameSideOf A B C D
helper_signatures.Elements.AreParallel.swap_left:
/-- "AB is parallel to CD" is the same as "BA is parallel to CD". -/
theorem AreParallel.swap_left (h : AreParallel A B C D) : AreParallel B A C D
helper_signatures.Elements.AreParallel.swap_right:
/-- "AB is parallel to CD" is the same as "AB is parallel to DC". -/
theorem AreParallel.swap_right (h : AreParallel A B C D) : AreParallel A B D C
helper_signatures.Elements.AreParallel.symm:
/-- If AB is parallel to CD, then CD is parallel to AB. -/
theorem AreParallel.symm (h : AreParallel A B C D) : AreParallel C D A B
helper_signatures.Elements.AreParallel.triangle:
/-- An end of one parallel is off the other: if AB is parallel to CD, then C
is not on the straight line AB, and ABC is a triangle. (Turned round with
`AreParallel.symm` and `.swap_right`, the same holds of D, and of A and B
beside CD.) -/
theorem AreParallel.triangle (h : AreParallel A B C D) : Triangle A B C
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop26:
/-- If two triangles have the two angles equal to two angles respectively, and one side equal to one
side, namely, either the side adjoining the equal angles, or that subtending one of the equal
angles, they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides and the remaining
angle to the remaining angle. -/
theorem Prop26 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hB : ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F) (hC : ∠ B C A = ∠ E F D)
    (hside : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ ∨ ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ ∧ ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop29:
/-- A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one
another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, and the interior angles on
the same side equal to two right angles. -/
theorem Prop29 {A B C D E F G H : Point} (hpar : AreParallel A B C D) (hAGB : Between A G B)
    (hCHD : Between C H D) (hEGH : Between E G H) (hGHF : Between G H F)
    (hBD : SameSideOf B D E F) :
    ∠ A G H = ∠ G H D ∧ ∠ E G B = ∠ G H D ∧ ∠ B G H + ∠ G H D = ∟ + ∟
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop29.alternate:
/-- The alternate angles. If the straight line PG is parallel to HQ, and P and
Q lie on opposite sides of GH, then the alternate angles PGH, GHQ are equal.
Euclid's figure is drawn about GH, each straight line produced beyond G and H
(`AreParallel.figure_alternate`), and I.29 does the rest. [I. 29] -/
theorem Prop29.alternate {P G H Q : Point} (hpar : AreParallel P G H Q)
    (hPQ : OppositeSidesOf P Q G H) : ∠ P G H = ∠ G H Q
helper_signatures.Elements.BookI.Prop4:
/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles
contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the
triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining
angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend. -/
theorem Prop4 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hA : ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F) :
    ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ ∧ △ A B C = △ D E F ∧ ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F ∧ ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E
helper_signatures.Elements.CommonNotion2:
/-- **Common Notion 2.** If equals be added to equals, the wholes are equal. -/
theorem CommonNotion2 {a b c d : Magnitude k} (h₁ : a = b) (h₂ : c = d) :
    a + c = b + d

theorem OppositeSidesOf.swap (h : OppositeSidesOf P Q A B) : OppositeSidesOf P Q B A
helper_signatures.Elements.OppositeSidesOf.symm:
/-- If P is on the other side of AB from Q, then Q is on the other side

theorem OppositeSidesOf.symm (h : OppositeSidesOf P Q A B) : OppositeSidesOf Q P A B

helper_signatures.Elements.Parallelogram:

helper_signatures.Elements.Parallelogram.sameSideOf:

helper_signatures.Elements.Tacit.add_comm:

helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle:

helper_signatures.Elements.Triangle.bac:

helper_signatures.Elements.angle_add_of_within:
/-- A straight line drawn from the corner of an angle through a point within it
cuts the angle into two. If R lies within the angle PVQ, on Q's side of VP
and on P's side of VQ, then the angle PVQ is made up of the angles PVR and

rather than of lines drawn and named. -/
theorem angle_add_of_within {V P Q R : Point} (hRQ : SameSideOf R Q V P)

theorem area_bac (A B C : Point) : △ A B C = △ B A C

I.4.enunciation: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend.

I.26.enunciation: If two triangles have the two angles equal to two angles respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely, either the side adjoining the equal angles, or that subtending one of the equal angles, they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides and the remaining angle to the remaining angle.

I.29.enunciation: A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, and the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles.

Does every proposition called by the proof unit in `lean_proof` do work towards its conclusion or a substantive intermediate step of Euclid's argument? Also check for artificial hypothesis uses. Judge this unit's uses of the supplied helper signatures; helper bodies are outside this question. Heath's sentences stand as `--` lines and `cited` gives exact enunciations. bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop34.bisect:
/-- The diameter bisects the parallelogram, said of its area: the parallelogram
ABCD, measured by its diameter AC, is double the triangle ABC. I.35–I.47 cite
I.34 for this ("the triangle ABC is half of the parallelogram EBCA; for the diameter
AB bisects it"). To halve by the other diameter, name the parallelogram from the
next corner (`Parallelogram.rotate`) and turn its area round with
`Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate`. [I. 34] -/
theorem Prop34.bisect {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea A B C D = △ A B C + △ A B C
bridges.Elements.Parallelogram.cross:
/-- The diameters of a parallelogram cross: in the parallelogram ABCD, some point
lies between A and C and between B and D. Its sides AB and DC are
parallel, so they do not cross, and `AreParallel.cross_or` leaves only the
diameters. -/
theorem Parallelogram.cross (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    ∃ X : Point, Between A X C ∧ Between B X D
bridges.Elements.Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate:
/-- A parallelogram has the same area whichever diameter cuts it: the parallelogram
ABCD measured by BD, as BCDA, is the same as measured by AC. -/
theorem Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea B C D A = quadArea A B C D

state.commentary:
Euclid now names the figure I.33 built, and never defines it. Heath observes that "when parallelograms have to be mentioned for the first time, Euclid calls them 'parallelogrammic areas'", and gathers from Proclus that "parallelogram", in Greek "parallel-lined", was Euclid's own word, suggested by I.33 and formed like "rectilineal" (vol. 1, p. 325). Our `Parallelogram` says just that: both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, the corners taken in order round the figure, here A, C, D, B.

The diameter BC, Euclid's word for a diagonal, falls on both pairs of parallels, and I.29 makes two pairs of alternate angles equal. With BC common, I.26 gives the remaining sides and angle. Common Notion 2 adds the angles at B and at C, once our proof shows that BC runs within the angles ABD and ACD, as the parallelogram, named from each corner, says. I.26 says nothing of areas, so for the halving Euclid goes back to I.4. Later proofs want the halving as an area, and we add `Prop34.bisect`: the parallelogram is twice either triangle.

**Which part is general?** Proclus, after Aristotle, calls the first part general, since only parallelograms have their opposite sides and angles equal, and the second not, since a diameter bisects circles and ellipses too: "the ancients, after investigating the fact that the diameter bisects an ellipse, a circle, and a parallelogram respectively, proceeded to investigate what was common to these cases" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 325). Heath doubts it. Proclus himself admits that the proposition presumes a four-sided figure, and "if we are entitled to the tacit limitation of the theorem to quadrilaterals in one part, we are equally entitled to it in the other" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 325).

Heath suspects that Proclus was alluding to Greek work on the diameters of all sorts of figures, which may have led to Apollonius' definition: a diameter of a bent line, which may be made up of straight lines as well as curves, bisects every straight line drawn across it parallel to a given straight line. A parallelogram's diameter is one in that sense too: "either diagonal of a parallelogram bisects all lines drawn within the parallelogram parallel to the other diagonal" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 326). Here Heath places an-Nairīzī's "neat construction for dividing a straight line into any number of equal parts", which uses I.33 and I.34 (vol. 1, p. 326).

**The modern way.** As vectors, $\mathrm{D = B + C - A}$, and the half-turn $z \mapsto \mathrm{B + C} - z$ about the middle of BC exchanges B and C and takes A to D. It carries the triangle ABC onto DCB and the angle ABD onto DCA, keeping every length, angle and area: the whole of I.34 at once.
state.heath_proof:
Let ACDB be a parallelogrammic area, and BC its diameter;

I say that the opposite sides and angles of the parallelogram ACDB are equal to one another, and the diameter BC bisects it.

For, since AB is parallel to CD,

and the straight line BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Again, since AC is parallel to BD,

and BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ACB, CBD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Therefore ABC, DCB are two triangles having the two angles ABC, BCA equal to the two angles DCB, CBD respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely that adjoining the equal angles and common to both of them, BC;

therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides respectively, and the remaining angle to the remaining angle; [I. 26]

therefore the side AB is equal to CD,

and AC to BD,

and further the angle BAC is equal to the angle CDB.

And, since the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD,

and the angle CBD to the angle ACB,

the whole angle ABD is equal to the whole angle ACD. [C.N. 2]

And the angle BAC was also proved equal to the angle CDB.

Therefore in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another.

I say, next, that the diameter also bisects the areas.

For, since AB is equal to CD,

and BC is common,

the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB respectively;

and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;

therefore the base AC is also equal to DB,

and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB. [I. 4]

Therefore the diameter BC bisects the parallelogram ACDB.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_proof:
/-- In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the
diameter bisects the areas. -/
theorem Prop34 {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A C D B) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ ∧ ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B ∧ ∠ A B D = ∠ A C D ∧
      △ A B C = △ D C B := by
  -- Let ACDB be a parallelogrammic area, and BC its diameter;
  have hBC : B ≠ C := h.2.symm.triangle.ne₁₃
  -- I say that the opposite sides and angles of the parallelogram ACDB are equal to one
  -- another, and the diameter BC bisects it.
  -- For, since AB is parallel to CD,
  have hpar₁ : AreParallel A B C D := h.2.symm.swap_left
  -- and the straight line BC has fallen upon them,
  have hAD : OppositeSidesOf A D B C := hpar₁.oppositeSidesOf h.sameSideOf.symm
  -- the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hABC_BCD : ∠ A B C = ∠ B C D := Prop29.alternate hpar₁ hAD
  -- Again, since AC is parallel to BD,
  have hpar₂ : AreParallel A C B D := h.1.swap_right
  -- and BC has fallen upon them,
  have hAD_CB : OppositeSidesOf A D C B := hAD.swap
  -- the alternate angles ACB, CBD are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hACB_CBD : ∠ A C B = ∠ C B D := Prop29.alternate hpar₂ hAD_CB
  -- Therefore ABC, DCB are two triangles having the two angles ABC, BCA equal to the two
  -- angles DCB, CBD respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely that adjoining the
  -- equal angles and common to both of them, BC;
  have hABC : Triangle A B C := hpar₁.triangle
  have hDCB : Triangle D C B := hpar₁.symm.swap_left.swap_right.triangle
  have hDC : D ≠ C := hpar₁.2.1.symm
  have hAC : A ≠ C := hpar₂.1
  have hB : ∠ A B C = ∠ D C B := hABC_BCD.trans (angle_symm hBC hDC)
  have hC : ∠ B C A = ∠ C B D := (angle_symm hBC hAC).trans hACB_CBD
  -- therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides
  -- respectively, and the remaining angle to the remaining angle; [I. 26]
  obtain ⟨hAB_DC, hAC_DB, -, hBAC_CDB⟩ :=
    Prop26 hABC hDCB hB hC (Or.inl (len_symm B C))
  -- therefore the side AB is equal to CD,
  have hAB_CD : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ := hAB_DC.trans (len_symm D C)
  -- and AC to BD,
  have hAC_BD : ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ := hAC_DB.trans (len_symm D B)
  -- and further the angle BAC is equal to the angle CDB.
  have hBAC : ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B := hBAC_CDB
  -- And, since the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD,
  -- and the angle CBD to the angle ACB,
  -- the whole angle ABD is equal to the whole angle ACD. [C.N. 2]
  /- BC falls within both angles: C within the angle ABD, and B within the
     angle ACD, as `Parallelogram.sameSideOf` says of the parallelogram named
     from each corner. -/
  have hABD : ∠ A B D = ∠ A B C + ∠ C B D :=
    angle_add_of_within h.rotate.rotate.rotate.sameSideOf h.rotate.rotate.sameSideOf.symm.swap
  have hACD : ∠ A C D = ∠ A C B + ∠ B C D :=
    angle_add_of_within h.sameSideOf.symm.swap h.rotate.sameSideOf
  have hABD_ACD : ∠ A B D = ∠ A C D := by
    rw [hABD, hACD, add_comm (∠ A C B)]
    exact CommonNotion2 hABC_BCD hACB_CBD.symm
  -- And the angle BAC was also proved equal to the angle CDB.
  -- Therefore in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one
  -- another.
  refine ⟨hAB_CD, hAC_BD, hBAC, hABD_ACD, ?_⟩
  -- I say, next, that the diameter also bisects the areas.
  -- For, since AB is equal to CD,
  have hBA_CD : ‖B A‖ = ‖C D‖ := (len_symm B A).trans hAB_CD
  -- and BC is common,
  have hBC_CB : ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := len_symm B C
  -- the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB respectively;
  have : ‖A B‖ = ‖D C‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := ⟨hAB_DC, hBC_CB⟩
  -- and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;
  have : ∠ A B C = ∠ D C B := hB
  -- therefore the base AC is also equal to DB,
  /- I.4 takes the corner of the given angle first: BAC and CDB, as in I.33. -/
  obtain ⟨hAC_DB', hBAC_CDB_area, -, -⟩ := Prop4 hABC.bac hDCB.bac hBA_CD hBC_CB hB
  -- and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB. [I. 4]
  have harea : △ A B C = △ D C B := by
    rw [area_bac A B C, hBAC_CDB_area, area_bac C D B]
  -- Therefore the diameter BC bisects the parallelogram ACDB.
  exact harea
  -- Q. E. D.

state.enunciation: In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the diameter bisects the areas.
state.heath_proof:
Let ACDB be a parallelogrammic area, and BC its diameter;

I say that the opposite sides and angles of the parallelogram ACDB are equal to one another, and the diameter BC bisects it.

For, since AB is parallel to CD,

and the straight line BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Again, since AC is parallel to BD,

and BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ACB, CBD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Therefore ABC, DCB are two triangles having the two angles ABC, BCA equal to the two angles DCB, CBD respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely that adjoining the equal angles and common to both of them, BC;

therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides respectively, and the remaining angle to the remaining angle; [I. 26]

therefore the side AB is equal to CD,

and AC to BD,

and further the angle BAC is equal to the angle CDB.

And, since the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD,

and the angle CBD to the angle ACB,

the whole angle ABD is equal to the whole angle ACD. [C.N. 2]

And the angle BAC was also proved equal to the angle CDB.

Therefore in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another.

I say, next, that the diameter also bisects the areas.

For, since AB is equal to CD,

and BC is common,

the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB respectively;

and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;

therefore the base AC is also equal to DB,

and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB. [I. 4]

Therefore the diameter BC bisects the parallelogram ACDB.

Q. E. D.

state.enunciation: Parallelograms which are on the same base and in the same parallels are equal to one another.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABCD, EBCF be parallelograms on the same base BC and in the same parallels AF, BC;

I say that ABCD is equal to the parallelogram EBCF.

For, since ABCD is a parallelogram,

AD is equal to BC. [I. 34]

For the same reason also

EF is equal to BC,

so that AD is also equal to EF; [C.N. 1]

and DE is common;

therefore the whole AE is equal to the whole DF. [C.N. 2]

But AB is also equal to DC; [I. 34]

therefore the two sides EA, AB are equal to the two sides FD, DC respectively,

and the angle FDC is equal to the angle EAB, the exterior to the interior; [I. 29]

therefore the base EB is equal to the base FC,

and the triangle EAB will be equal to the triangle FDC. [I. 4]

Let DGE be subtracted from each;

therefore the trapezium ABGD which remains is equal to the trapezium EGCF which remains. [C.N. 3]

Let the triangle GBC be added to each;

therefore the whole parallelogram ABCD is equal to the whole parallelogram EBCF. [C.N. 2]

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop34:
/-- In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the
diameter bisects the areas. -/
theorem Prop34 {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A C D B) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ ∧ ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B ∧ ∠ A B D = ∠ A C D ∧
      △ A B C = △ D C B
bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop34.bisect:
/-- The diameter bisects the parallelogram, said of its area: the parallelogram
ABCD, measured by its diameter AC, is double the triangle ABC. I.35–I.47 cite
I.34 for this ("the triangle ABC is half of the parallelogram EBCA; for the diameter
AB bisects it"). To halve by the other diameter, name the parallelogram from the
next corner (`Parallelogram.rotate`) and turn its area round with
`Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate`. [I. 34] -/
theorem Prop34.bisect {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea A B C D = △ A B C + △ A B C
bridges.Elements.Parallelogram.cross:
/-- The diameters of a parallelogram cross: in the parallelogram ABCD, some point
lies between A and C and between B and D. Its sides AB and DC are
parallel, so they do not cross, and `AreParallel.cross_or` leaves only the
diameters. -/
theorem Parallelogram.cross (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    ∃ X : Point, Between A X C ∧ Between B X D
bridges.Elements.Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate:
/-- A parallelogram has the same area whichever diameter cuts it: the parallelogram
ABCD measured by BD, as BCDA, is the same as measured by AC. -/
theorem Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea B C D A = quadArea A B C D

definitions.AreParallel:
/-- The straight lines `AB` and `CD` are parallel (Definition 23). -/
def AreParallel (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ C ≠ D ∧
    ∀ L M : Line, OnLine A L → OnLine B L → OnLine C M → OnLine D M → Parallel L M
definitions.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Length:
/-- A length (of a finite straight line). -/
abbrev Length := Magnitude .length
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Parallel:
/-- **Definition 23.** "Parallel straight lines are straight lines which, being in
the same plane and being produced indefinitely in both directions, do not meet
one another in either direction." -/
def Parallel (L M : Line) : Prop :=
  L ≠ M ∧ ¬ ∃ P : Point, OnLine P L ∧ OnLine P M
definitions.Parallelogram:
/-- The parallelogram `ABCD`, its corners taken in order: `AB` is parallel to
`CD`, and `BC` to `DA`. Euclid does not define it; he first speaks of
"parallelogrammic areas" in I.34. -/
def Parallelogram (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  AreParallel A B C D ∧ AreParallel B C D A
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area
definitions.len:
/-- The length of the finite straight line from `A` to `B`. Written `‖A B‖`. -/
noncomputable opaque len : Point → Point → Length
definitions.quadArea:
/-- The area of the four-sided figure `ABCD` (corners in order), measured as the
two triangles into which its diameter `AC` cuts it. -/
noncomputable def quadArea (A B C D : Point) : Area := △ A B C + △ A C D
