state.commentary:
Euclid cuts the figure into two triangles with DB. ABD goes to I.42, and DBC to I.44, which applies a parallelogram equal to it to GH, a side of the first. More sides mean more triangles, each applied in turn to the side the last one left. Our main theorem takes the figure as Euclid cuts it, the sum of ABD and DBC, because our `quadArea` would read ABCD along the other diameter, AC, and AC falls outside the figure when it has a corner pointing inwards at B or D.

**A figure that comes with its triangles.** The companions take a figure of any number of sides, given with the triangles it is cut into, and check the cutting: triangles that lie apart, no point inside two of them, so that the figure may even have a hole (`Prop45.apart`); or, as Euclid and Oliver Byrne cut it, triangles from one corner, checked to fit together (`Prop45.fan`). The parallelogram is equal to those triangles taken together. That another cutting gives the same whole, AC in place of DB, is the step Euclid takes for granted; David Hilbert proved it, for his measure of area.

**Do the triangles fit?** In Euclid's figure, A and C lie on opposite sides of DB, so ABD and DBC meet along DB and nowhere else. Put A and C on the same side and the triangles overlap. With more corners, the straight lines from one corner can fold back or come round on themselves. A later triangle may then lie over an earlier one or reach outside the figure, so the triangles together no longer give the figure. For `Prop45.fan` we check two things: neighbouring triangles lie on opposite sides of the straight line they share, and their angles at the corner together make less than four right angles. The hardest step, `Fitted.fan`, proves that these conditions let the triangles fit together without overlap. The proof follows the triangles round the corner one at a time, measuring how far round each point lies. Our angles are never greater than two right angles, so a point beyond that turn is measured as two right angles and something more. Euclid leaves this to his figure: four sides, two triangles, plainly apart.

Heath takes stock: "We have now learnt how to represent any rectilineal area, which can of course be resolved into triangles, by a single parallelogram having one side equal to any given straight line and one angle equal to any given rectilineal angle" (vol. 1, p. 347). A rectangle stands for a product, so applying one to a given straight line is, in his words, "the geometrical equivalent of algebraical *division*" (vol. 1, p. 347). The last step, a square equal to the figure, waits for II.14.

Proclus guesses that "it was in consequence of this problem that the ancient geometers were led to investigate the squaring of the circle as well" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 347): if any straight-sided figure can be made a parallelogram, why not a circle? Archimedes, he adds, proved a circle equal to the right-angled triangle whose sides about the right angle are the circle's radius and perimeter. But no construction with straight lines and circles can lay that perimeter out straight, as Ferdinand von Lindemann showed in 1882.

**The modern way.** With the cross product of [I.35](35.md), the figure's area is $\tfrac{1}{2}\lvert\mathrm{(B - A)} \times \mathrm{(D - A)}\rvert + \tfrac{1}{2}\lvert\mathrm{(B - D)} \times \mathrm{(C - D)}\rvert$. Write $\varepsilon$ for the given angle E and $a$ for the common side $\mathrm{KF} = \mathrm{GH}$. A parallelogram with a side $a$ in the angle $\varepsilon$ has area $a$ times its other side times $\sin\varepsilon$, so the breadths KH and HM are the areas of the two triangles, each divided by $a\sin\varepsilon$, and KM, their sum, is the area of the whole figure divided by $a\sin\varepsilon$: Heath's division, done once for each triangle.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABCD be the given rectilineal figure and E the given rectilineal angle; thus it is required to construct, in the given angle E, a parallelogram equal to the rectilineal figure ABCD.

Let DB be joined, and let the parallelogram FH be constructed equal to the triangle ABD, in the angle HKF which is equal to E; [I. 42] let the parallelogram GM equal to the triangle DBC be applied to the straight line GH, in the angle GHM which is equal to E. [I. 44]

Then, since the angle E is equal to each of the angles HKF, GHM, the angle HKF is also equal to the angle GHM. [C.N. 1]

Let the angle KHG be added to each; therefore the angles FKH, KHG are equal to the angles KHG, GHM.

But the angles FKH, KHG are equal to two right angles; [I. 29] therefore the angles KHG, GHM are also equal to two right angles.

Thus, with a straight line GH, and at the point H on it, two straight lines KH, HM not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles; therefore KH is in a straight line with HM. [I. 14]

And, since the straight line HG falls upon the parallels KM, FG, the alternate angles MHG, HGF are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Let the angle HGL be added to each; therefore the angles MHG, HGL are equal to the angles HGF, HGL. [C.N. 2]

But the angles MHG, HGL are equal to two right angles; [I. 29] therefore the angles HGF, HGL are also equal to two right angles. [C.N. 1]

Therefore FG is in a straight line with GL. [I. 14]

And, since FK is equal and parallel to HG, [I. 34] and HG to ML also, KF is also equal and parallel to ML; [C.N. 1; I. 30] and the straight lines KM, FL join them (at their extremities); therefore KM, FL are also equal and parallel. [I. 33]

Therefore KFLM is a parallelogram.

And, since the triangle ABD is equal to the parallelogram FH, and DBC to GM, the whole rectilineal figure ABCD is equal to the whole parallelogram KFLM.

Therefore the parallelogram KFLM has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal figure ABCD, in the angle FKM which is equal to the given angle E.

Q. E. F.
state.lean_proof:
/-- To construct, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure. -/
theorem Prop45 {A B C D E₁ E E₂ : Point} (hABD : Triangle A B D) (hDBC : Triangle D B C)
    (hE : Triangle E₁ E E₂) :
    ∃ K F L M : Point, Parallelogram K F L M ∧ ∠ F K M = ∠ E₁ E E₂ ∧
      quadArea K F L M = △ A B D + △ D B C := by
  -- Let ABCD be the given rectilineal figure and E the given rectilineal angle; thus it is
  -- required to construct, in the given angle E, a parallelogram equal to the rectilineal
  -- figure ABCD.
  -- Let DB be joined, and let the parallelogram FH be constructed equal to the triangle ABD,
  -- in the angle HKF which is equal to E; [I. 42] let the parallelogram GM equal to the
  -- triangle DBC be applied to the straight line GH, in the angle GHM which is equal to
  -- E. [I. 44]
  /- I.42 builds on half of the triangle's own base, so KH lies along BD and H
     falls on D: the Lean writes D wherever Euclid writes H, and in our figure KFLM
     overlaps ABCD. K lies between B and D, and F is on A's side of BD. -/
  obtain ⟨K, F, G, hBKD, hFA, hFKHG, hHKF, hFH⟩ := Prop42 hABD hE
  have hGHK : Triangle G D K := hFKHG.1.symm.swap_right.triangle.bac
  /- I.44's point for the side is taken across GH from K, so that KH and HM are
     "not lying on the same side", as I.14 will ask. -/
  obtain ⟨P, hPK, -⟩ := exists_oppositeSidesOf hGHK []
  obtain ⟨L, M, hMP, hGHML, hGHM, hGM⟩ := Prop44 hGHK.ne₁₂ hDBC hE hPK.triangle
  have hMK : OppositeSidesOf M K G D := hMP.trans_opposite hPK
  have hKD : K ≠ D := hGHK.ne₂₃.symm
  have hGD : G ≠ D := hGHK.ne₁₂
  have hFK : F ≠ K := hFKHG.1.1
  -- Then, since the angle E is equal to each of the angles HKF, GHM, the angle HKF is also
  -- equal to the angle GHM. [C.N. 1]
  have hHKF_GHM : ∠ D K F = ∠ G D M := CommonNotion1 hHKF hGHM
  -- Let the angle KHG be added to each; therefore the angles FKH, KHG are equal to the angles
  -- KHG, GHM.
  have hsum₁ : ∠ F K D + ∠ K D G = ∠ K D G + ∠ G D M := by
    rw [angle_symm hFK hKD.symm, hHKF_GHM, add_comm]
  -- But the angles FKH, KHG are equal to two right angles; [I. 29] therefore the angles KHG,
  -- GHM are also equal to two right angles.
  have hFG_KH : SameSideOf F G K D := hFKHG.rotate.sameSideOf.symm
  have h29a : ∠ F K D + ∠ K D G = ∟ + ∟ := Prop29.interior hFKHG.1.swap_left hFG_KH
  have hKHG_GHM : ∠ K D G + ∠ G D M = ∟ + ∟ := hsum₁.symm.trans h29a
  -- Thus, with a straight line GH, and at the point H on it, two straight lines KH, HM not
  -- lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles; therefore KH is
  -- in a straight line with HM. [I. 14]
  have hKHM : Between K D M := Prop14 hMK.symm (by
    rw [angle_symm hGD hKD]
    exact hKHG_GHM)
  -- And, since the straight line HG falls upon the parallels KM, FG, the alternate angles MHG,
  -- HGF are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hFK_HG : SameSideOf F K D G := hFKHG.rotate.rotate.sameSideOf
  have hMD : M ≠ D := ne_of_between (between_symm hKHM)
  obtain ⟨KM, hK_KM, hM_KM⟩ := Postulate1 K M (ne_of_between_ends hKHM)
  have hD_KM : OnLine D KM := on_line_of_between_ends hKHM hK_KM hM_KM
  obtain ⟨FG, hF_FG, hG_FG⟩ := Postulate1 F G hFKHG.2.2.1.symm
  have hKM_FG : Parallel KM FG := hFKHG.2.parallel hK_KM hD_KM hG_FG hF_FG
  have hMHGF : AreParallel M D G F :=
    AreParallel.of_parallel hMD hFKHG.2.2.1 hM_KM hD_KM hG_FG hF_FG hKM_FG
  have hMF : OppositeSidesOf M F D G := (hFK_HG.trans_opposite hMK.symm.swap).symm
  have hMHG_HGF : ∠ M D G = ∠ D G F := Prop29.alternate hMHGF hMF
  -- Let the angle HGL be added to each; therefore the angles MHG, HGL are equal to the angles
  -- HGF, HGL. [C.N. 2]
  have hsum₂ : ∠ M D G + ∠ D G L = ∠ D G F + ∠ D G L := CommonNotion2 hMHG_HGF rfl
  -- But the angles MHG, HGL are equal to two right angles; [I. 29] therefore the angles HGF,
  -- HGL are also equal to two right angles. [C.N. 1]
  have hML_HG : SameSideOf M L D G := hGHML.sameSideOf.swap
  have h29c : ∠ M D G + ∠ D G L = ∟ + ∟ := Prop29.interior hGHML.2.swap_right hML_HG
  have hHGF_HGL : ∠ D G F + ∠ D G L = ∟ + ∟ := CommonNotion1 hsum₂.symm h29c.symm
  -- Therefore FG is in a straight line with GL. [I. 14]
  have hFL : OppositeSidesOf F L D G :=
    hFK_HG.trans_opposite (hML_HG.symm.trans_opposite hMK.swap).symm
  have hFGL : Between F G L := Prop14 hFL hHGF_HGL
  -- And, since FK is equal and parallel to HG, [I. 34] and HG to ML also, KF is also equal and
  -- parallel to ML; [C.N. 1; I. 30] and the straight lines KM, FL join them (at their
  -- extremities); therefore KM, FL are also equal and parallel. [I. 33]
  obtain ⟨-, hFK_GH, -, -, -⟩ := Prop34 (A := F) (B := G) (C := K) (D := D) hFKHG
  obtain ⟨-, hGH_LM, -, -, -⟩ := Prop34 (A := G) (B := L) (C := D) (D := M) hGHML
  have hlen : ‖K F‖ = ‖M L‖ :=
    CommonNotion1 ((len_symm K F).trans hFK_GH) (hGH_LM.trans (len_symm L M)).symm
  obtain ⟨KF, hK_KF, hF_KF⟩ := Postulate1 K F hFK.symm
  obtain ⟨ML, hM_ML, hL_ML⟩ := Postulate1 M L hGHML.1.2.1
  obtain ⟨GD, hG_GD, hD_GD⟩ := Postulate1 G D hGD
  have hKF_GD : Parallel KF GD := hFKHG.1.swap_left.parallel hK_KF hF_KF hD_GD hG_GD
  have hML_GD : Parallel ML GD := hGHML.1.symm.parallel hM_ML hL_ML hG_GD hD_GD
  have hKF_ML : KF ≠ ML := fun e => by
    have hK_ML : OnLine K ML := e ▸ hK_KF
    have : ML = KM := line_unique (ne_of_between_ends hKHM) hK_ML hM_ML hK_KM hM_KM
    exact hML_GD.not_onLine (this ▸ hD_KM) hD_GD
  have hpar : AreParallel K F M L :=
    AreParallel.of_parallel hFK.symm hGHML.1.2.1 hK_KF hF_KF hM_ML hL_ML
      (Prop30.parallel hKF_GD hML_GD hKF_ML)
  have hdir : SameSideOf F L K M := by
    have hF : SameSide F G KM := hFG_KH.sameSide hK_KM hD_KM
    have hL : SameSide L G KM := hGHML.rotate.sameSideOf.sameSide hD_KM hM_KM
    exact SameSideOf.of_line (ne_of_between_ends hKHM) hK_KM hM_KM
      (same_side_trans (same_side_symm hF) (same_side_symm hL))
  obtain ⟨-, h33⟩ := Prop33 hpar hlen hdir
  -- Therefore KFLM is a parallelogram.
  have hKFLM : Parallelogram K F L M := ⟨hpar.swap_right, h33.symm.swap_right⟩
  -- And, since the triangle ABD is equal to the parallelogram FH, and DBC to GM, the whole
  -- rectilineal figure ABCD is equal to the whole parallelogram KFLM.
  have hwhole : quadArea K F L M = △ A B D + △ D B C := by
    rw [quadArea_add_of_parallelograms hFKHG.rotate.reverse hGHML.rotate.reverse hKHM hFGL,
      quadArea_reverse K D G F, hFKHG.quadArea_rotate, hFH,
      quadArea_reverse D M L G, hGHML.quadArea_rotate, hGM]
  -- Therefore the parallelogram KFLM has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal
  -- figure ABCD, in the angle FKM which is equal to the given angle E.
  refine ⟨K, F, L, M, hKFLM, ?_, hwhole⟩
  rw [angle_onRay_right (OnRay.of_beyond hKHM) hFK, angle_symm hFK hKD.symm]
  exact hHKF
  -- Q. E. F.

statement.note: With its companions: `Prop45.apart` takes any figure given with triangles that lie apart, `Prop45.fan` Euclid's division from one corner; `Prop45` his ABD, DBC.

route.note: Euclid shows two triangles. The companions repeat his second step for each triangle after the first, as Oliver Byrne draws it for three: `Prop45.append` is the second half of his proof, with the parallelogram so far given in place of the one I.42 makes, and `Prop45.sum` applies it to one triangle after another.

state.lean_statement:
theorem Prop45 {A B C D E₁ E E₂ : Point} (hABD : Triangle A B D) (hDBC : Triangle D B C)
    (hE : Triangle E₁ E E₂) :
    ∃ K F L M : Point, Parallelogram K F L M ∧ ∠ F K M = ∠ E₁ E E₂ ∧
      quadArea K F L M = △ A B D + △ D B C

attached_statements.I.45 apart:
theorem Prop45.apart {E₁ E E₂ : Point} (R : Apart) (hE : Triangle E₁ E E₂) :
    ∃ K F L M : Point, Parallelogram K F L M ∧ ∠ F K M = ∠ E₁ E E₂ ∧
      quadArea K F L M = R.area
attached_statements.I.45 append:
theorem Prop45.append {A B C K F L M E₁ E E₂ : Point} (hKFLM : Parallelogram K F L M)
    (hang : ∠ F K M = ∠ E₁ E E₂) (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hE : Triangle E₁ E E₂) :
    ∃ K' F' L' M' : Point, Parallelogram K' F' L' M' ∧ ∠ F' K' M' = ∠ E₁ E E₂ ∧
      quadArea K' F' L' M' = quadArea K F L M + △ A B C
attached_statements.I.45 fan:
theorem Prop45.fan {A₀ A₁ A₂ E₁ E E₂ : Point} {ps : List Point}
    (htri : ∀ s ∈ segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps), Triangle A₀ s.1 s.2)
    (hopp : ∀ t ∈ triples (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps), OppositeSidesOf t.1 t.2.2 A₀ t.2.1)
    (hA₀ : Magnitude.sum ((segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps)).map fun s => ∠ s.1 A₀ s.2) <
      ∟ + ∟ + (∟ + ∟))
    (hE : Triangle E₁ E E₂) :
    ∃ R : Rectilineal,
      R.pieces = (segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps)).map (fun s => (A₀, s.1, s.2)) ∧
      ∃ K F L M : Point, Parallelogram K F L M ∧ ∠ F K M = ∠ E₁ E E₂ ∧
        quadArea K F L M = R.area
attached_statements.I.45 figure:
theorem Prop45.figure {E₁ E E₂ : Point} (R : Rectilineal) (hE : Triangle E₁ E E₂) :
    ∃ K F L M : Point, Parallelogram K F L M ∧ ∠ F K M = ∠ E₁ E E₂ ∧
      quadArea K F L M = R.area
attached_statements.I.45 sum:
theorem Prop45.sum {E₁ E E₂ : Point} (ts : List (Point × Point × Point)) (hne : ts ≠ [])
    (hts : ∀ t ∈ ts, Triangle t.1 t.2.1 t.2.2) (hE : Triangle E₁ E E₂) :
    ∃ K F L M : Point, Parallelogram K F L M ∧ ∠ F K M = ∠ E₁ E E₂ ∧
      quadArea K F L M = Magnitude.sum (ts.map fun t => △ t.1 t.2.1 t.2.2)

named_declarations.Elements.BookI.Prop45.apart:
/-- **I.45, for any rectilineal figure, with any boundaries** (companion of I.45). To
construct, in a given rectilineal angle E, a parallelogram KFLM, its angle at K equal to E,
equal to a given rectilineal figure: the figure given with any division of it into
triangles, no point inside two of them (`Apart`), and "equal to the figure" meaning equal
to those triangles taken together (`Apart.area`). The figure may have a hole, touch itself
at a corner, or be in more than one piece. It is `Prop45.sum` for the figure's triangles;
lying apart is what makes their sum the figure's. Nothing is claimed of another division of
the figure. -/
theorem Prop45.apart {E₁ E E₂ : Point} (R : Apart) (hE : Triangle E₁ E E₂) :
    ∃ K F L M : Point, Parallelogram K F L M ∧ ∠ F K M = ∠ E₁ E E₂ ∧
      quadArea K F L M = R.area
named_declarations.Elements.BookI.Prop45.fan:
/-- **I.45, for a figure divided from one corner** (companion of I.45), as Euclid and Oliver
Byrne divide it. A figure with corners A₀, A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ, the list `ps` being A₃, …, Aₙ
(empty for a triangle), divided by the straight lines from A₀ into the triangles A₀A₁A₂,
A₀A₂A₃, …, A₀Aₙ₋₁Aₙ, one on each side `segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps)`. The division is checked:
each piece is a triangle; each two neighbouring triangles A₀Aᵢ₋₁Aᵢ and A₀AᵢAᵢ₊₁ lie on
opposite sides of the straight line A₀Aᵢ they share (one condition for each of
`triples (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps)`); and the angles A₁A₀A₂, …, Aₙ₋₁A₀Aₙ together are less than four
right angles. Then those triangles, in that order, are fitted together into one figure
(`Fitted.fan`); and, given a rectilineal angle E, there is a parallelogram KFLM, its angle
at K equal to E, equal to that figure, that is, to the triangles taken together. The figure
is read as the one with corners A₀, A₁, …, Aₙ in order round it; that its boundary is that
closed line is not stated in Lean. Nothing is claimed of another division.

The first conclusion is what the two conditions are for: without them the triangles from
A₀ may overlap, and need not be fitted. The parallelogram alone would follow from each
piece being a triangle, by `Prop45.sum`.

Euclid's ABCD with DB joined is the figure with corners D, A, B, C, its triangles DAB and
DBC: A and C lie on opposite sides of DB. Byrne's figure has its corners listed from its
re-entrant corner, from which both his straight lines are drawn. -/
theorem Prop45.fan {A₀ A₁ A₂ E₁ E E₂ : Point} {ps : List Point}
    (htri : ∀ s ∈ segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps), Triangle A₀ s.1 s.2)
    (hopp : ∀ t ∈ triples (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps), OppositeSidesOf t.1 t.2.2 A₀ t.2.1)
    (hA₀ : Magnitude.sum ((segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps)).map fun s => ∠ s.1 A₀ s.2) <
      ∟ + ∟ + (∟ + ∟))
    (hE : Triangle E₁ E E₂) :
    ∃ R : Rectilineal,
      R.pieces = (segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps)).map (fun s => (A₀, s.1, s.2)) ∧
      ∃ K F L M : Point, Parallelogram K F L M ∧ ∠ F K M = ∠ E₁ E E₂ ∧
        quadArea K F L M = R.area
named_declarations.Elements.Fitted.fan:
/-- **Euclid's and Oliver Byrne's division is a figure, when it is checked.** A figure given
by its corners A₀, A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ, the list `ps` being A₃, …, Aₙ, and divided by the straight
lines from A₀ into the triangles A₀A₁A₂, A₀A₂A₃, …, A₀Aₙ₋₁Aₙ, one on each side
`segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps)`. Suppose each is a triangle; each two neighbouring triangles,
A₀Aᵢ₋₁Aᵢ and A₀AᵢAᵢ₊₁, lie on opposite sides of the straight line A₀Aᵢ they share, that is,
Aᵢ₋₁ and Aᵢ₊₁ are on opposite sides of it (one condition for each of
`triples (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps)`); and the angles A₁A₀A₂, A₂A₀A₃, …, Aₙ₋₁A₀Aₙ at A₀ together are
less than four right angles. Then those triangles, in that order, are fitted together into
one figure: each is laid across the straight line A₀Aᵢ against the one before it, and meets
the earlier ones only along that straight line. The figure they make is read as the figure
with corners A₀, A₁, …, Aₙ in order round it; that its boundary is the closed line A₀A₁…AₙA₀
is not stated in Lean.

The two conditions are what make the triangles turn one way round A₀ and not come round on
themselves, so that they do not overlap. Euclid's ABCD, divided from D by DB, is the figure
with corners D, A, B, C: A and C are on opposite sides of DB, and the two angles at D,
each less than two right angles, are together less than four. -/
theorem Fitted.fan {A₀ A₁ A₂ : Point} {ps : List Point}
    (htri : ∀ s ∈ segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps), Triangle A₀ s.1 s.2)
    (hopp : ∀ t ∈ triples (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps), OppositeSidesOf t.1 t.2.2 A₀ t.2.1)
    (hA₀ : Magnitude.sum ((segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps)).map fun s => ∠ s.1 A₀ s.2) <
      ∟ + ∟ + (∟ + ∟)) :
    Fitted ((segments (A₁ :: A₂ :: ps)).map fun s => (A₀, s.1, s.2))
named_declarations.Elements.quadArea:
/-- The area of the four-sided figure `ABCD` (corners in order), measured as the
two triangles into which its diameter `AC` cuts it. -/
noncomputable def quadArea (A B C D : Point) : Area

definitions.Apart:
/-- **A rectilineal figure, given with triangles that lie apart** (Definition I.14: a figure
is "that which is contained by any boundary or boundaries"; Definition I.19: rectilineal
figures are "those which are contained by straight lines"): any division of it into
triangles, each named by its three corners, at least one; each a triangle; and no point
inside two of them. The figure is the triangles together. It may have a hole, as a square
with a smaller square cut from its middle has, may touch itself at a corner, and may be in
more than one piece. No order of the triangles is asked, and a triangle may lie against part
of a side of another. A figure given by gluing is one of these, its triangles lying apart by
`Fitted.inside_pairwise`. That every rectilineal figure, with any boundaries, can be cut
into triangles that lie apart is not stated in Lean. -/
structure Apart where
  /-- The triangles the figure is cut into. -/
  pieces : List (Point × Point × Point)
  /-- There is at least one. -/
  ne : pieces ≠ []
  /-- Each is a triangle: its corners are not on one straight line. -/
  triangle : ∀ t ∈ pieces, Triangle t.1 t.2.1 t.2.2
  /-- No point is inside two of them. -/
  apart : pieces.Pairwise fun s s' => ∀ Y : Point,
    InsideTriangle Y s.1 s.2.1 s.2.2 → ¬ InsideTriangle Y s'.1 s'.2.1 s'.2.2
definitions.Apart.area:
/-- **The area of a figure given with triangles that lie apart, as given**: the sum of its
triangles. As with `Rectilineal.area`, that another division of the same figure gives the
same sum is not proved here (Book I's gap catalogue, under I.45), so this is the area of the
figure with its division, not yet a measure of the figure alone. -/
noncomputable def Apart.area (R : Apart) : Area :=
  Magnitude.sum (R.pieces.map fun t => △ t.1 t.2.1 t.2.2)
definitions.AreParallel:
/-- The straight lines `AB` and `CD` are parallel (Definition 23). -/
def AreParallel (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ C ≠ D ∧
    ∀ L M : Line, OnLine A L → OnLine B L → OnLine C M → OnLine D M → Parallel L M
definitions.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
definitions.Corners:
/-- The triangle `t` has the corners `P`, `Q`, `R`: read from some corner, one way round or
the other, it is `(P, Q, R)`. So `PQ` is one of its sides, and `R` the corner opposite. -/
def Corners (t : Point × Point × Point) (P Q R : Point) : Prop :=
  t = (P, Q, R) ∨ t = (Q, R, P) ∨ t = (R, P, Q) ∨ t = (Q, P, R) ∨ t = (P, R, Q) ∨
    t = (R, Q, P)
definitions.Fitted:
/-- **Triangles fitted together into one rectilineal figure**, in the order listed.

* `single`: one triangle is a figure.
* `glue`: a figure, with a new triangle `PQX` laid against the side `PQ` of one of its
  triangles `t`, whose third corner is `R`. The new triangle lies across that side, `X` being
  on the other side of `PQ` from `R`; and it meets the triangles already there only along
  `PQ`: a point within or on the new triangle, and within or on one of the earlier ones,
  lies on the finite straight line `PQ`.

The new triangle goes at the end of the list. A figure made this way may be convex or not.
Every figure made this way is bounded by one closed line that neither crosses nor touches
itself, with no hole; and every such figure can be cut this way, since it can be cut into
triangles by straight lines joining its corners, and those triangles, listed so that each
after the first shares a side with one before it, with each later triangle named so that
its attached side is its first two corners, satisfy the rule: a later triangle meets an
earlier one that is not its neighbour only at an end of the side it is glued along.
Neither fact is stated in Lean. That no point is inside two of the triangles is stated, and
proved (`Fitted.inside_pairwise`). So every such figure has a division that is fitted, but
not every division of it is: a ring of triangles round a point inside it is not (below),
nor is a list whose later triangle is named from the wrong corner, as the square ABCD cut
along AC and listed ABC, ADC (the second must be named with AC as its first two corners,
ACD or CAD).

A ring of triangles closing up round a point, or round a hole, is not made this way, for its
last triangle would meet the others along two sides. A triangle laid against part of a
side, or against two sides in line, is not glued this way either; its figure is cut
differently. A figure with a hole cannot be cut so as to be glued. Any division of any
figure, with a hole or without, is taken given with triangles that lie apart (`Apart`), and
a fitted figure's triangles lie apart too. -/
inductive Fitted : List (Point × Point × Point) → Prop
  | single {A B C : Point} (h : Triangle A B C) : Fitted [(A, B, C)]
  | glue {ps : List (Point × Point × Point)} {t : Point × Point × Point} {P Q R X : Point}
      (hps : Fitted ps) (ht : t ∈ ps) (hside : Corners t P Q R)
      (hX : OppositeSidesOf X R P Q)
      (hmeet : ∀ Y : Point, OnOrInsideTriangle Y P Q X →
        ∀ s ∈ ps, OnOrInsideTriangle Y s.1 s.2.1 s.2.2 → OnFiniteLine Y P Q) :
      Fitted (ps ++ [(P, Q, X)])
definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.Magnitude.sum:
/-- **The sum of a list of magnitudes** of one kind: nothing for the empty list, and
otherwise the first added to the sum of the rest. So `Magnitude.sum [a, b, c]` is
`a + (b + (c + 0))`, which is `a + b + c`. -/
noncomputable def Magnitude.sum {k : Kind} : List (Magnitude k) → Magnitude k
  | [] => 0
  | a :: as => a + Magnitude.sum as
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnFiniteLine:
/-- `Y` lies on the finite straight line `PQ`: it is one of the ends, or between them. -/
def OnFiniteLine (Y P Q : Point) : Prop := Y = P ∨ Y = Q ∨ Between P Y Q
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.OnOrInsideTriangle:
/-- `Y` lies within the triangle `ABC` or on its boundary: inside it, on one of its sides
between two corners, or at a corner. -/
def OnOrInsideTriangle (Y A B C : Point) : Prop :=
  InsideTriangle Y A B C ∨ Between A Y B ∨ Between B Y C ∨ Between C Y A ∨
    Y = A ∨ Y = B ∨ Y = C
definitions.Parallel:
/-- **Definition 23.** "Parallel straight lines are straight lines which, being in
the same plane and being produced indefinitely in both directions, do not meet
one another in either direction." -/
def Parallel (L M : Line) : Prop :=
  L ≠ M ∧ ¬ ∃ P : Point, OnLine P L ∧ OnLine P M
definitions.Parallelogram:
/-- The parallelogram `ABCD`, its corners taken in order: `AB` is parallel to
`CD`, and `BC` to `DA`. Euclid does not define it; he first speaks of
"parallelogrammic areas" in I.34. -/
def Parallelogram (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  AreParallel A B C D ∧ AreParallel B C D A
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.Rectilineal:
/-- **A rectilineal figure with one boundary, given with its triangles fitted together**
(Definition I.19: "Rectilineal figures are those which are contained by straight lines"):
the triangles it is cut into, each named by its three corners, in an order in which they
fit together, with the proof that they do. The figure is the triangles together. -/
structure Rectilineal where
  /-- The triangles the figure is cut into, in the order they were fitted. -/
  pieces : List (Point × Point × Point)
  /-- They fit together into one figure. -/
  fitted : Fitted pieces
definitions.Rectilineal.area:
/-- **The area of a rectilineal figure, as given**: the sum of the triangles it is given
with, which do not overlap (`Fitted.inside_pairwise`) and make up the figure. That another
division of the same figure gives the same sum is not proved here (Book I's gap catalogue,
under I.45), so this is the area of the figure with its division, not yet a measure of the
figure alone. -/
noncomputable def Rectilineal.area (R : Rectilineal) : Area :=
  Magnitude.sum (R.pieces.map fun t => △ t.1 t.2.1 t.2.2)
definitions.SameSide:
/-- `SameSide A B L`: the points `A` and `B` lie on the same side of the
straight line `L`. (Neither of them is on `L`.) -/
opaque SameSide : Point → Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Triangle:
/-- **Definition 19.** A trilateral figure: three points not on one straight
line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop := ¬ Collinear A B C
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area

two triangles into which its diameter `AC` cuts it. -/

definitions.segments:

of `[A₁, A₂, A₃, A₄]` are A₁A₂A₃ and A₂A₃A₄. In a division from one corner A₀, the middle

triangles share, and the other two are their third corners. -/

  | p :: q :: r :: rest => (p, q, r) :: triples (q :: r :: rest)

state.enunciation: To construct, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABCD be the given rectilineal figure and E the given rectilineal angle; thus it is required to construct, in the given angle E, a parallelogram equal to the rectilineal figure ABCD.

Let DB be joined, and let the parallelogram FH be constructed equal to the triangle ABD, in the angle HKF which is equal to E; [I. 42] let the parallelogram GM equal to the triangle DBC be applied to the straight line GH, in the angle GHM which is equal to E. [I. 44]

Then, since the angle E is equal to each of the angles HKF, GHM, the angle HKF is also equal to the angle GHM. [C.N. 1]

Let the angle KHG be added to each; therefore the angles FKH, KHG are equal to the angles KHG, GHM.

But the angles FKH, KHG are equal to two right angles; [I. 29] therefore the angles KHG, GHM are also equal to two right angles.

Thus, with a straight line GH, and at the point H on it, two straight lines KH, HM not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles; therefore KH is in a straight line with HM. [I. 14]

And, since the straight line HG falls upon the parallels KM, FG, the alternate angles MHG, HGF are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Let the angle HGL be added to each; therefore the angles MHG, HGL are equal to the angles HGF, HGL. [C.N. 2]

But the angles MHG, HGL are equal to two right angles; [I. 29] therefore the angles HGF, HGL are also equal to two right angles. [C.N. 1]

Therefore FG is in a straight line with GL. [I. 14]

And, since FK is equal and parallel to HG, [I. 34] and HG to ML also, KF is also equal and parallel to ML; [C.N. 1; I. 30] and the straight lines KM, FL join them (at their extremities); therefore KM, FL are also equal and parallel. [I. 33]

Therefore KFLM is a parallelogram.

And, since the triangle ABD is equal to the parallelogram FH, and DBC to GM, the whole rectilineal figure ABCD is equal to the whole parallelogram KFLM.

Therefore the parallelogram KFLM has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal figure ABCD, in the angle FKM which is equal to the given angle E.

Q. E. F.

theorem Prop45 {A B C D E₁ E E₂ : Point} (hABD : Triangle A B D) (hDBC : Triangle D B C)

      quadArea K F L M = △ A B D + △ D B C

state.enunciation: On a given straight line to describe a square.
state.heath_proof:
Let AB be the given straight line; thus it is required to describe a square on the straight line AB.

Let AC be drawn at right angles to the straight line AB from the point A on it [I. 11], and let AD be made equal to AB; through the point D let DE be drawn parallel to AB, and through the point B let BE be drawn parallel to AD. [I. 31]

Therefore ADEB is a parallelogram; therefore AB is equal to DE, and AD to BE. [I. 34]

But AB is equal to AD; therefore the four straight lines BA, AD, DE, EB are equal to one another; therefore the parallelogram ADEB is equilateral.

I say next that it is also right-angled.

For, since the straight line AD falls upon the parallels AB, DE, the angles BAD, ADE are equal to two right angles. [I. 29]

But the angle BAD is right; therefore the angle ADE is also right.

And in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another; [I. 34] therefore each of the opposite angles ABE, BED is also right.

Therefore ADEB is right-angled.

And it was also proved equilateral.

Therefore it is a square; and it is described on the straight line AB.

Q. E. F.

bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop34:
/-- In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the
diameter bisects the areas. -/
theorem Prop34 {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A C D B) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ ∧ ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B ∧ ∠ A B D = ∠ A C D ∧
      △ A B C = △ D C B
bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop34.bisect:
/-- The diameter bisects the parallelogram, said of its area: the parallelogram
ABCD, measured by its diameter AC, is double the triangle ABC. I.35–I.47 cite
I.34 for this ("the triangle ABC is half of the parallelogram EBCA; for the diameter
AB bisects it"). To halve by the other diameter, name the parallelogram from the
next corner (`Parallelogram.rotate`) and turn its area round with
`Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate`. [I. 34] -/
theorem Prop34.bisect {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea A B C D = △ A B C + △ A B C
bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop46.square_eq:
/-- Squares described on equal straight lines are equal. Euclid assumes this in
I.48 ("since DA is equal to AB, the square on DA is also equal to the square on
AB"). Heath reports, under I.46, that Proclus proves it. Each square is a
parallelogram (`Prop28.square`), so the diameter AC cuts it into the triangles
ABC and ACD, right-angled at B and D; and I.4 makes these equal to the triangles
A'B'C' and A'C'D'. Here a square ABCD is "described on AB" when its far corners
C, D lie on one side of AB. [I. 4, I. 28] -/
theorem Prop46.square_eq {A B C D A' B' C' D' : Point} (h : Square A B C D)
    (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (h' : Square A' B' C' D') (hCD' : SameSideOf C' D' A' B')
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A' B'‖) : quadArea A B C D = quadArea A' B' C' D'
bridges.Elements.Parallelogram.cross:
/-- The diameters of a parallelogram cross: in the parallelogram ABCD, some point
lies between A and C and between B and D. Its sides AB and DC are
parallel, so they do not cross, and `AreParallel.cross_or` leaves only the
diameters. -/
theorem Parallelogram.cross (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    ∃ X : Point, Between A X C ∧ Between B X D
bridges.Elements.Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate:
/-- A parallelogram has the same area whichever diameter cuts it: the parallelogram
ABCD measured by BD, as BCDA, is the same as measured by AC. -/
theorem Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea B C D A = quadArea A B C D

definitions.AreParallel:
/-- The straight lines `AB` and `CD` are parallel (Definition 23). -/
def AreParallel (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ C ≠ D ∧
    ∀ L M : Line, OnLine A L → OnLine B L → OnLine C M → OnLine D M → Parallel L M
definitions.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Length:
/-- A length (of a finite straight line). -/
abbrev Length := Magnitude .length
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Parallel:
/-- **Definition 23.** "Parallel straight lines are straight lines which, being in
the same plane and being produced indefinitely in both directions, do not meet
one another in either direction." -/
def Parallel (L M : Line) : Prop :=
  L ≠ M ∧ ¬ ∃ P : Point, OnLine P L ∧ OnLine P M
definitions.Parallelogram:
/-- The parallelogram `ABCD`, its corners taken in order: `AB` is parallel to
`CD`, and `BC` to `DA`. Euclid does not define it; he first speaks of
"parallelogrammic areas" in I.34. -/
def Parallelogram (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  AreParallel A B C D ∧ AreParallel B C D A
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.SameSide:
/-- `SameSide A B L`: the points `A` and `B` lie on the same side of the
straight line `L`. (Neither of them is on `L`.) -/
opaque SameSide : Point → Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Square:
/-- **Definition 22.** "Of quadrilateral figures, a square is that which is both
equilateral and right-angled." The corners are `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`, in order. -/
def Square (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  ‖A B‖ = ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖C D‖ = ‖D A‖ ∧
    ∠ D A B = ∟ ∧ ∠ A B C = ∟ ∧ ∠ B C D = ∟ ∧ ∠ C D A = ∟
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area
definitions.len:
/-- The length of the finite straight line from `A` to `B`. Written `‖A B‖`. -/
noncomputable opaque len : Point → Point → Length
definitions.quadArea:
/-- The area of the four-sided figure `ABCD` (corners in order), measured as the
two triangles into which its diameter `AC` cuts it. -/
noncomputable def quadArea (A B C D : Point) : Area := △ A B C + △ A C D
definitions.rightAngle:
/-- The size of a right angle. Postulate 4 says all right angles are equal, so
it makes sense to have one name for their common size. Written `∟`. -/
noncomputable opaque rightAngle : Angle

state.heath_proof:
Let AB be the given straight line; thus it is required to describe a square on the straight line AB.

Let AC be drawn at right angles to the straight line AB from the point A on it [I. 11], and let AD be made equal to AB; through the point D let DE be drawn parallel to AB, and through the point B let BE be drawn parallel to AD. [I. 31]

But AB is equal to AD; therefore the four straight lines BA, AD, DE, EB are equal to one another; therefore the parallelogram ADEB is equilateral.

I say next that it is also right-angled.

For, since the straight line AD falls upon the parallels AB, DE, the angles BAD, ADE are equal to two right angles. [I. 29]

But the angle BAD is right; therefore the angle ADE is also right.

And in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another; [I. 34] therefore each of the opposite angles ABE, BED is also right.

state.lean_proof:
/-- On a given straight line to describe a square. -/
theorem Prop46 {A B P : Point} (hAB : A ≠ B) (hP : ¬ Collinear A B P) :
    ∃ D E : Point, Square A D E B ∧ SameSideOf D P A B ∧ SameSideOf E P A B := by
  -- Let AB be the given straight line; thus it is required to describe a square on the
  -- straight line AB.
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  -- Let AC be drawn at right angles to the straight line AB from the point A on it [I. 11],
  obtain ⟨C, hCP, hAC⟩ := Prop11 hAB ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB, hA_AB⟩ hP
  have hBAC : ∠ B A C = ∟ := hAC B ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB, hB_AB⟩ hAB.symm
  -- and let AD be made equal to AB; through the point D let DE be drawn parallel to AB, and
  -- through the point B let BE be drawn parallel to AD. [I. 31]
  /- A circle about A with distance AB gives D on the ray AC (Postulate 3).
     C need not lie beyond D. -/
  obtain ⟨D, hD, hAD⟩ := OnRay.exists_len_eq hAB hCP.triangle.ne₁₃
  have hDP : SameSideOf D P A B := SameSideOf.of_onRay hD hCP
  have hABD : Triangle A B D := hDP.triangle
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hDE_AB⟩ := Prop31.line (hABD.off_line hA_AB hB_AB)
  /- DE meets the parallel BE at E (`Prop31.parallelogram`). -/
  obtain ⟨E, -, hDABE⟩ := Prop31.parallelogram hDE_AB hD_DE hA_AB hB_AB hAB
  -- Therefore ADEB is a parallelogram; therefore AB is equal to DE, and AD to BE. [I. 34]
  have hADEB : Parallelogram A D E B := hDABE.rotate.reverse
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hADEB.2.1
  have hEB : E ≠ B := hADEB.1.2.1
  obtain ⟨hAB_DE, hAD_BE, -, -, -⟩ := Prop34 hADEB
  -- But AB is equal to AD; therefore the four straight lines BA, AD, DE, EB are equal to one
  -- another; therefore the parallelogram ADEB is equilateral.
  have h₁ : ‖A D‖ = ‖D E‖ := hAD.trans hAB_DE
  have h₂ : ‖D E‖ = ‖E B‖ :=
    hAB_DE.symm.trans (hAD.symm.trans (hAD_BE.trans (len_symm B E)))
  have h₃ : ‖E B‖ = ‖B A‖ :=
    (len_symm E B).trans (hAD_BE.symm.trans (hAD.trans (len_symm A B)))
  -- I say next that it is also right-angled.
  have hright : ∠ B A D = ∟ ∧ ∠ A D E = ∟ ∧ ∠ D E B = ∟ ∧ ∠ E B A = ∟ := by
    -- For, since the straight line AD falls upon the parallels AB, DE, the angles BAD, ADE are
    -- equal to two right angles. [I. 29]
    have h29 : ∠ B A D + ∠ A D E = ∟ + ∟ :=
      Prop29.interior hADEB.2.symm.swap_left hADEB.sameSideOf.symm
    -- But the angle BAD is right; therefore the angle ADE is also right.
    have hBAD : ∠ B A D = ∟ := (angle_onRay_right hD hAB.symm).trans hBAC
    have hADE : ∠ A D E = ∟ := by
      rw [hBAD] at h29
      exact CommonNotion3 (c := ∟) (d := ∟) (by rw [add_comm]; exact h29) rfl
    -- And in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one
    -- another; [I. 34] therefore each of the opposite angles ABE, BED is also right.
    obtain ⟨-, -, hBAD_DEB, hABE_ADE, -⟩ := Prop34 hADEB
    have hABE : ∠ A B E = ∟ := hABE_ADE.trans hADE
    have hBED : ∠ B E D = ∟ :=
      (angle_symm hEB.symm hDE).trans (hBAD_DEB.symm.trans hBAD)
    -- Therefore ADEB is right-angled.
    exact ⟨hBAD, hADE, (angle_symm hDE hEB.symm).trans hBED,
      (angle_symm hEB hAB).trans hABE⟩
  -- And it was also proved equilateral.
  have hequil : ‖A D‖ = ‖D E‖ ∧ ‖D E‖ = ‖E B‖ ∧ ‖E B‖ = ‖B A‖ := ⟨h₁, h₂, h₃⟩
  -- Therefore it is a square; and it is described on the straight line AB.
  have hsquare : Square A D E B := ⟨hequil.1, hequil.2.1, hequil.2.2, hright⟩
  have hEP : SameSideOf E P A B :=
    hADEB.rotate.rotate.rotate.sameSideOf.swap.symm.trans hDP
  exact ⟨D, E, hsquare, hDP, hEP⟩
  -- Q. E. F.

theorem Prop29 {A B C D E F G H : Point} (hpar : AreParallel A B C D) (hAGB : Between A G B)

definitions.AreParallel:
/-- The straight lines `AB` and `CD` are parallel (Definition 23). -/
def AreParallel (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ C ≠ D ∧
    ∀ L M : Line, OnLine A L → OnLine B L → OnLine C M → OnLine D M → Parallel L M
definitions.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Length:
/-- A length (of a finite straight line). -/
abbrev Length := Magnitude .length
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.OnRay:
/-- `P` lies on the straight line from `A` through `B`, on `B`'s side of `A`
(it may be `B` itself, or nearer, or beyond). -/
def OnRay (P A B : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ P ≠ A ∧ Collinear A B P ∧ ¬ Between P A B
definitions.Parallel:
/-- **Definition 23.** "Parallel straight lines are straight lines which, being in
the same plane and being produced indefinitely in both directions, do not meet
one another in either direction." -/
def Parallel (L M : Line) : Prop :=
  L ≠ M ∧ ¬ ∃ P : Point, OnLine P L ∧ OnLine P M
definitions.Parallelogram:
/-- The parallelogram `ABCD`, its corners taken in order: `AB` is parallel to
`CD`, and `BC` to `DA`. Euclid does not define it; he first speaks of
"parallelogrammic areas" in I.34. -/
def Parallelogram (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  AreParallel A B C D ∧ AreParallel B C D A
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.SameSide:
/-- `SameSide A B L`: the points `A` and `B` lie on the same side of the
straight line `L`. (Neither of them is on `L`.) -/
opaque SameSide : Point → Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Square:
/-- **Definition 22.** "Of quadrilateral figures, a square is that which is both
equilateral and right-angled." The corners are `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`, in order. -/
def Square (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  ‖A B‖ = ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖C D‖ = ‖D A‖ ∧
    ∠ D A B = ∟ ∧ ∠ A B C = ∟ ∧ ∠ B C D = ∟ ∧ ∠ C D A = ∟
definitions.Triangle:
/-- **Definition 19.** A trilateral figure: three points not on one straight
line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop := ¬ Collinear A B C
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area
definitions.len:
/-- The length of the finite straight line from `A` to `B`. Written `‖A B‖`. -/
noncomputable opaque len : Point → Point → Length
definitions.rightAngle:
/-- The size of a right angle. Postulate 4 says all right angles are equal, so
it makes sense to have one name for their common size. Written `∟`. -/
noncomputable opaque rightAngle : Angle

question.instructions:
Does every proposition called by the proof unit in `lean_proof` do work towards its conclusion or a substantive intermediate step of Euclid's argument? Also check for artificial hypothesis uses. Judge this unit's uses of the supplied helper signatures; helper bodies are outside this question. Heath's sentences stand as `--` lines and `cited` gives exact enunciations. In Lean, `have h : T := p` proves T by p and calls the result h; `obtain ⟨…⟩ := p` takes p apart into named pieces; `rw [h34, h37, …]` rewrites the goal by the equalities named. Follow uses through helper calls and tactics as well as explicit names. An anonymous binding or an unused hypothesis alone does not establish a defect. If both defects occur, choose `a dummy citation`.

docs/FORMALIZATION.md, section 5:
A checked intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid is legitimate, even if the
  final proof term could do without it.

criteria.a dummy citation: Some proposition call does no substantive work: its result neither supports the argument nor establishes a substantive intermediate fact, and merely supplies a citation while the step is done another way.
criteria.an artificial hypothesis use: No dummy citation is established, but a hypothesis is mentioned only so that it looks used, and does no substantive work.
criteria.cannot tell: What is given here is not enough to decide.
criteria.all do work: Every proposition call supports a later step or the conclusion, or establishes a substantive intermediate fact tied to a real sentence of Euclid. No hypothesis is mentioned merely to look used. With no proposition calls the citation part alone is vacuous; hypothesis use must still be inspected.

bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop34:
/-- In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the
diameter bisects the areas. -/
theorem Prop34 {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A C D B) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ ∧ ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B ∧ ∠ A B D = ∠ A C D ∧
      △ A B C = △ D C B
bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop34.bisect:
/-- The diameter bisects the parallelogram, said of its area: the parallelogram
ABCD, measured by its diameter AC, is double the triangle ABC. I.35–I.47 cite
I.34 for this ("the triangle ABC is half of the parallelogram EBCA; for the diameter
AB bisects it"). To halve by the other diameter, name the parallelogram from the
next corner (`Parallelogram.rotate`) and turn its area round with
`Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate`. [I. 34] -/
theorem Prop34.bisect {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea A B C D = △ A B C + △ A B C
bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop46.square_eq:
/-- Squares described on equal straight lines are equal. Euclid assumes this in
I.48 ("since DA is equal to AB, the square on DA is also equal to the square on
AB"). Heath reports, under I.46, that Proclus proves it. Each square is a
parallelogram (`Prop28.square`), so the diameter AC cuts it into the triangles
ABC and ACD, right-angled at B and D; and I.4 makes these equal to the triangles
A'B'C' and A'C'D'. Here a square ABCD is "described on AB" when its far corners
C, D lie on one side of AB. [I. 4, I. 28] -/
theorem Prop46.square_eq {A B C D A' B' C' D' : Point} (h : Square A B C D)
    (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (h' : Square A' B' C' D') (hCD' : SameSideOf C' D' A' B')
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A' B'‖) : quadArea A B C D = quadArea A' B' C' D'
bridges.Elements.Parallelogram.cross:
/-- The diameters of a parallelogram cross: in the parallelogram ABCD, some point
lies between A and C and between B and D. Its sides AB and DC are
parallel, so they do not cross, and `AreParallel.cross_or` leaves only the
diameters. -/
theorem Parallelogram.cross (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    ∃ X : Point, Between A X C ∧ Between B X D
bridges.Elements.Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate:
/-- A parallelogram has the same area whichever diameter cuts it: the parallelogram
ABCD measured by BD, as BCDA, is the same as measured by AC. -/
theorem Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea B C D A = quadArea A B C D

state.commentary:
Proclus notes that Euclid constructs a triangle but describes a square on a straight line, and Heath puts the difference so: "The *triangle* (or *angle*) is, so to say, pieced together, while the describing of a square on a given straight line is the making of a figure 'from' *one* side, and corresponds to the multiplication of the number representing the side by itself" (vol. 1, p. 348). So Euclid builds ADEB from AB alone, with a right angle, an equal straight line and two parallels, and only then proves it a square: equilateral and right-angled, as Definition I.22 asks. One step goes unnamed: "the angle ADE is also right" takes the right angle BAD from two right angles, and that is Common Notion 3.

Euclid's figure settles which side of AB the square stands on; his enunciation is silent. In our statement a given point settles it, and D and E are promised on its side, because I.47 needs its squares outward and I.48 describes three of them so. I.11 draws AC on that side, and a circle about A lays off AD equal to AB (Post. 3). Heath draws C beyond D; our proof leaves their order open.

**Equal squares, equal sides.** Euclid takes for granted in I.48 that squares on equal straight lines are equal, and the converse. Heath reports Proclus proving both here (vol. 1, pp. 348–349), and we prove them after I.46 as `Prop46.square_eq` and `Prop46.side_eq`. The first, Heath says, "is immediately obvious if we divide the squares into two triangles by drawing a diagonal in each" (vol. 1, p. 348): I.4 makes the triangles equal. For the converse Proclus sets the squares side by side; we prove it where they stand. I.3 cuts off from the greater side a straight line equal to the less, I.46 describes a square on it inside the greater square, and by I.34 the half of the one is a part of the half of the other, and so less.

**The modern way.** In the complex plane, turning AB about A through $\pi/2$ gives AD: $\mathrm{D = A} + i\mathrm{(B - A)}$, and $\mathrm{E = B} + i\mathrm{(B - A)}$ completes the square ADEB. Multiplying by $-i$ instead describes the square on the other side of AB, and the given point says which.
state.heath_proof:
Let AB be the given straight line; thus it is required to describe a square on the straight line AB.

Let AC be drawn at right angles to the straight line AB from the point A on it [I. 11], and let AD be made equal to AB; through the point D let DE be drawn parallel to AB, and through the point B let BE be drawn parallel to AD. [I. 31]

Therefore ADEB is a parallelogram; therefore AB is equal to DE, and AD to BE. [I. 34]

But AB is equal to AD; therefore the four straight lines BA, AD, DE, EB are equal to one another; therefore the parallelogram ADEB is equilateral.

I say next that it is also right-angled.

For, since the straight line AD falls upon the parallels AB, DE, the angles BAD, ADE are equal to two right angles. [I. 29]

But the angle BAD is right; therefore the angle ADE is also right.

And in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another; [I. 34] therefore each of the opposite angles ABE, BED is also right.

Therefore ADEB is right-angled.

And it was also proved equilateral.

Therefore it is a square; and it is described on the straight line AB.

Q. E. F.
state.lean_proof:
/-- On a given straight line to describe a square. -/
theorem Prop46 {A B P : Point} (hAB : A ≠ B) (hP : ¬ Collinear A B P) :
    ∃ D E : Point, Square A D E B ∧ SameSideOf D P A B ∧ SameSideOf E P A B := by
  -- Let AB be the given straight line; thus it is required to describe a square on the
  -- straight line AB.
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  -- Let AC be drawn at right angles to the straight line AB from the point A on it [I. 11],
  obtain ⟨C, hCP, hAC⟩ := Prop11 hAB ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB, hA_AB⟩ hP
  have hBAC : ∠ B A C = ∟ := hAC B ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB, hB_AB⟩ hAB.symm
  -- and let AD be made equal to AB; through the point D let DE be drawn parallel to AB, and
  -- through the point B let BE be drawn parallel to AD. [I. 31]
  /- A circle about A with distance AB gives D on the ray AC (Postulate 3).
     C need not lie beyond D. -/
  obtain ⟨D, hD, hAD⟩ := OnRay.exists_len_eq hAB hCP.triangle.ne₁₃
  have hDP : SameSideOf D P A B := SameSideOf.of_onRay hD hCP
  have hABD : Triangle A B D := hDP.triangle
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hDE_AB⟩ := Prop31.line (hABD.off_line hA_AB hB_AB)
  /- DE meets the parallel BE at E (`Prop31.parallelogram`). -/
  obtain ⟨E, -, hDABE⟩ := Prop31.parallelogram hDE_AB hD_DE hA_AB hB_AB hAB
  -- Therefore ADEB is a parallelogram; therefore AB is equal to DE, and AD to BE. [I. 34]
  have hADEB : Parallelogram A D E B := hDABE.rotate.reverse
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hADEB.2.1
  have hEB : E ≠ B := hADEB.1.2.1
  obtain ⟨hAB_DE, hAD_BE, -, -, -⟩ := Prop34 hADEB
  -- But AB is equal to AD; therefore the four straight lines BA, AD, DE, EB are equal to one
  -- another; therefore the parallelogram ADEB is equilateral.
  have h₁ : ‖A D‖ = ‖D E‖ := hAD.trans hAB_DE
  have h₂ : ‖D E‖ = ‖E B‖ :=
    hAB_DE.symm.trans (hAD.symm.trans (hAD_BE.trans (len_symm B E)))
  have h₃ : ‖E B‖ = ‖B A‖ :=
    (len_symm E B).trans (hAD_BE.symm.trans (hAD.trans (len_symm A B)))
  -- I say next that it is also right-angled.
  have hright : ∠ B A D = ∟ ∧ ∠ A D E = ∟ ∧ ∠ D E B = ∟ ∧ ∠ E B A = ∟ := by
    -- For, since the straight line AD falls upon the parallels AB, DE, the angles BAD, ADE are
    -- equal to two right angles. [I. 29]
    have h29 : ∠ B A D + ∠ A D E = ∟ + ∟ :=
      Prop29.interior hADEB.2.symm.swap_left hADEB.sameSideOf.symm
    -- But the angle BAD is right; therefore the angle ADE is also right.
    have hBAD : ∠ B A D = ∟ := (angle_onRay_right hD hAB.symm).trans hBAC
    have hADE : ∠ A D E = ∟ := by
      rw [hBAD] at h29
      exact CommonNotion3 (c := ∟) (d := ∟) (by rw [add_comm]; exact h29) rfl
    -- And in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one
    -- another; [I. 34] therefore each of the opposite angles ABE, BED is also right.
    obtain ⟨-, -, hBAD_DEB, hABE_ADE, -⟩ := Prop34 hADEB
    have hABE : ∠ A B E = ∟ := hABE_ADE.trans hADE
    have hBED : ∠ B E D = ∟ :=
      (angle_symm hEB.symm hDE).trans (hBAD_DEB.symm.trans hBAD)
    -- Therefore ADEB is right-angled.
    exact ⟨hBAD, hADE, (angle_symm hDE hEB.symm).trans hBED,
      (angle_symm hEB hAB).trans hABE⟩
  -- And it was also proved equilateral.
  have hequil : ‖A D‖ = ‖D E‖ ∧ ‖D E‖ = ‖E B‖ ∧ ‖E B‖ = ‖B A‖ := ⟨h₁, h₂, h₃⟩
  -- Therefore it is a square; and it is described on the straight line AB.
  have hsquare : Square A D E B := ⟨hequil.1, hequil.2.1, hequil.2.2, hright⟩
  have hEP : SameSideOf E P A B :=
    hADEB.rotate.rotate.rotate.sameSideOf.swap.symm.trans hDP
  exact ⟨D, E, hsquare, hDP, hEP⟩
  -- Q. E. F.

statement.note: The square stands on whichever side of AB a given point names.

theorem Prop46 {A B P : Point} (hAB : A ≠ B) (hP : ¬ Collinear A B P) :
    ∃ D E : Point, Square A D E B ∧ SameSideOf D P A B ∧ SameSideOf E P A B

named_declarations.Elements.BookI.Prop46.side_eq:
/-- Conversely, equal squares are described on equal straight lines. Euclid assumes
this too in I.48 ("therefore the square on DC is equal to the square on BC, so that
the side DC is also equal to BC"). Heath reports, under I.46, Proclus' proof, which
places the two squares side by side and then reasons through I.39, I.27, I.34
and I.26. We take another road, because a figure cannot be moved here (as
`Prop44.place` explains): one square has to be described afresh, and described
inside the other it is a part of it. Were AB less than A'B', cut off from A'B'
a straight line A'X equal to AB [I. 3], and describe on it a square A'ZYX on
the side of C' [I. 46]. It is equal to the square ABCD (`Prop46.square_eq`); Z
falls on A'D', short of D'; and each square is double the triangle its diameter
cuts off from A' [I. 34]. But the triangle XA'Z is a part of the triangle
B'A'D', and so less. [I. 3, I. 4, I. 28, I. 34, I. 46] -/
theorem Prop46.side_eq {A B C D A' B' C' D' : Point} (h : Square A B C D)
    (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (h' : Square A' B' C' D') (hCD' : SameSideOf C' D' A' B')
    (hsq : quadArea A B C D = quadArea A' B' C' D') : ‖A B‖ = ‖A' B'‖
named_declarations.Elements.BookI.Prop46.square_eq:
/-- Squares described on equal straight lines are equal. Euclid assumes this in
I.48 ("since DA is equal to AB, the square on DA is also equal to the square on
AB"). Heath reports, under I.46, that Proclus proves it. Each square is a
parallelogram (`Prop28.square`), so the diameter AC cuts it into the triangles
ABC and ACD, right-angled at B and D; and I.4 makes these equal to the triangles
A'B'C' and A'C'D'. Here a square ABCD is "described on AB" when its far corners
C, D lie on one side of AB. [I. 4, I. 28] -/
theorem Prop46.square_eq {A B C D A' B' C' D' : Point} (h : Square A B C D)
    (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (h' : Square A' B' C' D') (hCD' : SameSideOf C' D' A' B')
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A' B'‖) : quadArea A B C D = quadArea A' B' C' D'

definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Length:
/-- A length (of a finite straight line). -/
abbrev Length := Magnitude .length
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.SameSide:
/-- `SameSide A B L`: the points `A` and `B` lie on the same side of the
straight line `L`. (Neither of them is on `L`.) -/
opaque SameSide : Point → Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Square:
/-- **Definition 22.** "Of quadrilateral figures, a square is that which is both
equilateral and right-angled." The corners are `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`, in order. -/
def Square (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  ‖A B‖ = ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖C D‖ = ‖D A‖ ∧
    ∠ D A B = ∟ ∧ ∠ A B C = ∟ ∧ ∠ B C D = ∟ ∧ ∠ C D A = ∟
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area
definitions.len:
/-- The length of the finite straight line from `A` to `B`. Written `‖A B‖`. -/
noncomputable opaque len : Point → Point → Length
definitions.quadArea:
/-- The area of the four-sided figure `ABCD` (corners in order), measured as the
two triangles into which its diameter `AC` cuts it. -/
noncomputable def quadArea (A B C D : Point) : Area := △ A B C + △ A C D
definitions.rightAngle:
/-- The size of a right angle. Postulate 4 says all right angles are equal, so
it makes sense to have one name for their common size. Written `∟`. -/
noncomputable opaque rightAngle : Angle

state.enunciation: In right-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares on the sides containing the right angle.
state.heath_proof:
Let ABC be a right-angled triangle having the angle BAC right;

I say that the square on BC is equal to the squares on BA, AC.

For let there be described on BC the square BDEC, and on BA, AC the squares GB, HC; [I. 46] through A let AL be drawn parallel to either BD or CE, and let AD, FC be joined.

Then, since each of the angles BAC, BAG is right, it follows that with a straight line BA, and at the point A on it, the two straight lines AC, AG not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles; therefore CA is in a straight line with AG. [I. 14]

For the same reason BA is also in a straight line with AH.

And, since the angle DBC is equal to the angle FBA: for each is right: let the angle ABC be added to each; therefore the whole angle DBA is equal to the whole angle FBC. [C.N. 2]

And, since DB is equal to BC, and FB to BA, the two sides AB, BD are equal to the two sides FB, BC respectively; and the angle ABD is equal to the angle FBC; therefore the base AD is equal to the base FC, and the triangle ABD is equal to the triangle FBC. [I. 4]

Now the parallelogram BL is double of the triangle ABD, for they have the same base BD and are in the same parallels BD, AL. [I. 41]

And the square GB is double of the triangle FBC, for they again have the same base FB and are in the same parallels FB, GC. [I. 41]

[But the doubles of equals are equal to one another.]

Therefore the parallelogram BL is also equal to the square GB.

Similarly, if AE, BK be joined, the parallelogram CL can also be proved equal to the square HC; therefore the whole square BDEC is equal to the two squares GB, HC. [C.N. 2]

And the square BDEC is described on BC, and the squares GB, HC on BA, AC.

Therefore the square on the side BC is equal to the squares on the sides BA, AC.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.
state.lean_statement:
theorem Prop47 {A B C D E F G H K : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hright : ∠ B A C = ∟)
    (hBDEC : Square B D E C) (hD : OppositeSidesOf D A B C) (hE : OppositeSidesOf E A B C)
    (hABFG : Square A B F G) (hF : OppositeSidesOf F C A B) (hG : OppositeSidesOf G C A B)
    (hACKH : Square A C K H) (hK : OppositeSidesOf K B A C) (hH : OppositeSidesOf H B A C) :
    quadArea B D E C = quadArea A B F G + quadArea A C K H

statement.note: Proved for squares standing outward, as Euclid describes them; inward squares on the same sides are equal to these, as proved after I.46.

bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop34:
/-- In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the
diameter bisects the areas. -/
theorem Prop34 {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A C D B) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ ∧ ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B ∧ ∠ A B D = ∠ A C D ∧
      △ A B C = △ D C B
bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop34.bisect:
/-- The diameter bisects the parallelogram, said of its area: the parallelogram
ABCD, measured by its diameter AC, is double the triangle ABC. I.35–I.47 cite
I.34 for this ("the triangle ABC is half of the parallelogram EBCA; for the diameter
AB bisects it"). To halve by the other diameter, name the parallelogram from the
next corner (`Parallelogram.rotate`) and turn its area round with
`Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate`. [I. 34] -/
theorem Prop34.bisect {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea A B C D = △ A B C + △ A B C
bridges.Elements.BookI.Prop46.square_eq:
/-- Squares described on equal straight lines are equal. Euclid assumes this in
I.48 ("since DA is equal to AB, the square on DA is also equal to the square on
AB"). Heath reports, under I.46, that Proclus proves it. Each square is a
parallelogram (`Prop28.square`), so the diameter AC cuts it into the triangles
ABC and ACD, right-angled at B and D; and I.4 makes these equal to the triangles
A'B'C' and A'C'D'. Here a square ABCD is "described on AB" when its far corners
C, D lie on one side of AB. [I. 4, I. 28] -/
theorem Prop46.square_eq {A B C D A' B' C' D' : Point} (h : Square A B C D)
    (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (h' : Square A' B' C' D') (hCD' : SameSideOf C' D' A' B')
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A' B'‖) : quadArea A B C D = quadArea A' B' C' D'
bridges.Elements.Parallelogram.cross:
/-- The diameters of a parallelogram cross: in the parallelogram ABCD, some point
lies between A and C and between B and D. Its sides AB and DC are
parallel, so they do not cross, and `AreParallel.cross_or` leaves only the
diameters. -/
theorem Parallelogram.cross (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    ∃ X : Point, Between A X C ∧ Between B X D
bridges.Elements.Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate:
/-- A parallelogram has the same area whichever diameter cuts it: the parallelogram
ABCD measured by BD, as BCDA, is the same as measured by AC. -/
theorem Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea B C D A = quadArea A B C D

Elements.Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate: variable {A B C D E F X A' B' C' : Point} {L M N L₁ L₃ : Line}

definitions.AreParallel:
/-- The straight lines `AB` and `CD` are parallel (Definition 23). -/
def AreParallel (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ C ≠ D ∧
    ∀ L M : Line, OnLine A L → OnLine B L → OnLine C M → OnLine D M → Parallel L M
definitions.Between:
/-- `Between A B C`: the point `B` lies on the straight line through `A` and `C`,
strictly between them. -/
opaque Between : Point → Point → Point → Prop
definitions.Kind:
/-- The kinds of magnitude in Book I. -/
inductive Kind where
  | length
  | angle
  | area
  deriving DecidableEq
definitions.Length:
/-- A length (of a finite straight line). -/
abbrev Length := Magnitude .length
definitions.Line:
/-- **Straight line.** (Defs. 2–4) A `Line` is a whole straight line, extending
without end. Euclid's "finite straight line AB" is the pair of points `A`, `B`,
lying on such a line. -/
opaque Line : Type
definitions.Magnitude:
/-- A magnitude of a given kind: a length, an angle, or an area. -/
def Magnitude (k : Kind) : Type := (MagnitudeImpl k).type
definitions.MagnitudeImpl:
/-- A hidden carrier for each kind of magnitude. -/
opaque MagnitudeImpl : Kind → NonemptyType
definitions.OnLine:
/-- `OnLine A L`: the point `A` lies on the straight line `L`. -/
opaque OnLine : Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Parallel:
/-- **Definition 23.** "Parallel straight lines are straight lines which, being in
the same plane and being produced indefinitely in both directions, do not meet
one another in either direction." -/
def Parallel (L M : Line) : Prop :=
  L ≠ M ∧ ¬ ∃ P : Point, OnLine P L ∧ OnLine P M
definitions.Parallelogram:
/-- The parallelogram `ABCD`, its corners taken in order: `AB` is parallel to
`CD`, and `BC` to `DA`. Euclid does not define it; he first speaks of
"parallelogrammic areas" in I.34. -/
def Parallelogram (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  AreParallel A B C D ∧ AreParallel B C D A
definitions.Point:
/-- **Point.** "A point is that which has no part." (Def. 1) -/
opaque Point : Type
definitions.SameSide:
/-- `SameSide A B L`: the points `A` and `B` lie on the same side of the
straight line `L`. (Neither of them is on `L`.) -/
opaque SameSide : Point → Point → Line → Prop
definitions.Square:
/-- **Definition 22.** "Of quadrilateral figures, a square is that which is both
equilateral and right-angled." The corners are `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`, in order. -/
def Square (A B C D : Point) : Prop :=
  ‖A B‖ = ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖C D‖ = ‖D A‖ ∧
    ∠ D A B = ∟ ∧ ∠ A B C = ∟ ∧ ∠ B C D = ∟ ∧ ∠ C D A = ∟
definitions.Triangle:
/-- **Definition 19.** A trilateral figure: three points not on one straight
line, joined by three straight lines. -/
def Triangle (A B C : Point) : Prop := ¬ Collinear A B C
definitions.ang:
/-- The angle `ABC`, with vertex `B`. Written `∠ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque ang : Point → Point → Point → Angle
definitions.area:
/-- The area of the triangle `ABC`. Written `△ A B C`. -/
noncomputable opaque area : Point → Point → Point → Area
definitions.len:
/-- The length of the finite straight line from `A` to `B`. Written `‖A B‖`. -/
noncomputable opaque len : Point → Point → Length
definitions.quadArea:
/-- The area of the four-sided figure `ABCD` (corners in order), measured as the
two triangles into which its diameter `AC` cuts it. -/
noncomputable def quadArea (A B C D : Point) : Area := △ A B C + △ A C D
definitions.rightAngle:
/-- The size of a right angle. Postulate 4 says all right angles are equal, so
it makes sense to have one name for their common size. Written `∟`. -/
noncomputable opaque rightAngle : Angle
